Unfortunately my review will probably be washed down by the large amount of negative reviews this game has received, however I will take a stab at getting my voice out there to the people. First off, however, I want you to look at how many hours I have logged into this game. The amount of time I have spent in DayZ Standalone far surpasses any other game I have played on Steam, and for good reason. There is a lot of misconception going around the Steam reviews, and quite frankly many of the negative comments are filled with bigot hate towards the developers and a lack of understanding for how the early access model works in DayZ. Hopefully I can clear some of the confusion and give potential buyers some clarity on the title.
Let's rewind the clocks back to late 2013, a year after DayZ mod was released on Arma II. The survival sandbox genre had just exploded into the videogames scene, and every developer was trying to claim their stake in the land of the survivalist games. At the time, Bohemia Interactive had in their hands the most popular survivalist game on the market. Thousands of people played DayZ mod, and people loved the idea of an open-world survival game in which the elements and players are pitted against you. DayZ mod set the tone for what a survival game should be: challenging, unforgiving, and hard to top. Bohemia wanted to take the title and make it something greater, something much bigger and smoother than what the original mod intended to be. They knew that releasing a full version of the game on that clunky Arma II engine wouldn't cut it, so they had to make major improvements to bring the title into 2016 and beyond.
Instead of releasing the full DayZ Standalone game on the horrible Arma II engine, Bohemia made the decision to completely re-gut the engine and build a new one from scratch. FROM. SCRATCH. There are a few legacy modules that are getting carried over, but for the most part every aspect of the game is new (render, physics, lighting, etc). Anyone who has had any kind of development experience in video-games understands that this is a daunting task, a momentous task, a task that doesn't happen in one month or one year; No, creating a brand new engine takes years to develop, and this is where the root of the "problem" started.
DayZ Standalone went into early access in late 2013, and this is where they made their big mistake. The game simply wasn't ready. With no new engine components even being started on (plus it hit early access only 4 weeks into the development timeline, dear god), many early access players were left in disappointment when new features could not be pushed right away. People cried "fix zombies", but the zombies could not be fixed yet because an entirely new AI system was being created. People cried "fix FPS", but no FPS fix could be put in place because they were busy developing the new renderer. People wanted new vehicles, but vehicles could not be added yet because the physics system was being re-worked. There's no point in providing a "fix" for a mechanic in the game when that mechanic is going to be entirely replaced down the line anyways.
And so people got ♥♥♥♥♥♥, and fed up. "$20 for a Standalone title, and there's no fixes for these bugs?" Even I was at the point of rage, often times quitting DayZ Standalone for months at a time. People started saying that the developers weren't doing anything, that they "took the money and ran". But the real reality was that they were simply hard at work laying out the foundation for the title, unfortunately not being able to fix most bugs and issues at the time because they were so busy writing up new systems for the game to play on.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SO LET'S FAST FORWARD. It's late 2015 now, nearing 2016. DayZ Standalone has been in development for 2 years now. Has the game changed? Are any of the new engine models finished? Are zombies even fixed yet?
You bet your ♥♥♥ they are. If you were to ask me when I think the game should of been released to the public as early access, I would have said right now (version .59) would have been the time to do it. FINALLY, after 2 years of development, Bohemia Interactive is getting around to completing all of the upcoming engine changes and new foundation for the title. Let me make a quick list to get your hype train rolling:
New Renderer is nearly finished, should have "30 - 40 % FPS boost overall"
Zombie AI is brand new and fixed, zombies now have sense of smell and sight, don't clip through walls, are actually a challenge
Four vehicles currently in game: V3S, Sedan, Hatchback, and Bus. Arial vehicles confirmed, as well as bikes and boats
New vehicle physics system taken from GTA V (Bullet SDK). Full vehicle maintenance and parts
All servers persistent. Camps and items are saved after restart. You can create large camps now.
Tents, Barrels, vehicles, protector cases, and backpacks can all be used as base storage now. Stays persistent through server reset
Loot respawn fixed. Loot spawns in areas that make sense now, it is very hard to get access to good weapons and ammo
Sickness and Disease now a major factor of gameplay
Tons of new animals in the game with new Animal AI. They react to sight and sound, as well as naturally roam the map looking for ponds and fields to graze in.
Predator animals confirmed, including wolves and bears
map changes and new northern towns expand the map greatly from mod
Softskills soon to be implemented, aka the more you run the more fit you get. skills develop over time
Every building now enter able with loot
A ton of new weapons and cosmetic items (clothing) added into the game
character wear progession, such as growing beards and getting dirt / blood on yourself, soon to be implemented
Contaminated Zones confirmed and being worked on, the first being a military base up north
And soo so so much more. I could keep the list going forever but it honestly doesn't cover how much they've added into the game since launch.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
Anyone who says DayZ Standalone is dead, or that the developers have "taken the money and ran", or that the community is dead, quite frankly is full of ♥♥♥♥. The game is very much alive and so much better than it was when it started. Even though DayZ SA has been slow off the start compared to other survivalist games (H1Z1, Rust, ARK, Unturned, Miscreated, etc), I strongly believe it will come out on top as the best survivalist game when it is finished. No other survival game has this much attention to detail and realism as DayZ. No other survival game has the kind of studio resources and money that Bohemia has to put out a strong title. No other survival game has mastered the hardcore aspect of survival and struggle better than DayZ. Almost every other survival game was rushed out on a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ Unreal engine in an effort to reap money off the survivalist scene and try to outbeat Bohemia to the punch on features and gameplay. Games like Rust and H1Z1 fail to hit the bullseye on what a survival game should be. DayZ Standalone does this right and does it good. I would definitely recommend this game now, as it's about to surpass the ♥♥♥♥ outta all other games on the market. Go out there and start surviving!

So UNDERTALE is an RPG where no one has to die. The game has 3 routes: Pacifist, Neutral and Genocide. Neutral is the easiest because it means you have more health for bosses, but you don't get the outstanding emotional effects of the Pacifist and you'll have an AVERAGE time (also there are around 20 different Neutral endings). In the Genocide run you kill everyone and everything that gets in your way, meaning if you did a Pacifist run first you'll feel incredibly guilty for the deaths of all your friends and the bosses are incredibly difficult and you'll have a BAD time. Do I recommend this game? YES. YES I DO. 10/10 one of the best games I ever have played and ever will play. UNDERTALE.
Wow. I cannot even begin to explain the way I feel about this game. I'll try to keep it short, but I can't promise anything.
UNDERTALE has an amazing story, breathtaking soundtrack, silly humor, and hilarious characters. The game has multiple endings, which is something I've always wanted to try. It was an amazing experience.
The battle system is great. Choosing your actions based on how you want the story to unfold, and watching the characters' reactions, realizing how your actions affect others.. it's very satisfying and it feels real. The mechanics are very fun and smooth, and the framerate is nice.
The puzzles are fairly easy (by the time you play the game a second time, you should be able to complete most, if not all, of the puzzles quickly), and I wish it had a few harder ones, however I understand that puzzles are not the main focus of the game. And that's fine.
The boss battles are immensely fun and interesting. UNDERTALE seems to find a way to change it up at every boss fight, so battling constantly feels fun and it never gets old.
Once again, the soundtrack. Sometimes, I find myself sitting back and just listening to the soundtrack for a few seconds. It is truly amazing; it finds ways to implement parts of one song into another, so they all feel familiar yet new all at the same time. Not to mention the nice blend between retro-style and complex songs.
The world is vast and enjoyable. The different areas really help to contribute to the feeling that keeps the game from being stale. The colors blend nicely and the music really fits the theme.
As for age-appropriate questions, the game has some dark themes and disturbing images, but they're really not that bad.  There's no nudity, so that's not an issue. As for the humor, it's just silly fun times that will make you grin or even lose yourself in laughter. Nothing inappropriate that I can recall.
As for the length of the game, it took me less than ten hours for my first playthough, and it only got quicker after that for more Neutral Runs. However, time will vary depending on which ending you try to get. You can watch a movie that's only around two hours long and have it feel complete.  It's the same for this game. Even though it's short, it feels satisfying (ESPECIALLY when you achieve the true ending).
UNDERTALE is a masterpiece. It combines old and new mechanics and styles, making it the perfect game for someone who wants a fun and engaging RPG. And it's only ten dollars!
This game is truly amazing. If you haven't heard enough about it from the rest of the world, be my guest and read more. However, you'll get a better experience knowing as little as possible (that's why I tried to keep spoilers to a minimum here).
UNDERTALE. The RPG where you don't have to destroy anyone. Or do you? That's completely up to you.

Remember when all those people used to defend the devs with "It's in Alpha!" and "They're still fixing things!"?..... I'd love to hear them now. 3 years later. I'm ashamed of the devs and ashamed that Steam is still allowing this game on their store.

I understand that people have lost a lot of faith,,, but you gotta remember, Bohemia is still a comparitively small company, they can only do so much at one time.
Onto the review:
Let's get this out of the way now. YES DayZ DOES have a repitoire of bugs, but as stated prior, the game is in Pre-Alpha stage and Bohemia is still just a small company. DayZ puts you in Chernarus, a large area of land modeled after an identical area of land in the Czech Republic.  The combat, especially PvP (Person v. Person), is pulse-pounding & adrenaline rushing, once you hear that first shot or pop in your direction or open fire on enemies, you know it's gonna be rough. The landscape, from mountain to shore, is simply breathtaking, each little ambient detail having so much put into it, the cities are large and vast, the towns are small and reserved. The oceans? Holy cow, the detail put into the water is better than most games I've seen.
Alright I'm not going to blindly praise the game, let's get to the known bugs (Well, the ones I could remember):
-Sometimes you can't move or even access gear, namely stuff on the ground. It's mostly a desync issue I think.
-Some of the physics and collision detection aren't fully working yet, like some roofs you can't climb onto yet.
-Sometimes your person does the "retard slide", that is, if they bump a certain spot or wall or go down a steep incline, they start to uncontrollably slide in the direction where gravity is the most influential.
-Most cities (like Cherno or Elektro) have been known to cause massive drops in FPS, this is because DayZ runs on (or it used to) DirectX 9.
So do I recommend DayZ? Well... if you can understand (and get passed) it's bugs and flaws I promise that you won't regret paying 34 dollars\euros\whatever to experience this game. To reiterate, this game is still in Early-Alpha.
Cheers!

This game, THIS, GAME. There is no reason to hate this game. If I hear, one person say that they hate this beautiful game, just because it has 'bad graphics', or because it has something 'bad' with it, by pulling an excuse...Let's just say many of us, and I know many others will agree, they will have a very, VERY BAD TIME.
I mean just like, it's too freaking well-made to really hate! ALL of your choices, to either beating the monsters into submission, to being their best friend...or, foolishly, killing them all like they mean nothing to the world...it will matter. It doesn't pull a Telltale (Yes, I went THERE), and say that your actions matter when in reality they don't. It'll be the same ending...You'll get different reactions through the game, yes, but not the same ending. In Undertale, you'll be judged upon who you killed, who you spared...even some of the main characters, if you kill certain minor-character monsters...they WILL notice, and they will NOT sugarcoat it when they notice you did something screwed up. Even Flowey, a character we all know well, will CALL YOU OUT, FOR KILLING TORIEL! If a Naturally Evil character calls you out for killing someone like Toriel, then I think maybe, MAYBE the game actually matters!!!
In the end, great game, and for the haters? Why not you go back to your Call of Duty and Modern Warfare fights and cussing battles, because here, pulling that isn't going to be tolorated, and why? Because, a BAD TIME will come to you if you do.
EDIT: Also, for all you who say the 'fanbase is cringy'...just because the fanbase ruins the game, DOESN'T MEAN THE GAME IS BAD! Heck, the Call Of Duty fanbase makes it nearly unplayable for 90% of this world!!! So if you think you're going to attack a game just because of the game having a 'bad fanbase'...just remember, there's fans of the game who aren't so cringy, and who will actually listen to you...
as long as you don't attack US with insults and remarks that you easily know will spark an argument. So for once, everyone, use your brain when reading this, OK? Thanks.

Cant say I recommend DayZ even if you're hard-core its fairly boring in this day an age. Although the 'survival' aspects are intriguing at first with with staying hydrated and full of food this gets dull fast. What kills me though is how awful pvp and pve can be. For PVE the AI is just bad and for PVP you're either gunning down people with immunity until you run out of your very limited supply of food and ammo or being gunned down; in either case it gets dull fast.  The loot system (which if fixed might address some of these issues) is atrocious where you'll find dozens of weapons and no ammo (least not the type to fit your weapon) or tons of ammo and no weapons. If you're lucky you can run 15 to 20 minute to a good spot and find some but than you've got to run another 15 or 20 minutes back to the populated spots to find anyone.... than wait an additional 15 to 20 minutes camping... when your victim shows up it'll either be a fresh spawn which is no fun or rambo which sometimes can be slightly more fun. Either way the fight will last five seconds win or lose (unless you both chicken out an camp) than you've either got to run and pickup more gear, get in a lame glitchy melee fight (which the person you're fighting will have no gear) and/or wait another 15 to 20 minutes x2 again...They call it a running simulator for a reason and it seems unlikely it'll ever get out of early access ...The game is a glitchy money grab and a trap... Dont buy into the hype.

At its first release, Dayz seemed to have a promising concept. It was one of the first out in the "open world zombie survival" genre. But unfortunately, this game has made next to no progress whatsoever in its multiple year long early access. Its basically the same buggy unplayable mess it was at launch.
Expect to die out of nowhere frequently from bugs such and being pushed off of roofs and lagging out of buildings. The lag or 'vsync' in this game is the worst i have ever experienced. The entire server will freeze and people will be able to go and do whatever they want in the meantime. This ends up with newbies punching out geared players during times where they cant move. The optimization is as atrocious as the UI. With a powerful rig, you'll be lucky to maintain a playable framerate in any of the game's cities.
If you enjoy spending an hour and a half gearing up and finding your friends to spend 5 minutes in combat, this is the game for you. Cities are always a deathwish, but when you are not in them you will go hours at a time without seeing another player just to get killed on sight when you do have an encounter. Not to mention it has one of the crappiest playerbases in any game I have ever played, good luck finding an interaction that lasts longer than 5 seconds before getting shot. Also riddled with hackers on every server you can find. Not only are these hackers annoying, but they also have the ability to teleport and instantly kill everyone on the map, causing you to lose the hour you just spent gearing up. I had a lot of hope for this game at first and saw the potential for a great game, but unfortunately it has turned out to be a cash grab by greedy devs. For now, it is an unplayable, buggy, and boring game stuck in early access limbo, unlikely to gain any interesting content any time soon.
I would not recommend anyone waste their time or hard earned money on this incomplete, discarded game.

Undertale is truly a spectacular game I would recommend to anyone. As a long time fan of EarthBound, which inspired it, I can honestly say this game far outdoes EarthBound. The characters are witty, have entertaining but emotional backstories, the settings in which the game takes place are varied, the level of humor is self-aware and had me cracking up several times during my playthrough. The Soundtrack is phenomenal, the story touching and emotional, and it made me cry tears of joy and sadness throughout the course of the game several times - something very few games have made me do. It flips the RPG genre on it's head and introduces exciting and unique mechanics.
While their is a limited amount of sidequests and things to do; the game has tons of replay-ability for it's emotional story and soundtrack alone.
Truly, Undertale is a game worthy of cult classic status and of the huge fanbase it has created, and while I was hesitant when I first heard of it due to the large fanbase, I do not regret my decision to get this game at all and wish I had taken the plunge far sooner.
I very rarely give games this high of a score, but Undertale gets a perfect 10/10 from me.

Undertale is truly a spectacular game I would recommend to anyone. As a long time fan of EarthBound, which inspired it, I can honestly say this game far outdoes EarthBound. The characters are witty, have entertaining but emotional backstories, the settings in which the game takes place are varied, the level of humor is self-aware and had me cracking up several times during my playthrough. The Soundtrack is phenomenal, the story touching and emotional, and it made me cry tears of joy and sadness throughout the course of the game several times - something very few games have made me do. It flips the RPG genre on it's head and introduces exciting and unique mechanics.
While their is a limited amount of sidequests and things to do; the game has tons of replay-ability for it's emotional story and soundtrack alone.
Truly, Undertale is a game worthy of cult classic status and of the huge fanbase it has created, and while I was hesitant when I first heard of it due to the large fanbase, I do not regret my decision to get this game at all and wish I had taken the plunge far sooner.
I very rarely give games this high of a score, but Undertale gets a perfect 10/10 from me.

I've been playing video games since before I can remember. I grew up with my dad's SNES and have played hundreds if not thousands of games on a plethora of systems. I love gaming. However, many games these days lack a certain thing. It's not something you can really teach game developers to have. I've heard it of AAA publishers and indie gamers and it's true. Heart. You can't write a tried and true formula to give heart to a game. It cannot be done. Once a way of doing something becomes rote monotany all heart is gone. It's seen in the shooters of AAA titles. It's seen in the steampunk pixel art of indie. It's prevalent everywhere in the industry: a death of heart. Many games try to impress by making things bigger or better: more guns, infinite, randomly generated dungeons, a fine assortment of aged cheeses. It has come to the point where games feel more like drudgery than fun. An excuse to waste time finding the next "shiny cool."
Undertale is not drudgery. It reminds me of games like Journey or Cave Story, or even books like The Alchemist or The Little Prince, not because Undertale necessarily has elements it shares with these works, but because Undertale has heart. I could tell you about the features, its unique bullet hell rpg format, its pixel art charm. It would pointless, like describing a beautiful work of art to someone. There's no point and this game deserves better. I can only tell you how it made me feel. And it left me in awe. To say that this game is not one of the best games if not the best game of 2015 would be a gross injustice. The corny jokes reminded me of my friends from highschool. The characters felt like family. The story reminded me of my dreams. The message gives me hope. If you are someone who is tired of wading through the sea of a medium plagued by the tediousness of nothing new under the sun, try this game. Take a breath of fresh air.

A powerful and unique game which, despite me normally not tending to like games of it's sort, and not being very emotionally connected to characters in most games, really DID make me think in a different light.
The characters which are established do grow upon you, and seeing such horrors as their deaths in the Genocide run, or their happiness in the Pacifist run really do generate powerful emotions. Generally, I see games as JUST games, but this is one profound exception.
The way in which Undertale executes it's emotional manipulation is masterful - When I bought the game, hearing what seemed like exaggerated spiel about how it was some holy grail, I was ready to be disappointed. However... playing it drives some extreme feeling that your actions and relationships matter, so much so that after doing even the Neutral run, I found that attempting a Genocide run was emotionally draining.
In conclusion, Toby Fox's Undertale truly is a masterpiece of game development. Not the BEST game around, but that is subjective, as all people have different tastes. For a game of it's style it surely does appeal.

The characters which are established do grow upon you, and seeing such horrors as their deaths in the Genocide run, or their happiness in the Pacifist run really do generate powerful emotions. Generally, I see games as JUST games, but this is one profound exception.
The way in which Undertale executes it's emotional manipulation is masterful - When I bought the game, hearing what seemed like exaggerated spiel about how it was some holy grail, I was ready to be disappointed. However... playing it drives some extreme feeling that your actions and relationships matter, so much so that after doing even the Neutral run, I found that attempting a Genocide run was emotionally draining.
In conclusion, Toby Fox's Undertale truly is a masterpiece of game development. Not the BEST game around, but that is subjective, as all people have different tastes. For a game of it's style it surely does appeal.

Probably the greatest game i've played in years, and that's coming from someone who isn't all that big on RPGs. In addition to introducing a completely new gameplay style that uniquely and interestingly combines traditional RPG fighting with bullet-hell action (as well as throwing tricky but doable puzzles into otherwise ordinary hubworld exploration), Undertale also offers a wide variety of memorable characters and fresh humor, as well as a somewhat confusing yet touching storyline that really knows how to pull the player in.
It's selection of characters is very unlike most RPGs, in that they aren't completely bland and unimaginative with underwhelming flat personalities, nor are they really ♥♥♥♥ing annoying pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥and make you want to kill all of them (except Mettaton; ♥♥♥♥ him). Though most of Undertale's cast consists of comic relief, a good chuck of 'em also have deeper personalities and stories behind them.
My only real complaint is how short the game is; I beat it in less than six hours. However, there are three ways to play the game, each one revealing a different ending; you can either try not to kill as many enemies as possible, just kill all of them or attempt to create a balance between the two. Though a relatively easy little thing, it's still quite an impressive piece of artwork for something created in Gamemaker.

My personal game of the year for 2015.
Play it.
That is all. The less said the better; it really is something that deserves to be experienced unspoiled.

I was gifted this game in December of 2015 and completed it (all 3 ((if you haven't played / live under a rock and havent encountered spoilers, you'll find out soon enough)) ) a while ago. What can I say about this game that others haven't? Little to none, I suppose. So without an alternative I find myself compelled to speak honestly.
I'm more of an atmosphere kind of guy, but I do have a soft spot for narrative that comes with a catch. I have to be emotionally invested in the game in one way or another and boy let me tell you, it captured my heart n' soul. I wont give vague gerenics revolving around character, plot, theme, etc. Instead let me tell you this and this alone. I'm usually a stoic; I try to be resourceful in looking for best outcomes, I'm very objective when it comes to working at something (this includes games at times).
As I went on my first playthrough I became invested as I said before and by the end I finished AVERAGE. But towards the very end, one part struck me and struck me hard. I mean very hard. I felt something that I haven't felt in the longest time from a game and that's actual emotion, and I don't mean love, happiness, or pleasure. I felt guilt, remorse, regret, an agonizing need to be penitent; helpless at a hand of justice for a sin that I could've avoided, like a knife twisting my heart and by my own doing, no less. It was real.
To do that took something more. Toby Fox, if you ever see this I have two messages: "Thank you" & "Whatever / whoever you were to make this... don't ever change from that." 10/10 would absolutely recommend to anyone who asks.

Right, I've now played this game enough to have a better understanding of it. Here's why I advise to steer clear of this game:
- The game is buggy as hell. Animals will glitch through walls and rocks, so you can be killed in your sleep by them. Deer drop chicken meat, which is just lazy on the devs' part. Sounds are bugged, creating distortions or ambient sounds in the wrong place. Item descriptions are also wrong, with many items having the same description as another, or having incorrect information in them.
- You are never safe. When you log out, your body stays exactly where it is, completely vulnerable. If you crash while exploring, you're basically dead. You can try logging off in your house, but it doesn't take much for someone to break into where you're sleeping and just murder you. I don't know who thought this was a good idea, but it really doesn't make sense.
- Offline raiding is a big thing. When you aren't on, your base is unprotected and open for anyone to blow their way into it. Since you're also still visible to them, you're just a sitting duck while they raid you. Then you log in later to find you're dead and, more than likely, your sleeping bag/bed (which you use to respawn at your base) has been destroyed, meaning you've now lost where your home is.
- It takes far too long to set yourself up initially. You log in completely naked, with just a rock for gathering resources and a torch to light at night. The rock gets you barely anything and the torch just attracts players with weapons to you. By the time you have enough to make a small base, someone else will have already killed you and taken all your loot. This happens repeatedly, so you can spend hours without ever making a base, just running around being killed by others.
- Building is a pain. If you're making honeycombed walls, where each cell is there to keep people out, there is no way to effectively upgrade it all. You can't reach inside, so anything behind a wall is lost to you. The tool cupboards are also a pain, since only one covers a wide area, so if it breaks or gets found, that entire area is exposed. But if you want to hide it, it means you can't have friends access it later, to allow them to build.
- If you get raided by someone with a rocket, there will be splash damage on your building. But you can't see what's damaged without standing right up close to it, which makes rebuilding and repairing a long and annoying task. If you've been raided like that, it's usually easier just to start fresh somewhere else, which is also annoying.
- Turrets are a pain. Not fighting them, but actually maintaining them. They require authorisation on them to stop them shooting you, so if you place one down while your ally is offline, they will be killed when they log back in. But if you leave it off for them, someone else will likely break in and auth on themselves, then turning your turret against you. You also can't see at a glance how much ammo they have, so checking them for reloading is a pain. They also waste their ammo on animals like deer, horses, chickens or boars, which won't harm you.
- It's a killer on the GPU. I'm getting heat levels of 90 celsius, unless I put the fan on 100% and then I get around 80 celsius, but it sounds like a jet engine taking off. No other game causes such a drastic change, and this happens even at lowest settings for Rust.
- There is no easy single-player/private server option. I'm not sure why, since Garry's Mod had it, but you can't just save a map with your own creations to work on whenever you like in private, without fear of it being destroyed by someone else. You have to go out of your way to set one up, which most gamers can't or won't do.
- The game works on a tedious level system. You need to grind resources repeatedly just to build better things. But you don't get levels for building, only for finding loot, gathering resources, or crafting things. It makes it a slow and boring way to improve yourself.
- All servers are wiped regularly. Around 1 - 4 weeks, everything you've worked on to build will be wiped clean. Your levels are gone. Your loot is gone. You start from scratch AGAIN. This means you never get invested in the game and everything is ultimately pointless.
- The game relies on players making mods for it. There are a number of quality of life issues that vanilla Rust just doesn't have, but server-owners make mods for. Why these haven't been added as standard to Rust is beyond me.
- The player base is cancerous. It's a survival game that's more about surviving other people than the environment. Most of the time, you'll be naked, with nothing but a rock, and someone in full gear at a much higher level than you will kill you. Not for any reason, but because they can. This behaviour can go as far as targetting certainly players repeatedly, constantly attacking the same base each time it's rebuilt, or griefing for the sake it. There's no sense of community because the ultimate goal of the game is non-existant, so they make PvP the goal.
- This game has been "released" for 3 years now and it's STILL in alpha. This "early access" is an excuse for the devs to put out a game that's not finished and will never be finished, all while delivering a sub-par product. Don't waste your time buying it.
- There's already microtransactions. Most of the decent skins for weapons and clothes are on the Steam Market, with some selling at silly prices (one was at £50). You get the chance to get them randomly added to your Steam Inventory, but in all the time I've played I've only unlocked 6 things, and all of them are awful. Any game that asks you to spend more money to get all of the features in it is one to steer clear of.
Edit: DO NOT BUY THIS GAME. There was a recent update that complete broke the whole system. What it did was allow anyone at all to build within the radius of your personal area (usually a tool cupboard keeps people from building in your base). This meant that it just helped raiders to raid you. Now they also plan to make it harder for people to build big bases, so you'll be more likely to get raided AND you won't be able to repair as easily after a raid. They've been busy adding stupid items like tables and chairs (which no one can use), and giving raiders and even easier time of it (even though it's already extremely easy for them), instead of trying to get the game out of its permanent alpha status.
Steer clear. This game is cancerous.

Probably the greatest game i've played in years, and that's coming from someone who isn't all that big on RPGs. In addition to introducing a completely new gameplay style that uniquely and interestingly combines traditional RPG fighting with bullet-hell action (as well as throwing tricky but doable puzzles into otherwise ordinary hubworld exploration), Undertale also offers a wide variety of memorable characters and fresh humor, as well as a somewhat confusing yet touching storyline that really knows how to pull the player in.
It's selection of characters is very unlike most RPGs, in that they aren't completely bland and unimaginative with underwhelming flat personalities, nor are they really ♥♥♥♥ing annoying pieces of♥♥♥♥♥♥and make you want to kill all of them (except Mettaton; ♥♥♥♥ him). Though most of Undertale's cast consists of comic relief, a good chuck of 'em also have deeper personalities and stories behind them.
My only real complaint is how short the game is; I beat it in less than six hours. However, there are three ways to play the game, each one revealing a different ending; you can either try not to kill as many enemies as possible, just kill all of them or attempt to create a balance between the two. Though a relatively easy little thing, it's still quite an impressive piece of artwork for something created in Gamemaker.

My personal game of the year for 2015.
Play it.
That is all. The less said the better; it really is something that deserves to be experienced unspoiled.

Right, I've now played this game enough to have a better understanding of it. Here's why I advise to steer clear of this game:
- The game is buggy as hell. Animals will glitch through walls and rocks, so you can be killed in your sleep by them. Deer drop chicken meat, which is just lazy on the devs' part. Sounds are bugged, creating distortions or ambient sounds in the wrong place. Item descriptions are also wrong, with many items having the same description as another, or having incorrect information in them.
- You are never safe. When you log out, your body stays exactly where it is, completely vulnerable. If you crash while exploring, you're basically dead. You can try logging off in your house, but it doesn't take much for someone to break into where you're sleeping and just murder you. I don't know who thought this was a good idea, but it really doesn't make sense.
- Offline raiding is a big thing. When you aren't on, your base is unprotected and open for anyone to blow their way into it. Since you're also still visible to them, you're just a sitting duck while they raid you. Then you log in later to find you're dead and, more than likely, your sleeping bag/bed (which you use to respawn at your base) has been destroyed, meaning you've now lost where your home is.
- It takes far too long to set yourself up initially. You log in completely naked, with just a rock for gathering resources and a torch to light at night. The rock gets you barely anything and the torch just attracts players with weapons to you. By the time you have enough to make a small base, someone else will have already killed you and taken all your loot. This happens repeatedly, so you can spend hours without ever making a base, just running around being killed by others.
- Building is a pain. If you're making honeycombed walls, where each cell is there to keep people out, there is no way to effectively upgrade it all. You can't reach inside, so anything behind a wall is lost to you. The tool cupboards are also a pain, since only one covers a wide area, so if it breaks or gets found, that entire area is exposed. But if you want to hide it, it means you can't have friends access it later, to allow them to build.
- If you get raided by someone with a rocket, there will be splash damage on your building. But you can't see what's damaged without standing right up close to it, which makes rebuilding and repairing a long and annoying task. If you've been raided like that, it's usually easier just to start fresh somewhere else, which is also annoying.
- Turrets are a pain. Not fighting them, but actually maintaining them. They require authorisation on them to stop them shooting you, so if you place one down while your ally is offline, they will be killed when they log back in. But if you leave it off for them, someone else will likely break in and auth on themselves, then turning your turret against you. You also can't see at a glance how much ammo they have, so checking them for reloading is a pain. They also waste their ammo on animals like deer, horses, chickens or boars, which won't harm you.
- It's a killer on the GPU. I'm getting heat levels of 90 celsius, unless I put the fan on 100% and then I get around 80 celsius, but it sounds like a jet engine taking off. No other game causes such a drastic change, and this happens even at lowest settings for Rust.
- There is no easy single-player/private server option. I'm not sure why, since Garry's Mod had it, but you can't just save a map with your own creations to work on whenever you like in private, without fear of it being destroyed by someone else. You have to go out of your way to set one up, which most gamers can't or won't do.
- The game works on a tedious level system. You need to grind resources repeatedly just to build better things. But you don't get levels for building, only for finding loot, gathering resources, or crafting things. It makes it a slow and boring way to improve yourself.
- All servers are wiped regularly. Around 1 - 4 weeks, everything you've worked on to build will be wiped clean. Your levels are gone. Your loot is gone. You start from scratch AGAIN. This means you never get invested in the game and everything is ultimately pointless.
- The game relies on players making mods for it. There are a number of quality of life issues that vanilla Rust just doesn't have, but server-owners make mods for. Why these haven't been added as standard to Rust is beyond me.
- The player base is cancerous. It's a survival game that's more about surviving other people than the environment. Most of the time, you'll be naked, with nothing but a rock, and someone in full gear at a much higher level than you will kill you. Not for any reason, but because they can. This behaviour can go as far as targetting certainly players repeatedly, constantly attacking the same base each time it's rebuilt, or griefing for the sake it. There's no sense of community because the ultimate goal of the game is non-existant, so they make PvP the goal.
- This game has been "released" for 3 years now and it's STILL in alpha. This "early access" is an excuse for the devs to put out a game that's not finished and will never be finished, all while delivering a sub-par product. Don't waste your time buying it.
- There's already microtransactions. Most of the decent skins for weapons and clothes are on the Steam Market, with some selling at silly prices (one was at £50). You get the chance to get them randomly added to your Steam Inventory, but in all the time I've played I've only unlocked 6 things, and all of them are awful. Any game that asks you to spend more money to get all of the features in it is one to steer clear of.

What it did was allow anyone at all to build within the radius of your personal area (usually a tool cupboard keeps people from building in your base). Now they also plan to make it harder for people to build big bases, so you'll be more likely to get raided AND you won't be able to repair as easily after a raid. Since this game is in Alpha (where it's been for like, 3 years) I won't comment on the multitude of performance issues, which make the game almost unplayable unless you manipulate your Steam launch settings.  I've put 180 hours into DayZ, and I've come to the conclusion that this game is for you if you are:
A. A sociopath
B. Enjoy long-distance running in videogames (which requires all of the patience of real running with none of the benefits from actually running)
Let's back up.  If you haven't played DayZ, you're probably thinking of this as a Zombie Survival game, but it really isn't.  The zombies and actual survival basics aren't difficult.  You can easily outrun zombies, they are very easy to dodge, and they hardly do any damage.  You can punch them to death for crying out loud!  In my 180 hours, I've never been killed by a zombie.  Survival is trivial; food and water are plentiful and easy to find almost immediately.  The real danger is other players.
And this is why I do not recommend DayZ.  If you're hoping for meaningful experiences/interactions with other players, prepare to be mostly disappointed.  In my experience, your player interactions will consistent of the following:
A.  50% will simply shoot you on sight, regardless of whether you have weapons or identify yourself as friendly.
B.  25% will pretend to be friendly and, as soon as they get a chance, attack/kill you.
C.  15% are legitimate friendly.  Some will offer to help or team up with you, others will simply ignore you.
D.  10% will attempt to hold you up and rob you.  After they tie you up, they'll most likely break your legs so you can only crawl around, and then they'll force disinfectant down your throat so you die a slow, terrible death.  Experienced players simply refuse to comply with holds ups since they know they will get killed at the end of it anyway.
Why do people act like this?  Well, I think there are three main reasons.  First, they are basically anonymous.  You can't see anyone's name in game without checking their pulse, which is almost impossible to do without their compliance (forced or otherwise).  Second, unless you get a lucky spawn/loot, it takes a good while (half an hour to an hour on average) to get some decent gear/weaponry.  By killing you, they basically set you back to square one.  If you had a friend you were playing with, you have to either continually kill yourself until you get a respawn near their location, or you have to suck it up and run for who knows how long to meet up with them.  Sociopaths get a kick out of wasting your time.  Finally, there's very little possibility of retaliation or revenge, and people take full advantage of that.  After killing you, you're able to hear the other player for a few seconds (long enough for them to taunt you/call you a few racial epithets).  30 seconds later, you'll respawn with nothing but the clothes on your back in a totally random location throughout the world.  The chances that you respawn near them, find a weapon, and then exact revenge are extremely remote, and other players know this.  Sociopathy without consequence.
Don't get me wrong; the game can be fun, especially if you're playing with a couple of friends.  However, of my 180 hours, I've spent maybe 40 hours in actual combat/meaningful interactions.  The other 140 hours were spent running around, looking for a weapon, and committing suicide.
This isn't a zombie survival game, it's an open-world third/first person shooter/murder simulator.  Even then, the combat mechanics are pretty crappy (controls are awkward and melee combat is a total mess).  Consider the type of game you're *actually* buying, and if you're still interested, go buy Call of Duty instead.

Wow.
Just, wow.
I'm at a literal loss of words. This game...
...It's an absolute MASTERPIECE.
Undertale is my Favourate of 2015.
Graphics
The graphics are a simple 8-bit style, and although it's considered "generic" because of the whole "8 bit indie game made by one guy" sort of thing, this game uses it properly. I know, that seems really weird, but it's true. If you play the game and take a certain route, the final boss WILL blow your mind with the visuals. Not much here to say, it's not what's supposed to make this game so noteworthy, but it's still acceptable nonetheless.
Gameplay
Undertale is a lot like Earthbound in many ways, the most notable trait being the turn based combat and how it's portrayed. Nowadays, LOTS of games have opportunities where you can spare or kill a certain character and decide their fate. Their flaw, however, is that the said death often is just shrugged off, both in the game's world AND in real life. Undertale takes this concept and cranks it up a notch, leaving literally every single character's fate in your hands. You can go for a pacifist run and kill no one, and this is the one I would highly recommend going for if you do decide to purchase this masterpiece. There's also the neutral ending, which is the most common of the bunch but has one of the most creative final bosses I've ever seen in video games. I won't spoil much, but it will BLOW your mind, you can trust me on that. There's also the genocide run, which is incredibly difficult to pull off because of how emotionally difficult it is to actually kill this lovable cast of monsters. The combat itself is like Earthbound's, as said earlier. This being said, Undertale takes yet another step forward, adding bullet hell and platforming to the mix and blends the two perfectly, making the game far more exciting, while keeping the original RPG elements.
Story
This is the very core of why Undertale is such an unforgettable experience. Of course, though, you shouldn't be shocked at this point, because most of the internet will agree with me on that. The cast of characters is so diverse and unique, each one having traits to make them likable or the one you'd love to kill on a genocide run. For example, you have Sans, my favorite of the bunch. He's a laid back, prankster, and easy going skeleton who has a brother named Papyrus. What Papyrus lacks in intelligence, he makes up for with a big heart for humans. You also have Flowey, who immediately will creep you out because of how ruthless he is. As for the plot itself, it's one big emotional rollercoaster you would want to ride over and over and over again. It has its hilarious moments, since the writing is surprisingly well done, while it has its sad moments, too. What takes the cake on all of this, though, is that it literally makes you rethink everything you knew about video games. The fourth wall is also broken often, and this is done in the most clever and creative ways. It's like Kid Icarus: Uprising, except Undertale does it far better. I almost forgot, too, but every action in this game will be remembered by the characters, long after you actually beat it. People have called this game a "sentient being" and I can actually agree with them on that. Trust me, Undertale is literally perfect for storytelling, and I won't be shocked if you cried a bit. It's hard not to, and with such a unique cast of lovable characters, it further justifies my point.
Audio
I have a friend who also loves Undertale, and the one thing he seems to point out about it is the soundtrack. I can't blame him, because it's really catchy. Remember how I said this game was my Shovel Knight of 2015? I wasn't kidding about that, it has the awesome soundtrack to go with it. You have Bonetrousle, the sinister, yet lighthearted and catchy tune that fits Papyrus. There's the Spider Dance, Muffet's theme. This theme is a lot more evil but far more catchy, and is one of my personal favorites. The king of the bunch, however, is one that didn't directly originate from Undertale: Megalovania. Sans' theme is slowly becoming an iconic boss theme, as it has been used in two different times in the past, and this variation is definitely my favorite of the three. You also have some humorous songs, namely the Dogsong. I won't get too in-depth with that one, but I need to say this now: GEEEET DUNKED ON! There is no voice acting, but why does that even matter? This game doesn't need it. Overall, this game has some high quality music, and I love it that way.
Replayability
As I said earlier, this game has multiple endings. Want to know what makes it interesting, though? The characters will remember EVERYTHING you've done. I mean that, too. Mess with the game's files and try to beat it that way, I dare you. With the multiple endings, the replayability is far more dependent on you. If you have no soul, you'll probably try and do a genocide run while doing the other two runs as well. Maybe you'll try and do a pacifist one so you don't have to go through the pain of killing anyone, then do a neutral, and finish with a genocide ending. Just remember, EVERY choice will be remembered permanently.
Verdict
Undertale is easily my GotY at this point in time, but it's also one of the most creative games I've ever seen. This is an absolute masterpiece, and I really hope it wins a LOT of awards. Do I recommend this game? Well, I'll join the internet on this one and say, "Of course!" Just be ready to stock up on spaghetti, because you'll need it while you stress-eat and do a playthrough of this gem.

Undertale is an amazing game with very few faults. I won't spoil the game, but I'll give a basic sypnosis: you are a human who fell down Mt. Ebott and and find out you are in the underground. The underground is a place were monsters fled to several years ago, after they had lost a war with the humans. There is more about the story I want to say, but undertale is a game best experienced blind.
There are three ways to play this game: Pacifist (were you don't kill or more commonly refered to SPARE anyone), Genocide (where you activley try and kill everything), and Neutral ( where you kill whoever you want and SPARE whoever you want). This is made through an incredibly inovative battle system. One where during your turn you can try and kill your enimies or talk to them. However during the enemies turn it turns into a bullet hell game where you have to try to doge a bunch of attacks coming towards you at once.
The complaints I have about undertale are nitpicks at best. It seems at some points there are huge difficulty spikes for no reason. Some of the random encounters you have in this game are in my opinion harder than some boss fights in the game. Another small compliant I have with the game is the out of battle sprites not being very detailed. For example when one of the characters is saying something realy sad and emotional there that character is with her srite haveing her smile and nothing else. Again it's just a small nitpick that breaks from the emersion a little bit.
Overall undertale is an amazing game that I think you should pick up right now. I promise that you will get enjorment out of this game. Weather that means you just like it or think it's the best thing scince toilet paper. I mean it's only ten bucks. Just buy this game already!

We paid these guys because we were so hyped for this game to be finished, they made so much money before even starting that Dean Hall just ran off in the woodworks with millions in his pockets. On to the pros; the game looks great on a Geforce 980 and up (I personally used a 960, 980ti, and a 1070 to test). Rust has come a long way since then, no longer do I have to download the game in my browser each time I wish to play it. The game has a certain depth that is uncommon amongst any game I have ever played. Because, there is always something to do in Rust.
The Rust that you could be buying (or playing already) is in my opinion the third iteration of the game and if I had to be objective it is honestly the best it's ever been. The game (although advertised as alpha) is more complete than the vast majority of early access games on the market. It's free of bugs, rich in features and has the hardest working game dev team I have ever seen.
If you're someone who is creative, adventurous and enjoys running around naked with a rock in your hand. Then rust is the perfect match for you.

Since I earlier wrote this review, a few of the problems I thought had been tackled. I'm also impressed by the activity of the developers.
I do recomend this game, however, there are a few things to note.
It is still very much in development, however, the developers update frequently and add plenty of new things, to the extent to which if you stop playing for a while, there's so much more added that you almost have to relearn the game! Depending on how you like your games, this may be a selling point or a caution.
One major critisism was the push towards clan gameplay - The game was ruled by clans during some updates. If clan gaming is your thing, this game is great, however, for solo players like me being put up against a clan of 5 or 6 is almost impossible, and the recent updates have made this even worse. Not to mention every single clan is a bunch of absolute ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s. However, the newer changes have seemed to deal with a few of these problems. Clans will of course always be the most powerful
, but it feels far more playable now.
Recently, the gunplay has been hugely improved, which is a big plus. With the huge update with the exp system, the game has somewhat taken a huge step in balancing (although resulting in the unfortunate side effect of helping clans). It's a lot of fun to pick up and play for a while.
One last gripe from potato players like me; optimisation is not great right now, however the developers are working hard to fix this.
All in all, I love this game, and it's constantly improving. (I'm sorry legacy fans, I find that version awful) I trust the developers and believe this game will be a worthwhile buy, and the money I put into it was well worth the entertainment; although you may wish to wait for a sale. On sale, BUY IT.

Rust as many of you know is a full survival game. The survival aspect of this game is pretty spot on. Where as most survival games, you need to work hard to get enough food to survive, but you also have to do it with caution as the wild life in this game can be pretty ferocious. A boar is just as dangerous as a wolf or bear.
There are many servers with plenty of players. The are a fair amount of cheaters, but not as bad as in early Rust. Since the game doesn't have a PvE setting you have to kill or be killed, and you will most likely not get shown pity or any remorse for trying to be friendly. There are some servers that are PvE and the owners will punish you for killing players. A good one is Plague's PvE. Plague (the owner) is pretty cool and has a good community and the people are nice.
Rust has a dynamic survival feature that many games I've seen/played don't have. It has caves that can go on for ages, fish traps, copying the genes of plants to grow your farms production, and the everyday struggle of getting food, water, ores, wood, and variety of other items you'll need to survive Rust. Their are plenty of weaponry ranging from spears, to bows, to guns, even to a flame thrower  (who doesn't love using a flame thrower on that bear at your door :P).

I never liked 2D games of any kind. I find it extremely difficult to get immersed without that third dimention. Undertale however achieved this and so, so much more.
The storyline is one of the best I've ever seen in a game, on par with the likes of Kingdom Hearts or Uncharted in my opinion. It makes you question all pre-conceptions of RPGs and other games alike. You make a huge connection with the characters regardless of your moral choices, and boy do those choices have an impact.
The music is catchy, memorable, and absolutely fantastic. Definitely another one of the strong points. I find myself listening to them again and again.
If I had any critisisms it would be that once you've finished you feel an Undertale shaped hole in your heart. This game is the definition of one-of-a-kind, there's nothing else like it in quite the same way.
There's a HUGE amount of re-playability value, although you may not want to after you've finished for reasons that you will no doubt discover once you start playing for a while.
This game is definitely worth picking up, it's changed my outlook on 2D games entirely. However I think I may have shot myself in the foot a bit, because I feel I quite possibly could have started with the best one out there. It's all downhill from here for me....

This game is everything you could want in a real apocalyptic survival game. First and foremost, it is in beta, any complaints about lag, glitches and the like are just silly because that's the whole point of a game going through alpha/beta, otherwise it would just be called released.
Second and what should be more important: gameplay. The concept is basic but great, you wake up with nothing (realistically no stat pants couldn't hurt haha) and every piece of resource you need you have to gather. One issue on some servers is that resources aren't spawning quickly enough or at all from what I hear, but that's because the game is in alpha... aside from spawning rates resource execution is great, maybe in the future they will reskin some rocks to look like discarded metal for realism, but as far as gameplay goes it's all the same. In a real survival situation you wouldn't find piles of a variety of resources naturally, just some wood and minerals. Animals are scarce in some areas and that's completely realistic too, unless you're on a farm, if there was real life apocalypse you would not see bears and boars walking around main paths constantly.
The sleeping bag is a great feature. You can save a spawn point and use a metal door to hopefully keep your things safe. This allows you to actually form alliances and make friends, but doesn't add a "haven/neutral" point in the game which makes it so much more exciting.
Lastly community discussion. Yes, the people are mean and vicious, and perhaps they are kids (I like how that's become an insult these days, it's a videogame for Christ's sake!). This is what makes this game great. Who expects there to be tons of people out there willing to help others and extend trust and a welcoming hand to total strangers in an apocalypse? Most people you run into will be desperate and selfish, some well run the other direction because they are scared, lots will become bullies because they can and a few will begin to band together in these beginning stages of hard times. This is what I've come across so far playing the game, and this is what makes it pee your pants scary...what I assume you were looking for when you bought this game.
For anyone who wants a nice community with easy to gather resources and mobs that hit you for 3% of your health, play minecraft. For those who played for 30 mins or an hour and got tired of crap server lag and crashes, and glitchy gameplay just keep in mind it's in alpha and will get better. If you don't have the patience put it on the backburner for later enjoyment!

Rust as many of you know is a full survival game. The survival aspect of this game is pretty spot on. Where as most survival games, you need to work hard to get enough food to survive, but you also have to do it with caution as the wild life in this game can be pretty ferocious. A boar is just as dangerous as a wolf or bear.
There are many servers with plenty of players. The are a fair amount of cheaters, but not as bad as in early Rust. Since the game doesn't have a PvE setting you have to kill or be killed, and you will most likely not get shown pity or any remorse for trying to be friendly. There are some servers that are PvE and the owners will punish you for killing players. A good one is Plague's PvE. Plague (the owner) is pretty cool and has a good community and the people are nice.
Rust has a dynamic survival feature that many games I've seen/played don't have. This is one of the best games I've played in a long time. It's rare when I play through a game more than once or twice, while with Undertale I did so more than three times--and that's not counting watching others play through it as well. Yes, you know where the story's heading and what's going to happen, but when it affects everyone in a different manner, where even minor decisions change dialogue and responses later on, it's damn amazing.
Not to even mention the music. The soundtrack for this game on its own is already great, but paired with characters, scenes, and the story itself it can get downright emotional. I don't tend to react physically to sad or happy scenes, but throw in thematic music during an explanation of the pain one family and their entire race went through and I might've cried--a lot.
Lastly, the characters stick so much with you afterwards. Some appear to fit stereotypes, but develop and show different aspects of themselves. Others appear to be one way on one playthrough, then show a completely different side upon the player choosing to play contrary to how they did before. Even the characters you hardly see in the game have so much buried and hinted about them that it's normal not to be able to find out much about them just from playing through the game once or twice. It's decently short--a typical playthrough tends to be six to eight hours--but certainly replayable.

Borderlands 2 is a game for those that enjoy the feeling of finding awesome equipment hidden in a massive pile of other stuff.
Sure, you don't NEED to go in-depth with this game. On the first playthrough you can get by with just picking up gear as you travel along, choosing stuff that looks better than your current gear, and maybe occasionally buying something in the vendor that looks handy. The deeper you go down the rabbit hole however, the more there is to discover.
The story is decent for a First Person Shooter (albeit one with RPG elements), and dialogue is often amusing to a degree. Handsome Jack, the main antagonist is a cartoon villain with M rated attitudes. He believes, or at least pretends to believe that he is the good guy, and you are just a "Filthy Bandit.".
Graphically, the game has a lot more variations in design and color scheme than it's predecessor (which was brown, brown, and a bit of color here and there). Cell shaded graphics with thick, graphic novel like outlines is the style of the game, and does a good job of separating it from the average FPS.
Now, on to the gameplay itself!:
Action is often fast paced and exciting. So long as you don't allow yourself to get too far ahead of the enemy levels, you'll find battles where you have to fight hard to win. The game does a decent job of easing you into the various elements, such as different gun types (Pistol, SMG, Assault/Combat Rifle, Shotgun, Revolver, Rocket Launcher, and Sniper Rifle), the importance of a good shield, grenade mods (alter the way your grenade behaves, including damage bonuses and special effects), Class Mods (Class-specific devices which can boost skills, and have other effects like increasing fire rate with specific weapon types), and lastly Relics (Device which generally boost damage or defence in some way). Equipment rarity is also made fairly clear. It goes White, Green, Blue, Purple, Magenta, Orange, Seraph, and Pearlescent. The final two rarities (Pearlescent and Seraph) are special. Seraphs require you to have at least one of the season pass DLC to obtain (and you need all 4 of the Season Pass DLC to obtain all the Seraph rarity items), and as to Pearlescent rarity weapons, you need to be in Ultimate Vault Hunter Mode (Playthrough 3) for them to have a chance of being spawned. Don't assume that a blue is automatically better than a green rarity item, even at the same level. Experiment!
Playable Characters and Skills:
There are 4 included playable characters, and two DLC characters. Each class has it's ups and downs, and a special game changing skill unique to them. For example, Salvador (Gunzerker) will dual-wield guns when his action skill is active, meaning TWICE THE FIREPOWER. Axton (Commando) drops a turret, which damages enemies and draws aggression away from you. Maya (Siren) locks an enemy's movements for a short time, allowing you to get in free hits. Zer0 turns invisible for a few seconds and launches a decoy, and his first attack made whilst in this mode does increased damage. The DLC characters are Gaige (Mechromancer) who launches a flying robot that attacks nearby enemies, and Kreig (Psycho); a schizophrenic musclebound maniac that will whale on everything within reach with increased offensive and defensive capabilities and can even throw his axe at more distant targets.
Aside from the action skills unique to the character, there are various other skills that you can put points into, and have an effect on gameplay in some way. For example, increasing fire rate or damage for a few seconds after a kill is made. Each character has 3 skill trees, each ending with a final gamechanging skill modifier. For example, Zer0's Bloodlust (Melee) tree ends with the Many Must Fall perk, which will instantly re-deploy the hologram if he kills the enemy with one melee strike. As mentioned before, Class Mods unique to a character class will boost certain skills. It's possible for them to go as high as +6, meaning some skills can be boosted to 11, as the normal limit on points you can put into most skills is 5, though some skills are only 1 (those usually affect the way you play).
Plus, there is a gun that shoots swords....EXPLODING swords...In DLC4 (Tiny Tina's Assault on the Dragon Keep). So yeah, there is that too.

This is an updated review for the recent 0.60 update. If you don't know what DayZ is, DayZ is a standalone version of the very popular DayZ mod on Arma 2. This mod blew up because of it being a hardcore survival mod. You had to eat and drink and kill zombies. This is the same idea for this but i believe it is still as good as that.
DayZ has many pros and many cons, but the pros overshadow the cons.
Pros:
- A realistic survival experience
- Many servers to play on
- Great RP (for those looking for roleplay)
- Intense firefights for supplies
- Large map
- 60 player servers
- Many towns and cities to explore
Con:
-Still in development
- Bugs that occur very rarely
- Hard to get in
- Can be very difficult at first
Honestly, It comes down to weather or not the pros overshadow the cons. The gameplay is great in this game. If you are looking for a hardcore survival experienece, pick up DayZ today

I don't care about how bad the fanbase can get, the game itself is something that should be experienced by everyone.
When I first saw Undertale on the front page of steam, I had no idea what it was. Apparently I was behind on all the hype building up around this game, but it looked intriguing from the store page and had a small sale going on, so I got it.
Little did I know that I was lucky: playing Undertale blind without the internet spoiling anything. Some have had their chance to play the game ruined by spoilers or people yelling at them to play genocide or pacifist, and if that hurt your opinion of the game I can see why.
That being said, SPOILERS from now on about the game are likely to pop up in my writing here. There is too much to black out with the spoiler option. If you were somehow able to avoid all the information going around about this game, I would recommend you stop reading now and play the game blind while you still have the chance.
Anyway, when I started up the game, I really didn't know what to expect.
The beginning sequences quickly made me start caring for the world because the world was caring for me (well, my character that is). Never mind the talking flower, I thought, I have a loving caring mom Toriel and a warm house now.
...and I accidentally killed her.
I wanted to go back and fix things, but there was no way I would start over on a first playthrough, so I continued on to the main world. At first, I was a little put off by the change in tone when the 2 silly skeletons showed up, still feeling bad about Toriel, but I really enjoyed learning about the characters and the little snowy town Snowdin. The cave sections with Undyne were mesmerising (with spine-tingling music), but eventually I came to the science lab in the volcano. This is the point where I almost quit playing, because Alphy's stupid anime jokes and Mettaton's existence were annoying me beyond belief.

But, after a day of not touching the game, I decided to go back.
The first playthrough of Undertale can't be a true pacifist run. So, on this first playthrough, I got the normal neutral ending. At this point, I still felt bad about the beginning of the game, and the game itself did not let me forget about what I'd done. Flowey continued to mess with the game, saving and loading it and "corrupting" the whole thing before our final fight, when I beat him. Now I was given the option of sparing or killing some evil foliage.
And you know what, I spared him. At this point I was still a bit annoyed at the game's anime jokes, but the overall feeling Undertale left me with was... hard to describe.
This was before I did the true pacifist run.
Following neutral, I started up the game again, and almost couldn't believe it when characters started mentioning things about my previous playthrough. I had started over, but the game didn't forget anything I had done in my previous life. Now I was Determined (sorry) to befriend and spare everything in my path.
This is point where I really, really started to care about everything and everyone around me. It didn't matter how stupid papyrus and san's jokes were, or how aggressive Undyne was, there was no way in hell I could hate any of these people (monsters?) As I continued on playing, taking more and more abuse from enemies and still saying hello to them, still helping them with their problems, and still telling them that they mattered, the more it warmed my heart (that's so cheesy, but it's true). Then came the final boss, where (I don't mind saying this) I cried. The final battle: the music, the chaotic attacks, the dialogue, holding on through it all somehow - it's unbelievably powerful and the ending hug and forgiveness is too much to handle.
I know it's been said before, but I'll repeat it here: you don't play Undertale, Undertale plays you. It's still hard to sum up, but Undertale made me care. It made me question quite a few morality choices, made me wonder about all the secrets hidden behind the scenes (Gaster?), and, all-in-all, made a world worth experiencing several times over.
The bullet hell combat is great, the music is excellent, and the graphics, while a mess in many ways, work out great in the end. I'll probably come back and edit this
if I can come up with a way to accurately describe how this game worked so well.
Until then, I really do think it;s worth most of the praise it recieves.
It's not perfect, but what game is? I wish the fans would chill out a bit and stop deepthroat forcing memes and pics everywhere, but they can do what they want on open sites. Just know that it hurts lots of people's opinions of this game. And it's hip and cool to hate Undertale, apparently. Ignoring that, this game was an unforgettable experience for me, still one of the best games I've ever played.
Coming back to this later: there may be games with better gameplay (though Undertale did a bullet hell/turn-based mashup really, really well), but I can't think of any other game that's had a better "journey" - the experience from start to finish and all the little nuances in between. I've lost sleep over the story, and the mysteries people still haven't figured out (again, Gaster). Even crazier is that the magic hasn't changed over multiple playthroughs. It still works even when I know exactly what's going to happen. How does it do that?

This is one of those rare games that you really shouldn't miss. Let me explain.
I like RPG's but the combat has bored me in many of the turn based games lately. If that's the case, hell, even if you don't like RPG's at all, Undertale is incredible. The combat, or lackthereof if thats what you choose, is fun and quick backed by INCREDIBLE music. Did I say the music was incredible? It is. I regret not getting the bundle with the soundtrack.

If I were to describe video games in an extremely complicated metaphor that tied in mammals, reptiles, ethnic food, and figures from mythology, Borderlands 2 would be something like a Platypus-Snake-JapaneseSesameChicken-Surma.
Platypus: Why a platypus? Because Platypuses/Platypeese/Platypii are unique. They're a weird hybrid thing that is actually pretty cool. Borderlands is practically a second cousin of the platypus, with all that uniquity. The best way I can think to explain it would be to draw up the image of an MMO. MMOs let you run around, level up, dump skill points everywhere, find loot to kill things to find more loot of varying rarity, and some of them let you enter instanced dungeon areas to kill monsters with your friends (Where applicable).
Borderlands is pretty similar to that, but it's a first person shooter. You pick a class, get killed first thing off, and then start your adventure as the semi-official minion of the incessantly talking Wheatley/Gir mashup named Claptrap(More like shut-your-trap, amirite?). Your adventure will have you killing enemies for random loot, levelling up to get different perks that let you build your own style of character, and taking side quests from NPCs. the whole game is like one of those aforementioned instanced dungeons, where you can drag up to three friends (Or, should you lack those, random people online that probably hate you just because they are the internet) and go monster slaying. I've heard that if your friend takes your loot, you can stop being friends and then challenge him to a now-unfriendly duel to kill him and take what's rightfully yours. I wouldn't know, because I don't really..... have... friends. And I hate the internet people.
In summary: Borderlands 2 is an FPSMMO but not MMO because instead of being massive multiplayer it's like 4 multiplayer, but still retains all the typical trimmigns of one of the nicer MMOs. It's like halo with quests.
After your head finishes exploding at how fun that sounds, carry on reading.
Snake: Snakes look pretty cool, and they make neat sounds.
You know what else looks cool?
I do! I have awesome curly hobbit hair like Frodo.
But I'm not the only cool-looking thing around. Cel-shaded graphics are pretty neat as well. Borderlands 2 has a really cool art style that makes it super obvious you're playing Borderlands and not something else. For the easily confused, it may be nice to be able to tell what game you're playing at a glance.
Sound-wise, it's wunderbar (German for wonderful. Also useful: "Der Mann isst das Kind" means "I like children", which is good to know because people trust you more if you like children). Everyone's voiced, and they voiced real nice. Guns sound like guns. Bad guys sound like bad guys and say things like "I will kill you" before making guns noises come out of their guns.
Japanese Sesame Chicken: HOLY CHILDREN OF GOD SESAME CHICKEN IS GOOD. I order it every time I go to a Japanese restaurant, much in the same way I ordered Borderlands 2. fun is good, and Borderlands 2 is fun. Everyone is funny, and you can't spell funny without fun. You can't spell gun without un, and you can't spell fun without un. You also can't spell undertaker without un, but that's not applicable here.
Dialogue is full of funny things, a couple of which made me pause the game so I could laugh for a while (Claptrap talking about his own voice is my favorite line so far).
Surma: Surma is the Finnish god of violent death, if wikipedia tells the truth. Science has been performed to prove that wikipedia is true. So scientifically speaking, (Is that what scientology is?) Surma is real, and Surma is in this game a lot because you will death-initely be violently death-ing a whole death-ing lot of things with all your fancy guns you pick up (Which feel great by the way. Some shooters feel horrible, and other just "feel right" or something). Lots of fun stat comparing to be had, so you can put that statistics* class to use for once. It seems like Surma might be the only god in here though, besides maybe the god of fun if that's a thing (Sheogorath?).
All your quests will boil down to "walk here" followed by "shoot the bad things" (Don't worry, they are bad things like enemies, so it's fine to shoot them. Claptrap addresses this as well, if you are suffering any moral twinges about this.) and then "pick up the things" and then finally "take the thing to the guy" to get a profitable return. So not much variety. the story behind each will be different, ranging from r/interesting to "You srsly ask me do this."
The complete Platypus-Snake-JapaneseSesameChicken-Surma package:
