A poorly contrived sequal to an otherwise competant shooter.
In Borderlands 2 you'll find lazy texturing in the case of snow which is simply a white square copy-pasted over most of the terrain, no improvement to the graphics other than some physx effects when you miss your target.  Enemy hit boxes are buggy as hell, point-blank shots from a shotgun or riotgun can somehow miss the target, headshots can quite often totally miss even when aimed perfectly, there's very few new enemies, most of them just being recycled from the first game.  The storyline is poorly written at best, simply putting you as another vault hunter looking for another vault, but then for some reason completely ignoring that first premise and having you fight in a resistance faction against some terribly annoying guy that does nothing but irritate you over the radio as you progress through dull and empty terrain, that's when you're not playing corridor shooter in most of the areas.
Most weapons you find won't work how you want them to.  Want an assault rifle with a reasonably large clip and maybe some elemental effect?  Too bad, most of the ones you'll find have very small clips and use 2-3 bullets per shot, meaning you have to go through the incredibly long 2+ second reload time after every 4th bullet, making it a totally useless weapon, one of the most ridiculous ones I've found was a shotgun with a 3 round clip, that used 3 rounds per shot, with the description 'fires as fast as you can pull the trigger'.  It's almost impossible to find a weapon that you'll actually enjoy using, and in a first person shooter, that's extremely bad design.
Borderlands 1 was known for it's comedy and humour, sadly Borderlands 2 gets all it's 'humour' from internet memes and parodies, it has no original jokes of it's own and most of the comedy is so bad you'd wish you hadn't heard them say it.  Claptraps in the first game were funny because they were air-headed and silly, in BL2 they're purposefully annoying, and as such, you just wish they'd shut up.
All Borderlands 2 is really is a boring and irritating slog through same-old same-old situations from a company that really has no idea how to make a good game.  BL1 was a one trick pony, but since then they've had Duke Nukem Forever, Aliens: Colonial Marines and this to show how bad they really are.  If you own Borderlands 1 and were thinking of buying this, don't bother, just play BL1 again and you'll get a better experience than anything this could offer.

In short, do not try to play this game if you intend to Solo or go in with a small group. This is not a survival game, this is a PvP battleground in disguise. This game is only fun for people in huge clans and groups. Everybody else will only feel anger and frustration.
The game mechanics and graphics themselves are satisfying. The problem with the game is the experience itself, which is quite horrible. High level players shoot everybody on sight, there is no human interaction. If you meet somebody with a gun on the road (and you will), they will kill you every single time and waste all your progress.
High level players raid and grief bases constantly to the point of abusiveness because they have nothing else to do. (ever seen the YT comments section? Those are the people playing Rust). And since you are level dependent, you will be facing off against advanced firearm wielding opponents armed with bows and spears all the time, without a chance of crafting equal weaponry till many gameplay hours later.
There is no way of properly fortifying your base if you don't have massive resources. (high level players will blow your walls in smaller houses away with C4 and such). And since there's so many of them it is no problem for them to amass the necessary resources. They can easily steal any buildings you create this way, invalidating all your progress.
The only solution to the problem is joining a bigger group of people and grinding your level through to the point where you can create competitive weaponry. But if you play in a smaller group like me, you will have to waste your time away trying to cope against insurmountable odds. Even if you manage to fortify and equip yourself, if you don't have a clan that plays 24/7 your base will be offline raided.
=========== Verdict ============
Ultimately I gave Rust a negative rating because of all the frustration it caused. There was a lot of fun to be had, but all that got overshadowed by constantly griefing, frustration, and simple abusiveness. Worst of all, it wasted my time.
Now if you like what you heard and would like to join this cesspool of violence, griefing, toxicity, and gang fighting; be my guest and go join a clan, the game's mechanics are definitely solid. Me personally though, I rather go play Battlefield and have actual fun without the grind.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

We dont play DayZ for action pack shoot outs, now there are those and they are great fun but if you buy the game expecting that all the time your going to be disapointed. We play DayZ for the experience of taking a player with nothing, dragging him through hell with you and still come out on top. We play for the experience of taking that player with either it be a broken leg, starvation, cold, dehydration, bites, or even a bullet wound, and see him be brought back to full heath. We play for the experience of climbing a mountain mind numbingly slow to be rewarded with a gleam of sunlight and a view over all of the northeastern airstrip and surrounding towns. We play DayZ because we become attatched to our character, in other games such as GTA or CoD you dont care if you get killed. Maybe it will take a bit of cash or drop your KD a bit but who really cares. In DayZ its very differnt, you die all your stuff and hard work is gone, and you start from square one again. We care about our characters and take time to think of a plan or to scout out an area, we dont just charge in guns blazing because the chance of losing everything is too great. If you start getting shot at you get scared with your character, because you dont want to see the guy who triped and broke his leg, rolled 1000m for a piece of cloth to make a splint, then get up and find a gun with three oh so precious bullets, get shot and die. We play DayZ because its immersive experience is like none other, its truely a great game.

This game is honestly an amazing survival game, possibly the best I've seen, but there's a huge problem in it right now. If you don't have any friends to team up with every time you play, or you just want to survive in the game alone, then get used to starting from scratch every single day. It's impossible to survive on your own and actually do well in this game. Clans just have too much power, and if you're new to a server, then for the first few days that you go on that server you're going to get wiped out everytime as you level up to get your first gun. I like to think I represent the average gamer. I have a job that I have to go to most days, so I don't have a ton of time to put into videogames, I can usually play for 4 hours usually, give or take depending on the day, and I don't have a ton of friends to play with, maybe one other friend who might have the game and sometimes is willing to play. To actually craft your first reliable ranged weapon, a bow, takes a few hours of straight farming for the xp, then even more time to actually get the resources to make it. That's assuming you're able to go under the radar long enough to not be interupted by constant deaths and slaughters for no reason. Clans are impossible to even consider taking down, and usually even if you're able to build a little hut out of metal, they'll still get in overnight while you're sleeping and take you out without even giving you a chance. That happens so often it gets to the point I'm just discouraged from playing anymore. I know there isn't a lot Facepunch can do about raiders, it's apart of the game and they can't just remove it, but something needs to be done to give solo players a chance. It's to the point where I'll build a 2x2 metal house and spend all day making it, just to wake up the next morning and find it raided and me dead. I find my house again and try to rebuild, then I have to go to work, and when I get home I'm raided, they blocked off my cabinet, and walled me in so my only option is to use the kill command. I trust eventually the devs will do something about this, and when they do I'll change my recommendation, but for now I only recommend it to someone with 4 or 5 friends who have the game too and can all team up to kick the little guy.

Welcome, to Undertale. This game is amazing. You play as a fallen human named Frisk, finds themselves in a place known as The Underground. Throughout the game, you fight bosses, meet new monsters, and get endings.
Now for the review.  I'll base this off of 3 major things in a game, Its game play, its replay ability, and its community.
For starters, the game play is pretty nice, and pretty basic, nothing special there, but then, when i first tried out the battle, my mind was changed. instead of the usual RPG battle screen i'm used to (which is usually fight, items, and flee) I saw the "FIGHT" the "ACT" the "ITEMS" and "MERCY" 2 of which are relevant. Usually in RPG's you have fighting and items and fleeing, but in undertale, you have the option to spare enemies. This blew my mind to pieces because I've always learned to fight and kill enemies in games. But anyway, lets get back to the topic. Another game play aspect is how characters behave. you have a comedic skeleton, his childish brother, a goat mom, a goat dad, a goat son, a fish, a robot, and a weeaboo dinosaur. these characters make for a perfect "Humerus" game play aspect, with a plot twist. And no, i did not forget about flowey, the supposed antagonist in this game, it depends on how you play the game.
Next up, replay ability. this one won't be as long, because replay ability is not a big factor.
Anyway, this game may seem like it has a lot of replay ability, but it really doesn't. Its only fun after about 2 runs and a supposed "True" reset, which doesn't fully reset.
and finally, the moment I've been waiting for, the community. Jesus, what a horrible place to be in general. I mean seriously, what the actual ♥♥♥♥ happened to this community, it just.... auuhhg. you know what? no, i'm done, i cannot finish this review, this community is just horrible
My final review on the game is..... 9.5 skeletons out of 10

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding pie recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1. 6 tablespoons unsalted butter
2. 1/2 cup white sugar
3. 1/2 cup brown sugar
4. 1/4 cup water
5. 1/4 teaspoon cinnamon
6. 1 pinch salt
7. 5 apples - peeled, cored and sliced
8. 1 pastry for double-crust pie
Directions:
1. Preheat oven to 425 degrees F (220 degrees C).
2. Combine butter, white sugar, brown sugar, water, cinnamon, and salt in a saucepan over medium heat. Bring to a boil, remove from heat and set aside.
3. Roll out half the pastry to fit a 9-inch pie plate. Place bottom crust in pie plate; pour in apple slices.
4. Roll out top crust into a 10-inch circle. Cut into 8 (1-inch) wide strips with a sharp paring knife or pastry wheel. Weave the pastry strips, one at a time, into a lattice pattern. Fold the ends of the lattice strips under the edge of the bottom crust and crimp to seal.
5. Pour butter-sugar mixture over top of pie, coating the lattice, and allowing any remaining sauce to drizzle through the crust.
6. Bake in the preheated oven for 15 minutes. Reduce heat to 350 degrees F (175 degrees C), and bake until the crust is golden brown, the caramel on the top crust is set, and the apple filling is bubbling, 35 to 40 more minutes. Allow to cool completely before slicing.

We dont play DayZ for action pack shoot outs, now there are those and they are great fun but if you buy the game expecting that all the time your going to be disapointed. We play DayZ for the experience of taking a player with nothing, dragging him through hell with you and still come out on top. We play for the experience of taking that player with either it be a broken leg, starvation, cold, dehydration, bites, or even a bullet wound, and see him be brought back to full heath. We play for the experience of climbing a mountain mind numbingly slow to be rewarded with a gleam of sunlight and a view over all of the northeastern airstrip and surrounding towns. We play DayZ because we become attatched to our character, in other games such as GTA or CoD you dont care if you get killed. Maybe it will take a bit of cash or drop your KD a bit but who really cares. In DayZ its very differnt, you die all your stuff and hard work is gone, and you start from square one again. We care about our characters and take time to think of a plan or to scout out an area, we dont just charge in guns blazing because the chance of losing everything is too great. If you start getting shot at you get scared with your character, because you dont want to see the guy who triped and broke his leg, rolled 1000m for a piece of cloth to make a splint, then get up and find a gun with three oh so precious bullets, get shot and die. We play DayZ because its immersive experience is like none other, its truely a great game.

Borderlands 2 is a FPS RPG set on the desolate world of Pandora, ruled by bandits, fought over by various corporations for its wealth of resources.
Set 5 years after the first borderlands, both Atlas and Dahl have fled pandora, leaving behind their remnants. A new company has arisen to take their place however - Hyperion. Power hungry and searching for a vault, their CEO employs the likes of you to find them. However, you are betrayed, and left to die. The games story follows you as you attempt to take revenge, and defeat Handsome Jack, CEO of hyperion.
Play as the two-gun rambo-style Salvidor, the Gunzerker, or Zer0, the deadly, sneaky assasin who's a master of blade and sniper. Maya, the siren, can support and heal teammates, while controlling the battlefield with her magical powers. Axton and Gaige can summon robots to help them fight, though axton is more of a hange behind cover kind of guy, while gaige has trouble aiming, but packs quite the punch.
Hunt for loot and kill bosses, though sometimes their loot is...well...rare.

I have played many survival games in the past, and sadly, this game is still very similar to all of the others I've played. It can be fun, don't get me wrong, but you could get the same experience of spawn, grind, die, and repeat from all of the other survival games currently on the market for much cheaper.
Rust's core gameplay mechanics right now seem to be focused on how many of your friends you can gather into one server. It's basically a social waiting game. All you need to do to be successful is to get 4+ people into your clan, grind for several days at a time, all while contructing a massive fortress of stone and sheet metal. Once you've completed that you'll probably all have AK's, thousands of 5.56 rounds, a couple C4, and several charges of fresh spawn murder.
Another negative thing about this game's mechanics is the grinding. It seems to be impossible to escape from it, as just every single survival game includes this. In Rust, you spawn in at lvl 0, you hit a tree and a node for about five minutes just to get to lvl 1, and then you have to repeat that until you get to lvl 3 just to get stone tools. Then you craft tools, make a crappy twig shack, and then a member of a huge clan with a suppressed tommygun will raid your base and ransack all of the loot that you spent four hours obtaining. The only way to prevent this, like said before, is to get a group of 4+ friends and just grind your way up the ladder until you can build a "impenetrable" compound and craft AK's.
Weapons in this game won't do you justice until you get to about lvl. 20. A hunting bow will do nothing against bears and the clan of 4 with metal armor that you're bound to have to fend off. Crossbows are slightly better, but it's so damn slow to reload that you're forced to 1 shot headshot someone (which might not be possible depending on their armor). The eoka pistol is a pile of garbage and the waterpipe shotgun can only kill freshspawns at point blank. You're practically defenseless if you're found by someone with a better weapon and armor or a bear with those weapons. Only once you get your vengeful little hands on a revolver or above can you actually kill things. Need to defend your log cabin that you grinded for three hours to build from an attacking clan? Just craft yourself something better than the waterpipe shotgun and rally around your three other friends.
Unless you want to run this game on Minecraft graphical settings you'll need to spend over a grand just to get the recommended specs, and even then you probably won't get to play on Ultra with a stable 60fps.
The only good thing I can say about this game is that it's a great time killer and if you actually manage to get decent weapons you can take out your frustration on anyone you please. 4/10 don't buy unless you have three other friends to play with

The only bosses in the game that gave me trouble were Undyne the Undying and Sans, but after you beat them they all of a sudden become to easy because you know their patterns.
The overworld segments aren't much better. Every puzzle in the game has been done a million times before in other, better games, and they don't really get spiced up. The only one I kinda enjoyed were the little space shooter puzzles in Hotland.
Also if I wanted to be invested in these, give me more RPG elements and new powers to play with. When I play an RPG, I'm excited to level up to see what new powers I get and how strong my character becomes. In Undertale, there is no benefit to anything in battle and with a rather mediocre story (I'll touch on that later), there is practically no reason I want to progress through the game. Sparing monsters doesn't take more effort than killing them either, so that's lame also.
Second: Characters
Every character in the game can be explained in 10 words or less, and they're not all that easy to get emotionally attached too. Toriel is a caring but overly worried mother, Papyrus is a naive dreamer that cooks spaghetti, Undyne is an angry♥♥♥♥♥♥fish, you see what I mean? And they also always drive their personalities to the ground. I don't NEED a million cutscenes to show that Papyrus sucks at puzzles and he's an idiot, I get it. The only characters that are good are Sans and Flowey, and even then Flowey ends up becoming a typical anime villian and Sans ends up becoming a typical anime protector type character. How the hell do people fear the genocide run so much if all the characters are so bland and one-note? Mettaton literally exists just to justify how much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥character Alphys is.
What bothers me more is that they all rely on "meme power", and it's the only thing that keeps these characters alive, ESPECIALLY Temmie, Papyrus, Sans, and pretty much everyone else. For an RPG, that's inexcusable.
Third: Story
Plain and simple, the story sucks, and you've pretty much heard it before. Its so cheesy and obvious I fail to see how it gives people the feels. Every ending is so predictable, pretentious, and anime that it becomes just laughable rather than emotional. The journey isn't much better either. Infact, nothing much happens through the game besides the ending scenes. It's another "FRENDSHPI BEATS ALLL" game, and its so obvious about it that I begin to cringe to the point that my stomach begins to hurt.
Fourth: Music
The only redeeming quality of Undertale. It's not that great, but damn is it sadly the best part of the game. If you haven't listened to these already, I recommend Waterfall, CORE, Metal Crusher, Death By Glamour, ASGORE, Hopes and Dreams, and especially Battle Against A True Hero.
Conclusion: This game pretty much represents everything wrong with Indie games. If a normal AAA Game made a game like this, it'll be passed off a mediocre, but just because it's indie means it gets a free pass. I hope aspiring indie developers don't fall for this games hype and make something much better, enjoyable, and less pretentious.
Only play if you want to know why the hell people love it so much. Maybe you'll something I don't, who knows, but just avoid at all costs, don't fall for its hype, and stay clear of it. You can spend that $10 on something better.

Absolutely FANTASTIC adventure.  Gives me hopeful visions and terrifying nightmares all in one package.  It actually makes me want to vomit.

In short, do not try to play this game if you intend to Solo or go in with a small group. This is not a survival game, this is a PvP battleground in disguise. This game is only fun for people in huge clans and groups. Everybody else will only feel anger and frustration.
The game mechanics and graphics themselves are satisfying. The problem with the game is the experience itself, which is quite horrible. High level players shoot everybody on sight, there is no human interaction. If you meet somebody with a gun on the road (and you will), they will kill you every single time and waste all your progress.
High level players raid and grief bases constantly to the point of abusiveness because they have nothing else to do. (ever seen the YT comments section? Those are the people playing Rust). And since you are level dependent, you will be facing off against advanced firearm wielding opponents armed with bows and spears all the time, without a chance of crafting equal weaponry till many gameplay hours later.
There is no way of properly fortifying your base if you don't have massive resources. (high level players will blow your walls in smaller houses away with C4 and such). And since there's so many of them it is no problem for them to amass the necessary resources. They can easily steal any buildings you create this way, invalidating all your progress.
The only solution to the problem is joining a bigger group of people and grinding your level through to the point where you can create competitive weaponry. But if you play in a smaller group like me, you will have to waste your time away trying to cope against insurmountable odds. Even if you manage to fortify and equip yourself, if you don't have a clan that plays 24/7 your base will be offline raided.
=========== Verdict ============
Ultimately I gave Rust a negative rating because of all the frustration it caused. There was a lot of fun to be had, but all that got overshadowed by constantly griefing, frustration, and simple abusiveness. Worst of all, it wasted my time.
Now if you like what you heard and would like to join this cesspool of violence, griefing, toxicity, and gang fighting; be my guest and go join a clan, the game's mechanics are definitely solid. Me personally though, I rather go play Battlefield and have actual fun without the grind.

Damn, what an incredibly overrated game,
First of all: Gameplay
The battle system is really cool, at first. Then you realize the bosses are the only enemies that take full advantage of the battle system and even then it's still "Fisherprice: My First Touhou Game". The bosses have weird handicaps with them that I can't understand, like Toriel purposely not aiming for you if your health is low, Papyrus not even killing you, Flowey have CHECKPOINTS of all things, and I don't think the true final boss can even kill you. The only bosses in the game that gave me trouble were Undyne the Undying and Sans, but after you beat them they all of a sudden become to easy because you know their patterns.
The overworld segments aren't much better. Every puzzle in the game has been done a million times before in other, better games, and they don't really get spiced up. The only one I kinda enjoyed were the little space shooter puzzles in Hotland.
Also if I wanted to be invested in these, give me more RPG elements and new powers to play with. When I play an RPG, I'm excited to level up to see what new powers I get and how strong my character becomes. In Undertale, there is no benefit to anything in battle and with a rather mediocre story (I'll touch on that later), there is practically no reason I want to progress through the game. Sparing monsters doesn't take more effort than killing them either, so that's lame also.
Second: Characters
Every character in the game can be explained in 10 words or less, and they're not all that easy to get emotionally attached too. Toriel is a caring but overly worried mother, Papyrus is a naive dreamer that cooks spaghetti, Undyne is an angry♥♥♥♥♥♥fish, you see what I mean? And they also always drive their personalities to the ground. I don't NEED a million cutscenes to show that Papyrus sucks at puzzles and he's an idiot, I get it. The only characters that are good are Sans and Flowey, and even then Flowey ends up becoming a typical anime villian and Sans ends up becoming a typical anime protector type character. How the hell do people fear the genocide run so much if all the characters are so bland and one-note? Mettaton literally exists just to justify how much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥character Alphys is.
What bothers me more is that they all rely on "meme power", and it's the only thing that keeps these characters alive, ESPECIALLY Temmie, Papyrus, Sans, and pretty much everyone else. For an RPG, that's inexcusable.
Third: Story
Plain and simple, the story sucks, and you've pretty much heard it before. Its so cheesy and obvious I fail to see how it gives people the feels. Every ending is so predictable, pretentious, and anime that it becomes just laughable rather than emotional. The journey isn't much better either. Infact, nothing much happens through the game besides the ending scenes. It's another "FRENDSHPI BEATS ALLL" game, and its so obvious about it that I begin to cringe to the point that my stomach begins to hurt.
Fourth: Music
The only redeeming quality of Undertale. It's not that great, but damn is it sadly the best part of the game. If you haven't listened to these already, I recommend Waterfall, CORE, Metal Crusher, Death By Glamour, ASGORE, Hopes and Dreams, and especially Battle Against A True Hero.
Conclusion: This game pretty much represents everything wrong with Indie games. If a normal AAA Game made a game like this, it'll be passed off a mediocre, but just because it's indie means it gets a free pass. I hope aspiring indie developers don't fall for this games hype and make something much better, enjoyable, and less pretentious.
Only play if you want to know why the hell people love it so much. Maybe you'll something I don't, who knows, but just avoid at all costs, don't fall for its hype, and stay clear of it. You can spend that $10 on something better.

Damn, what an incredibly overrated game,
First of all: Gameplay
The battle system is really cool, at first. Then you realize the bosses are the only enemies that take full advantage of the battle system and even then it's still "Fisherprice: My First Touhou Game". The bosses have weird handicaps with them that I can't understand, like Toriel purposely not aiming for you if your health is low, Papyrus not even killing you, Flowey have CHECKPOINTS of all things, and I don't think the true final boss can even kill you. The only bosses in the game that gave me trouble were Undyne the Undying and Sans, but after you beat them they all of a sudden become to easy because you know their patterns.
The overworld segments aren't much better. Every puzzle in the game has been done a million times before in other, better games, and they don't really get spiced up. The only one I kinda enjoyed were the little space shooter puzzles in Hotland.
Also if I wanted to be invested in these, give me more RPG elements and new powers to play with. When I play an RPG, I'm excited to level up to see what new powers I get and how strong my character becomes. In Undertale, there is no benefit to anything in battle and with a rather mediocre story (I'll touch on that later), there is practically no reason I want to progress through the game. Sparing monsters doesn't take more effort than killing them either, so that's lame also.
Second: Characters
Every character in the game can be explained in 10 words or less, and they're not all that easy to get emotionally attached too. Toriel is a caring but overly worried mother, Papyrus is a naive dreamer that cooks spaghetti, Undyne is an angry♥♥♥♥♥♥fish, you see what I mean? And they also always drive their personalities to the ground. I don't NEED a million cutscenes to show that Papyrus sucks at puzzles and he's an idiot, I get it. The only characters that are good are Sans and Flowey, and even then Flowey ends up becoming a typical anime villian and Sans ends up becoming a typical anime protector type character. How the hell do people fear the genocide run so much if all the characters are so bland and one-note? Mettaton literally exists just to justify how much of a♥♥♥♥♥♥character Alphys is.
What bothers me more is that they all rely on "meme power", and it's the only thing that keeps these characters alive, ESPECIALLY Temmie, Papyrus, Sans, and pretty much everyone else. For an RPG, that's inexcusable.
Third: Story
Plain and simple, the story sucks, and you've pretty much heard it before. Its so cheesy and obvious I fail to see how it gives people the feels. Every ending is so predictable, pretentious, and anime that it becomes just laughable rather than emotional. The journey isn't much better either. Infact, nothing much happens through the game besides the ending scenes. It's another "FRENDSHPI BEATS ALLL" game, and its so obvious about it that I begin to cringe to the point that my stomach begins to hurt.
Fourth: Music
The only redeeming quality of Undertale. It's not that great, but damn is it sadly the best part of the game. If you haven't listened to these already, I recommend Waterfall, CORE, Metal Crusher, Death By Glamour, ASGORE, Hopes and Dreams, and especially Battle Against A True Hero.
Conclusion: This game pretty much represents everything wrong with Indie games. If a normal AAA Game made a game like this, it'll be passed off a mediocre, but just because it's indie means it gets a free pass. I hope aspiring indie developers don't fall for this games hype and make something much better, enjoyable, and less pretentious.
Only play if you want to know why the hell people love it so much. Maybe you'll something I don't, who knows, but just avoid at all costs, don't fall for its hype, and stay clear of it. You can spend that $10 on something better.

After previously recommending this game, I can no longer recommend it.
The game has a lot of potential.  The gunplay is amazing.  Base building is amazing.  The game, for 687 hours, was very enjoyable for me.  I loved Rust.  I played many successful solo wipes on high population servers, and I lived and died with several groups of my friends.  I met most of my Steam friends on Rust as well.
However, some of the most recent updates in Rust have been the worst I have seen in my opinion.  It is no longer possible to play Rust as a solo player.  Building cabinets have literally 0 purpose now, and Rust is now orientated towards playing with a large group of people to survive and win.  There is no playing solo anymore.
The community is toxic.  Very toxic.  Most players are immature little kids that continually harass you and offline raid you. The new raiding system promotes offline raiding moreso than ever, and makes it more difficult for anyone to prevent an offline raid unless you live with a group of many players that have a lot of resources they can put towards base building. The animal AI is terrible.  There is no PVE aspect of the game except for the occassional helicopter that flys around every 2-3 hours (which, by the way, is always taken down by the group of 10 that lives next to Dome every server.)
Unless you have 9 other friends to play this game with, expect to get raided very early on.  Expect to have all the stuff you worked hard for taken away from you as soon as you get it.
This review has nothing to do with the PVP aspect of the game.  The PVP is fantastic.  However, there are too many drawbacks in this game.  Offline Raiding, the Toxic Community, the terrible AI, and many other aspects make this game terrible.

Rust is a FPS PVP survival game. If you're familiar to Hurtworld, H1Z1; then this will be pretty much similar. At first you will be stranded from at the coast, with just a Rock and Torch, injured and hungry. You are to find resources around the map and build your way up to making your base. While at the same time cross-pathed with some mean players or even the AI helicopters. Getting to kill the helicopter is hard too, with this ongoing community of raging wars. The game is built to be PVP, in a real harsh world.
Rust have generally revolved alot from the beginning stages, where players can still pot-lucked themselves when hunting out the barrels for blueprints to get some lucky items. However after the developers have changed the gameplay system to an EXP leveling system. Now it's pretty hard for new players whom have joined the game. Especially the game of being the nothing-on-hand continues to be poor, while the fully-loaded continues to get richer. With this system in mind, it's hard even for players to reach the top level of leveling system. Generally I've seen most of the players get raided at around Level 12 onwards. Where you have gathered your resources to make your Furnace and smelt some Metal Fragments. Ready for some Gunpowder crafting, and make guns.
For networking, most of the official servers are located in the US, Australia, and Hong Kong. But most of them are stranded with raided houses, it's nearly impossible to survive out there where there's already ongoing players whom have build them long ago. While some still continues to play them, but have shifted to modded servers instead. It's just basically pointless for players to build all the way up for days, and to be destroyed by C4 detonations within seconds. Although modded servers practice a way, that they will wipe the servers every monthly, or bi-weekly basis to get new players to come back and climb the ladder again. It's a vicious cycle.
None to say most of the servers are still pretty mean towards players, or rather shoot-on-sight basis. It's hard to get team players if you were to be playing single. So get this game if you're going to play with friends, by means they are active in their gameplay too. Since raiding can happen anytime, online or offline. You wouldn't want to get back the next day only to see your sleeping body to be emptied out and slaughtered.
If you're looking for more friendly survival games out there, I suggest you play Unturned, Don't Starve Together instead. It's still a survival but in a PVE role yet still able to team together. Moreover the server reset are more frequent there than here. Where you nearly survive less than just a week, while the wipe is a month later.
It will be good to have the players to choose probably 3 teams, on the first day of the wipe. Thereafter players whom just came in later to only have to choose within that 3 teams and play along-side with them, and unable to swap teams. So at least it's still a PVP with raging war going on, meaning three factions team fighting each other and also the neutral party of the AI helicopters. Yet still able to get incoming players to join the team with the growing of faction parties. It's like hiring more players to join and fight for the war. This makes players to have a better objective in game, than to think whether should I just roam around killing players, and only to hide when the AI helicopters come. Or should the teams form an alliance and gun down the AI helicopters? Now that's another diplomacy system that Rust developers have to think of.

The original UNDERTALE is an awesome shooter. A must-play for fans of the FPS genre alongside Half-Life and DOOM. The lovecraftian aesthetic and design for the monsters and levels is very unique and creates a unique, almost horror-like atmosphere that blends very well with the frenetic, high-octane shooting.
For the Steam version of this game specifically, I would say buy on sale (it usually goes for a buck). The reason for this is that you're buying an outdated version of GLUndertale which has a lot of notable issues, particularly the inability to increase resolution past 1920x1080 and the inability to adjust FOV, which can be frustrating since you'll have to tinker with it for a while just to get it to run outside of a blurry miniscule window.
Definitely buy it for the data files and ID1 folder so you can bring it into a more modern UNDERTALE engine and you'll have a blast!

It was a fun game for the first couple of hours. We played on a good server, built, had some fun, yet there was something missing. The game could be fun in itself with encounters and such, and I would recommend the game if everyone played on an roleplaying server, but everyone doesn't have that oppurtunity, therefore I'm rating the game based on just joining a normal server. At an high populated server, it is very hard to survive and base raiding will occur, a lot. But as I've mostly, and almost only played on a low populated server, I will rate the game out of that experience. Rust is a fun game, and at start, there's a lot of things to do, but after a while it just loses character. It stops being fun out of the sole reason that there's basically nothing to do, it has lost it's charm. Everything is just the same, you mine, you build, you mine, you build, etc. Of course this might not be the case in regards to an roleplaying server, were you will have the oppurtunity to experience amazing encounters, not get killed on site, etc. If I'm going to start playing rust again, it will be on an rp server, and sure that will be something that I can enjoy, but you can't ask everyone to sign up for rp servers. Some people just want an casual experience, and if you want that I can't recommend this game, but if you are willing to sign up for an rp server, and really go all in, I do recommend this game.

The game could be fun in itself with encounters and such, and I would recommend the game if everyone played on an roleplaying server, but everyone doesn't have that oppurtunity, therefore I'm rating the game based on just joining a normal server. At an high populated server, it is very hard to survive and base raiding will occur, a lot. But as I've mostly, and almost only played on a low populated server, I will rate the game out of that experience. Rust is a fun game, and at start, there's a lot of things to do, but after a while it just loses character. It stops being fun out of the sole reason that there's basically nothing to do, it has lost it's charm. Everything is just the same, you mine, you build, you mine, you build, etc. Of course this might not be the case in regards to an roleplaying server, were you will have the oppurtunity to experience amazing encounters, not get killed on site, etc. If I'm going to start playing rust again, it will be on an rp server, and sure that will be something that I can enjoy, but you can't ask everyone to sign up for rp servers. Some people just want an casual experience, and if you want that I can't recommend this game, but if you are willing to sign up for an rp server, and really go all in, I do recommend this game.

Similar to the TV show 'Lost', after playing Rust for a while it's clear the developers have no idea what the final iteration of the game will look like. First the blueprint system was removed and was replaced by the XP system, then it was put back in again alongside the XP. There are frequent tweaks here and there, new items and places to explore.
On the one hand you could say the devs are listening to the players and changing the game accordingly, on the other you could question whether or not they have a clue about where Rust is going, and what it'll finally look like. The game is still in Alpha - and that doesn't look like changing any time soon. There are some performance issues - I have a GTX 970 and experience the most horrendous frame rate drops from time to time.
Despite all these issues though, Rust is a brilliant game. It's raw, terrifying, exhilarating, frustrating and down right annoying all at the same time. The community at times can be awful - think ten year olds who kill on sight when you've just started. But if you find a good server, get a friend or two; you will have an enormous amount of fun.

This is a re-written review, concentrating on the recent changes in Rust. This game is currently not recommended. Some time ago I had a positive review, which is rare for an Early Access to get a thumbs-up from me.
The new XP system has made this game a huge grind and time consuming. I played loads of it on my week off, but I did not feel rewarded for it. It is a MINDLESS grind right now. I completely do NOT recommend it in its current state. You spend a lot of time into gaining levels and get extremely little in return. No thank you - if anyone thinks this is fair, please do re-evaluate your time and think if it could be spent more useful (even in gaming), because it can.
Facepunch, I do not think that XP system is a complete disaster, therefore there are three ways Rust can become playable again:
1)You go back to Blueprint system - a boring move and it will still consume some hours from players to get better gear, but there are at least chances to get cool stuff early on and working together actually PAYS OFF.
2)You boost the rate of the XP gain around 5 times. I have to spend more than 3 hours to get a metal hatchet/Waterpipe (W-pipe available earlier from the get go)?!? That is stupid and does not balance anything, only consume our time!
3)A friend of mine had an idea that the first 10 levels are available to you from the beginning. There isn't anything extreme there - some clothes, basic gear, primitive weapons. And the remaining level gaining rate is being boosted 1,5x or 2x. People get stuff earlier, but it is better than spending 6 hours and maybe getting something that you can actually use for more advanced farming and ancient-method killing, which is bullcr@p!!!
Thanks to anyone who might or might not have read this. I will be waiting for changes to occur and if anything positive comes out, my review will adapt as well.

Similar to the TV show 'Lost', after playing Rust for a while it's clear the developers have no idea what the final iteration of the game will look like. First the blueprint system was removed and was replaced by the XP system, then it was put back in again alongside the XP. There are frequent tweaks here and there, new items and places to explore.
On the one hand you could say the devs are listening to the players and changing the game accordingly, on the other you could question whether or not they have a clue about where Rust is going, and what it'll finally look like. The game is still in Alpha - and that doesn't look like changing any time soon. There are some performance issues - I have a GTX 970 and experience the most horrendous frame rate drops from time to time.
Despite all these issues though, Rust is a brilliant game. It's raw, terrifying, exhilarating, frustrating and down right annoying all at the same time. The community at times can be awful - think ten year olds who kill on sight when you've just started. But if you find a good server, get a friend or two; you will have an enormous amount of fun.

This is a re-written review, concentrating on the recent changes in Rust. This game is currently not recommended. Some time ago I had a positive review, which is rare for an Early Access to get a thumbs-up from me.
The new XP system has made this game a huge grind and time consuming. I played loads of it on my week off, but I did not feel rewarded for it. It is a MINDLESS grind right now. I completely do NOT recommend it in its current state. You spend a lot of time into gaining levels and get extremely little in return. No thank you - if anyone thinks this is fair, please do re-evaluate your time and think if it could be spent more useful (even in gaming), because it can.
Facepunch, I do not think that XP system is a complete disaster, therefore there are three ways Rust can become playable again:
1)You go back to Blueprint system - a boring move and it will still consume some hours from players to get better gear, but there are at least chances to get cool stuff early on and working together actually PAYS OFF.
2)You boost the rate of the XP gain around 5 times. I have to spend more than 3 hours to get a metal hatchet/Waterpipe (W-pipe available earlier from the get go)?!? That is stupid and does not balance anything, only consume our time!
3)A friend of mine had an idea that the first 10 levels are available to you from the beginning. There isn't anything extreme there - some clothes, basic gear, primitive weapons. And the remaining level gaining rate is being boosted 1,5x or 2x. People get stuff earlier, but it is better than spending 6 hours and maybe getting something that you can actually use for more advanced farming and ancient-method killing, which is bullcr@p!!!
Thanks to anyone who might or might not have read this. I will be waiting for changes to occur and if anything positive comes out, my review will adapt as well.

XP SYSTEM = KILLED THE GAME

Rust has lost it's vibe.
It's completely gone.
The abundance of cheaters (seeing 9 players banned within 5 minutes is worrysome). To admin abuse just because they have the willpower to do so. Not to mention the inevitible grind that is still the XP system. I'll be addressing this all one by one below:
The abundance of cheaters
Alright. So yeah, official servers ♥♥♥♥in blow donkey dongs when it comes to legitimate players. We all know to stay far away from that grey area of the server browser. Although community and modded are not too far off from themselves. You think only private accounts and people with low hours are cheating? Think again. Hours mean absolutely nothing; oh yeah, that player also was level 86 on Steam. It's absolutely TOO easy to cheat in this game. EAC does a horrible job of automatically detecting cheats, since you can technically ESP for 8 hours and never ESP again and NEVER be banned. In all honesty; ditch EAC. Get BattlEye. OR make a more intrusive anticheat. Yes, privacy is key but what about this concept that was made for a game emulator I was a "dev" for a few years ago...
"When the users accept the ToS of the game; in section X,x. It states that the game developer's anti-cheat will take preiodic screenshots of the GAME WINDOW only while the player is playing. When a player logs a kill or other large statistic based information, a screenshot is taken and uploaded to a cloud server where the developers can easily assess if such player is ESPing or cheating at all, thus resulting in an account termination."
This system would be a little intrusive. ALTHOUGH, it would not be able to take a screenshot of anything BUT your game window. Even if you had layered windows above the game window; it would not show any of that. Just like OBS's and other game capture apps, it can constrain to a specific window rather than an entire screen.
Aside from that being a possible way of getting the cheating situation in rust taken care of. Cheating in rust has blown out the fun my group and I used to have. We log in. Work our asses off hitting nodes, picking up♥♥♥♥♥♥on the ground, breaking barrels in order to make a god damn pistol, to have it taken from us by someone who is using an external program.
Admin abuse
This goes without saying. It happens here and there, although I don't think that the server admins should be dictators over their servers. After all FP makes the game that allows them to host servers. FP should have some sort of final say in how they can handle their servers. (Unfair bans, cheat accusations without reason or evidence, ect)
"The Grind"
Boy, bet you thought you would never hear that again. Too bad. The linear system of XP doesn't make any sense for rust. Neither do the temporary blueprints. It's still something a raider can take from you extremely easy if you started late on the server. Problems I can see with the XP system
Joining a server even one week late means you are too far behind to enjoy the wipe
Getting raided on a server and moving is not possible due to the point above
60 hours to get a metal facemask to survive an extra bullet to the head, okay
The "dramatic" feeling of Rust and the overall excitement of discovering something random each new wipe was nice, which is the opposite of the XP system
Grind and grind to get a weapon so you can defend yourself during a grind
Now I speak for myself and my group on this. None of us like the XP system and we have all logged 2k hours on record each. Give or take 400ish. Getting raided on one server and building back up is almost as difficult as going to a new server and fighting AK's with bows. Atleast with the BP system we had a CHANCE of getting an AKBP and a CHANCE of defending ourselves against those who are already level 34+.
Nonetheless, the wipes are too similar with the XP system. It's the same every wipe. Go smack a tree or a barrel and somehow "learn" how to make explosives. It doesn't fit the feel of rust or make any sense. Blueprints actually tied the game together fairly well. They just needed more tweaking. As for the game dying because of XP. I've seen it. Those who say they haven't are lyin right out their poop chute. I have noticed a large decline in players recently.

When I first played Rust, I was like... WOW.
The graphics are nice, a few graphics bugs but hey its an alpha, so no biggie.
Leveling is cool. If you die, you get to keep your skill levels, your unlocks etc, just your character loses everything he/she has on him/her.
Also, you can set respawn points to get back to your base once you die. Cool!
So while I died a few times, being killed by wolves and bears, trying to figure stuff out, it was not in vain. Quickly I learned how it goes, and from there on, dying was becoming way more difficult.
But here is the problem. There are no challenges. If you play PvP, yea, the other players are the challenge. But it ain't fun from what I've read in the reviews so I went straight to PvE.
Well, obtaining food is easy, ressources too. So teching up is basically grinding. Which is not bad in itself. The problem is, there is nothing to fear. Wolves are easily defeated with relatively basic equipment, bears too, which leaves NOTHING else that could be a challange.
Dear developers... WHY?????
The game in itself is great, but its just sort of a foundation with no building on it. Well, what do I mean by that?
There are no threats. This game would be PERFECT for a zombie scenario. Spawn areas with no or few zombies. More zombies in the rest of the map. Zombie migrations to survive by defending or running away. (walking dead challenges...)
Wolves could come in packs, too. Hungry, dangerous dogs. Big lizards. Snakes...... Boars could fight back, at least when they have newborns. Agressive single Elephants that damage what ever they want. Whales, sharks that make passing water difficult. There could be illnesses. Monsters of any kind. etc...
I'd have a thousand more ideas...
But nothing. just nothing. *sigh* So, in my view, the game is great, but it lacks crucial content.
I already can feel people telling me to go PvP, but well, thanks, but no thanks. Joining on a sever where everyone has a time advantage on me? No thanks. Without any allies, getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥killed (yea my character is female, thanks rust) until I leveled up enough to stand a slight chance? No thanks.
So my verdict:
Great game, but lacks crucial content to keep me playing PvE, wrong PvP concept to make me wanna play it. So not great enough to recommend.

Similar to the TV show 'Lost', after playing Rust for a while it's clear the developers have no idea what the final iteration of the game will look like. First the blueprint system was removed and was replaced by the XP system, then it was put back in again alongside the XP. There are frequent tweaks here and there, new items and places to explore.
On the one hand you could say the devs are listening to the players and changing the game accordingly, on the other you could question whether or not they have a clue about where Rust is going, and what it'll finally look like. The game is still in Alpha - and that doesn't look like changing any time soon. There are some performance issues - I have a GTX 970 and experience the most horrendous frame rate drops from time to time.
Despite all these issues though, Rust is a brilliant game. It's raw, terrifying, exhilarating, frustrating and down right annoying all at the same time. The community at times can be awful - think ten year olds who kill on sight when you've just started. But if you find a good server, get a friend or two; you will have an enormous amount of fun.

This is a re-written review, concentrating on the recent changes in Rust. This game is currently not recommended. Some time ago I had a positive review, which is rare for an Early Access to get a thumbs-up from me.
The new XP system has made this game a huge grind and time consuming. I played loads of it on my week off, but I did not feel rewarded for it. It is a MINDLESS grind right now. I completely do NOT recommend it in its current state. You spend a lot of time into gaining levels and get extremely little in return. No thank you - if anyone thinks this is fair, please do re-evaluate your time and think if it could be spent more useful (even in gaming), because it can.
Facepunch, I do not think that XP system is a complete disaster, therefore there are three ways Rust can become playable again:
1)You go back to Blueprint system - a boring move and it will still consume some hours from players to get better gear, but there are at least chances to get cool stuff early on and working together actually PAYS OFF.
2)You boost the rate of the XP gain around 5 times. I have to spend more than 3 hours to get a metal hatchet/Waterpipe (W-pipe available earlier from the get go)?!? That is stupid and does not balance anything, only consume our time!
3)A friend of mine had an idea that the first 10 levels are available to you from the beginning. There isn't anything extreme there - some clothes, basic gear, primitive weapons. And the remaining level gaining rate is being boosted 1,5x or 2x. People get stuff earlier, but it is better than spending 6 hours and maybe getting something that you can actually use for more advanced farming and ancient-method killing, which is bullcr@p!!!
Thanks to anyone who might or might not have read this. I will be waiting for changes to occur and if anything positive comes out, my review will adapt as well.

(Ok I'm changing this review for the better.  Don't be fooled by my hours because I have over 17 hours offline.)
After not having internet for a week I decided to go back to Undertale because I was bored. This was the best decision I've made this summer.  Undertale is one of my new favourite games because of it's humour, art style, and storyline.
If you're the kind of guy (or girl) who likes dumb AND witty humour everything in this game will make you smile.  There are jokes where it flat out tells you what's funny and then there are jokes that you have to really look closely at to understand.  There are even jokes stretched out across different story branches but I won't spoil them for you!
The art style is kind of hard to pin point exactly, some scenes remind me of an old DOS game but others are just plain SNES or NES style pixel art.  It's a really pleasing game to look at.  From the detailed battle sprites to the scenery and landscapes nothing goes un-noticed, for the exception of small items in the world like in the Junkyard.  Never the less it's all well done, big or small.
Next up I'm going to talk about the storylines, there are 3 main plot lines in Undertale.  The most popular being the Pacifist Route in which you spare every creature you encounter, I did this route first and you should too as it really ties together the story in a feel good way.  Next is the Genocide Route where you do the exact opposite of the Pacifist Route, KILL EVERYTHING.  When I say everything I mean EVERYTHING, every single damn monster you encounter?  Kill it.  This route isn't for the faint of heart and if you've grown attached to the characters in the story, well then prepare your♥♥♥♥♥♥for a bumpy un-lubed anal♥♥♥♥♥♥of emotions and feelings.  Also the Genocide Route has the hardest boss fights ever so ♥♥♥♥ that.  Last but not least is the Neutral Route.  In this route you can really do whatever you want, there aren't a lot of rules.  Want to kill a particular character you don't like?  Go ahead, you're not evil but you aren't great either.  Mercy and Fight can be used equally in this route and will give you an appropriate ending depending on who you have killed/spared and who you haven't.  For any new players the Neutral Ending will be the first ending you get in Undertale on your first playthrough no matter what, doesn't matter if you kill everything or spare everything you're going to get a neutral ending.
Obviously the story is the biggest part to this game as evident by my significantly larger paragraph than the others I wrote.  But that's just because there's more to talk about and more to describe in that catagory.  This game is really well done and is obvious why it gained such a cult following so fast.
(TL;DR The art is good. The humour is good.  The story is good.  Go play it.  Also it has a good soundtrack.  Again go play it.)

Borderlands 2 is a quite nice game. I played it on Playstation 3 by the way, which is why I have very little playtime on PC. The artstyle suites the game well and gameplay is enjoyable enough.
What Borderlands 2 is more than anything is a great sequel to Borderlands 1 in many respects. Where Borderlands 1 had only desert environments and repetitive enemies, characters and colours, Bordelands 2 features desert, glacier, urban, tundra and plain environments, much more colour and variation in enemies and more distinct weapons. There is now more that defines gun brands and small aditions such as the 'badass rank' system are welcome.
The game's story is still really simple and does not hold up the game. There are some obvious plotholes regarding the beginning of the game and most things that happen during the story are predictable. The game's strength is in the gamplay aspect.
Mostly thanks to its cell-shaded artstyle, this game is not demanding at all. It is nice that this game makes good use of Nvidea PhysX, which makes the battles a lot more hectic. Another bad thing which I exclusively found in the PC version was that DLC related locations in the game world and DLC characters were all shown, but whenever you tried to select any one of them the game would switch to the steam store page of the DLC that this location or character is unlocked with. This is frustrating because it constantly points out the things you don't have and can be considered annoying advertising within the game. The PhysX makes the PC port good enough.
So, personally I found this game to be quite fun, but that surely won't apply to everyone.

Rust has lost it's vibe.
It's completely gone.
The abundance of cheaters (seeing 9 players banned within 5 minutes is worrysome). To admin abuse just because they have the willpower to do so. Not to mention the inevitible grind that is still the XP system. I'll be addressing this all one by one below:
The abundance of cheaters
Alright. So yeah, official servers ♥♥♥♥in blow donkey dongs when it comes to legitimate players. We all know to stay far away from that grey area of the server browser. Although community and modded are not too far off from themselves. You think only private accounts and people with low hours are cheating? Think again. Hours mean absolutely nothing; oh yeah, that player also was level 86 on Steam. It's absolutely TOO easy to cheat in this game. EAC does a horrible job of automatically detecting cheats, since you can technically ESP for 8 hours and never ESP again and NEVER be banned. In all honesty; ditch EAC. Get BattlEye. OR make a more intrusive anticheat. Yes, privacy is key but what about this concept that was made for a game emulator I was a "dev" for a few years ago...
"When the users accept the ToS of the game; in section X,x. It states that the game developer's anti-cheat will take preiodic screenshots of the GAME WINDOW only while the player is playing. When a player logs a kill or other large statistic based information, a screenshot is taken and uploaded to a cloud server where the developers can easily assess if such player is ESPing or cheating at all, thus resulting in an account termination."
This system would be a little intrusive. ALTHOUGH, it would not be able to take a screenshot of anything BUT your game window. Even if you had layered windows above the game window; it would not show any of that. Just like OBS's and other game capture apps, it can constrain to a specific window rather than an entire screen.
Aside from that being a possible way of getting the cheating situation in rust taken care of. Cheating in rust has blown out the fun my group and I used to have. We log in. Work our asses off hitting nodes, picking up♥♥♥♥♥♥on the ground, breaking barrels in order to make a god damn pistol, to have it taken from us by someone who is using an external program.
Admin abuse
This goes without saying. It happens here and there, although I don't think that the server admins should be dictators over their servers. After all FP makes the game that allows them to host servers. FP should have some sort of final say in how they can handle their servers. (Unfair bans, cheat accusations without reason or evidence, ect)
"The Grind"
Boy, bet you thought you would never hear that again. Too bad. The linear system of XP doesn't make any sense for rust. Neither do the temporary blueprints. It's still something a raider can take from you extremely easy if you started late on the server. Problems I can see with the XP system
Joining a server even one week late means you are too far behind to enjoy the wipe
Getting raided on a server and moving is not possible due to the point above
60 hours to get a metal facemask to survive an extra bullet to the head, okay
The "dramatic" feeling of Rust and the overall excitement of discovering something random each new wipe was nice, which is the opposite of the XP system
Grind and grind to get a weapon so you can defend yourself during a grind
Now I speak for myself and my group on this. None of us like the XP system and we have all logged 2k hours on record each. Give or take 400ish. Getting raided on one server and building back up is almost as difficult as going to a new server and fighting AK's with bows. Atleast with the BP system we had a CHANCE of getting an AKBP and a CHANCE of defending ourselves against those who are already level 34+.
Nonetheless, the wipes are too similar with the XP system. It's the same every wipe. Go smack a tree or a barrel and somehow "learn" how to make explosives. It doesn't fit the feel of rust or make any sense. Blueprints actually tied the game together fairly well. They just needed more tweaking. As for the game dying because of XP. I've seen it. Those who say they haven't are lyin right out their poop chute. I have noticed a large decline in players recently.

When I first played Rust, I was like... WOW.
The graphics are nice, a few graphics bugs but hey its an alpha, so no biggie.
Leveling is cool. If you die, you get to keep your skill levels, your unlocks etc, just your character loses everything he/she has on him/her.
Also, you can set respawn points to get back to your base once you die. Cool!
So while I died a few times, being killed by wolves and bears, trying to figure stuff out, it was not in vain. Quickly I learned how it goes, and from there on, dying was becoming way more difficult.
But here is the problem. There are no challenges. If you play PvP, yea, the other players are the challenge. But it ain't fun from what I've read in the reviews so I went straight to PvE.
Well, obtaining food is easy, ressources too. So teching up is basically grinding. Which is not bad in itself. The problem is, there is nothing to fear. Wolves are easily defeated with relatively basic equipment, bears too, which leaves NOTHING else that could be a challange.
Dear developers... WHY?????
The game in itself is great, but its just sort of a foundation with no building on it. Well, what do I mean by that?
There are no threats. This game would be PERFECT for a zombie scenario. Spawn areas with no or few zombies. More zombies in the rest of the map. Zombie migrations to survive by defending or running away. (walking dead challenges...)
Wolves could come in packs, too. Hungry, dangerous dogs. Big lizards. Snakes...... Boars could fight back, at least when they have newborns. Agressive single Elephants that damage what ever they want. Whales, sharks that make passing water difficult. There could be illnesses. Monsters of any kind. etc...
I'd have a thousand more ideas...
But nothing. just nothing. *sigh* So, in my view, the game is great, but it lacks crucial content.
I already can feel people telling me to go PvP, but well, thanks, but no thanks. Joining on a sever where everyone has a time advantage on me? No thanks. Without any allies, getting♥♥♥♥♥♥♥killed (yea my character is female, thanks rust) until I leveled up enough to stand a slight chance? No thanks.
So my verdict:
Great game, but lacks crucial content to keep me playing PvE, wrong PvP concept to make me wanna play it. So not great enough to recommend.

I'm just going to be straight forward and say that DayZ is a pretty good game. It's one of the better open world survival games that one can sit down, play for a couple hours, and then pick it up again the next day. Playing with friends makes for an even better experience. Yeah, it has its fair share of bugs, but that's what you can expect from an early access game. Did both your legs break because you opened a door? That's okay because the game is still in alpha.
That being said, the development of DayZ is ridiculously slow. Waiting time between updates can be several months to three quarters of a year. Whoever says that DayZ has "weekly updates" is just flat out wrong. There's no debate there. The developers have serious issues with adding new content before the older bugs are fixed. Vehicle spawns are almost non-existant but that's okay because the likely hood of being shot while driving a vehicle is probably close to 90%. It's like team deathmatch with a handful of zombies thrown into the mix. Considering that the crafting system is basic and there's no real point to farming yet, I don't really blame people for going around killing fresh spawns on sight. There isn't a whole lot to do after you get geared up.
On top of that, the character you play as is one of the most whiny little children I have ever seen. It's aggravating when the player character constantly complains "I'm hungry"/"I'm thirsty"/"I'm cold"/"My feet hurt"/"My face is melting because I sat by the fire for 5 seconds". Yes. We get it. I'll feed your the moment I find a can of bacon.
It's a bit of fun for a couple hours but definitely not worth the forty dollars. I wouldn't pay more than ten dollars for this game seeing as the developers seem to have taken everyone's money and run away with it. Of course, if you're dead set on buying the game, by all means fill your boots. I just hope I'll still be alive to see my great grandchildren play the beta.

As I died screaming between a wolf’s jaws, collapsing in the snow that dusts the top of the mountains while listening to it gnaw through virtual flesh, I had a realization: survival games are fun as long as they are about the threat of death.
Death itself is underwhelming: a gateway to an ever-increasing set of chores and tasks that you must repeat in order to recover your lost progress. Inevitably, the process eventually repeats, and the to-do list gets longer and less fulfilling, which sounds a little bit like hell and a little bit like a parable about the human condition. Rust [official site], the multiplayer survival game from Facepunch Studios, seems comfortable with both analogies.
If you’re not familiar with Rust, or if you only know it as the Survival Game with Lots of♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ it’s actually a weirder and more interesting game than it first appears to be. You wake up in a strange landscape, cold and naked with nothing but a torch and a rock to your name. Then, after a few minutes of trial-and-error exploration of Rust’s wilderness, you can start building crude tools out of loose materials, then using those tools to harvest more material to build better tools, etc. The tech tree runs from Stone Age materials all the way to automatic weapons and heavy body armor. Survival in Rust can become a fairly comfortable survivalist’s fantasy if you stay alive long enough… but death comes swiftly and with little warning.
Rust is the closest I’ve ever come in a videogame to feeling like I was living in The Most Dangerous Game or The Ruum or any of those pursuit-and-survival classics that students read every year in middle school. Every player you meet is potentially a mortal threat or a potential ally, which is common enough for a survival multiplayer game, except that Rust also functions a bit like a social experiment. It’s like someone gave Stanley Milgram a private island, a private army, and an endless supply of willing prisoners and said, “See what you can make happen here.”
Every few hours in-game, a cargo plane flies overhead and makes a supply drop that draws players from all around the map into a highly charged, dangerous confrontation over the mere possibility of treasure. There might be nothing very special in those supply drops… but there might be advanced gear that would be difficult or impossible to craft yourself.
Alternately, an attack helicopter sometimes appears to hunt down and kill any players that it manages to see, and its appearance is as chilling as it is unexplained. It’s existence is contrived, like everything else in Rust’s deserted, semi-industrial wilderness, but still unsettling. It’s something that forces me to consider what Rust looks like from above, as a bunch of half-naked, violent, and greedy people try and create peace and security for themselves in a setting of profound anarchy.
But eventually, you die. You didn’t hide quickly enough and the helicopter mows you down in the open, or you were too busy stalking a deer to notice someone has been stalking you for the past few minutes and literally all you hear is a shot before the world turns red and you drop to the ground. Or you die in the dumbest of ways: taking a shortcut over a mountain, and a wolf walks up a near-vertical cliff face to surprise you at the exact moment that you don’t have any of your good weapons equipped in the hotbar. A few impotent stabs with your spear later (a weapon with the worst hit-detection in the game) and you’re back to square one: naked and alone.
Well, almost. Rust is also a game about securing property rights in an anarchic world, a John Locke essay with a flintlock blunderbuss and magical crafting items. When you die, you have the option to wake-up again at a sleeping bag you’ve left somewhere out in the world. Ideally, inside a home you’ve built next to a supply cache and behind a locked door. With a little foresight, you can leave an inheritance for yourself of decent tools, materials, and weapons so that you can get right back to your survival saga of living by your wits and slowly becoming predator rather than prey in this hostile world. If you build a tool cabinet inside, then nobody else can construct anything near your stuff, letting you securely lay claim to territory. After a couple deaths, I was building two of everything and jamming my hilltop fortress full of weapons and material.
But some loss of progress is inevitable, and if you get on a bad run, that little rainy-day fund will get depleted and eventually you’re back to being alone with a rock and virtual genitalia (which will, of course, be the name of my forthcoming memoir). At that point, Rust becomes a far less joyous and evocative experience and something a lot more like shift-work. The first time you hunt a half-dozen animals and smelt enough metal ore to create advanced weapons and armor you feel like Ash in Army of Darkness. The fourth time you do it, and you’re chopping down yet another tree with a stone hatchet, or chasing a deer around some rocks? It starts to feel like survival might be a punishment rather than a goal.
The weird thing is, I think that’s contributed to a strange sense of community on some servers. A year or so ago, Rust sounded like a game full of half-naked sociopaths killing each other in front of a pig’s skull. Now, while there’s still a heavy air of distrust that hangs over the proceedings, there’s also more respect and cooperation. Neighbors ask to borrow tools to get back on their feet. Warnings go out regarding particularly violent players who are causing trouble. It’s not that Rust is turning into some kind of utopian experiment, but it’s definitely less the anarchy that it was in the past. Live, and let live seems to be the rule in Rust, unless someone has REALLY nice stuff and you have a clear shot.
There is an irony to success in Rust: the better you are at surviving, the less that will actually happen. Just before writing this, I spent a couple hours upgrading my building, building new weapons and ammunition, and collecting extra supplies to keep behind a new electronic lock. I have windows that afford me a view in every direction, and a kind of parapet on the third floor from which I can shoot down at anyone who starts trying to batter down my walls. I spend most of my time hiding from other players now, or hiding from the helicopter, or watching out for bears and wolves. When I think about a typical session of Rust, it’s a catalog of things that didn’t happen, of risks successfully avoided and bets wisely hedged. The brilliance of Rust is that it demands a lot of suspenseful work, attention, and planning to make sure that it remains uneventful.

Undertale is a lot more than meets the eye.
I was expecting a simple, lighthearted and quick game. I wasn't expecting a beautiful journey that tore my heart out and put it back together, or characters that had me falling in love over and over again. I certainly wasn't expecting such an emotional experience.
The gameplay mechanics are incredibly clever. I truly enjoyed how each encounter was made unique through the ACT selection. By figuring out how to spare a monster, you get to know the monster as well.
The writing is brilliant. The overarching story (the general one) is one that we've heard before - the dominant, more powerful race wins a war and it leads to the oppression of the other race. However, it's the way Undertale is executed that sets it above other games and stories with similar themes. The dialogue is quirky, engaging and at times very thought-provoking (I'm looking at you, Sans...). Once again, each encounter tells a little story of its own, whether it's Shyren enjoying the spotlight or Napstablook making a hat out of tears, and these little stories not only make the world a richer place to play in, but also grow your own identity within the playable character. Your actions become a part of them, and thus the character become a reflection of yourself (AKA it's a choice-based game, and you really feel it).
Many may not agree with me when I say that I love the artwork. At many times it is simple. The playable character sprite certainly is. But it does what it needs to do, and every so often (*coughcough* Waterfall *coughcough*) it whips out a view so spectacular you WISH SCREENCAPS WOULD WORK SHEESH.
I don't think I need to go into the score. Youtube has enough evidence that the Undertale OST has left its mark. I got the album and it's all I listen to, but it still brings me back to the countless unforgettable moments that made me love the game in the first place. When I listen to the music, I really feel like I am back in the Underground.
With everything I've mentioned it might be surprising to hear that I was hesitant in purchasing this game. I thought it would be overrated because there was so much hype surrounding it. After 30 hours of gameplay, I think it's safe to say I was proven wrong. Undertale deserves every bit of hype it's gotten and every cent it's made. This game blew me away. Undertale has my highest recommendation and is one of my favourite games to date.
