When I bought this game, I was completely aware of the acclaim this title has. However, when I was starting my first playthrough, I set forth with an ounce of scepticism, thinking this would turn out to be yet another example of bandwagon-praise-train to downtown Circlejerksville of a game.
Having completed the 'Neutral' to 'True pacifist' ending, I'm glad to say that I was woefully wrong.
You can find out more below:
Gameplay in Undertale is essentially divided between two screens: Overworld and combat screen.
is literally the world that you can explore and progress through: This is where you meet new characters, solve puzzles, progress and whatnot.
The areas themselves are varied and interesting, and although most of them don't really blow you away with beauty, they still serve their purpose quite well. Majority of the puzzles are more a slight hindrance than an actual brainteaser (one of the characters actually even holds your hand as they literally walk you through one of the tu-toriel *ba-dum-ts* rooms (you'll get it later)).
The combat screen let's you confront the monsters, and fight or spare them. The most barebones version of this is as follows: First, you choose and action (like attack, spare, consume and item, etc.) and you defend yourself against a
. This is nicely balanced, and if you can't beat an enemy, you can only blame yourself.

Let me start this out by saying that this is an excellent game. It comes from an excellent mod, it's probably one of the more in-depth "survival games," out there, and the only real problem that it seems to have is that unless you've got the SuperComputer 5000 from Futuresoft, you'll have to run this on minimum settings.
That being said (That I do legitimately like this game/concept), I cannot recommend it to anyone. I left this game in the dust maybe about 6 months ago, and upon returning, all the core problems of being in "alpha state," are still there. Teleporting zombies. Bleeding out for no reason. Crumbly loot tables. Desync and horrible lag for no apparent reason. I could go on for ages about the community being absolutely cancer, and how much this game has taught me to hate and avoid people IRL and in-game, but I won't - that's not the developer's problem.
The problem is that the dev's of this game have made upwards of TWELVE MILLION DOLLARS (not even COUNTING crowdsourcing funds!) and haven't done a THING with it. Oh, certainly, they've added features and items. You can't deny that - I totally agree! There's more items and ways to craft and do unique things then more or less any game that I've seen that *isn't about* crafting items. The sheer amount of loot and weapons is incredible, and it's all modelled brilliantly!
The problem is that it's been nearly 3 years, and I still have to hold my breath and pray when I go down a ladder, because there's a *high* probability that I'll just clip through it and fall to my death. The problem is that I've got an i7 CPU, 16GB of RAM, and a 4GB graphics card - all water cooled - and it makes my machine scream for mercy. The problem is that I can't even safely hide from the main enemies of the game because they can GO THROUGH WALLS. The problem is that the mere act of logging out of a server has about an 80% chance of erasing all the progress I've made for the day!
When this is finally released (sometime in the 2020's), I'd tell you to make it a first-day purchase. I can see the potential; I can practically *taste* the potential from this title. The dev's are obviously talented and know what they're doing in terms of game feel and mechanics. Till then? Save your money. These dudes have made more then enough to make a AA game - much less what amounts to a standalone game that's been in constant development for three years that still somehow has less meat then their mod of the same name.
TL;DR
Don't buy now, wait till release (if it ever gets released).

There are a lot of negative reviews on here, so I feel like I should chime in.
Most people seem to be complaining about what Rust isn't, not what Rust is. And they're generally making these points by comparing "old Rust" to the current version. Although I bought this game over a year ago, I didn't actually try playing it until recently...which means that I don't have the "old system" to compare it to.
The only thing I can actually review is the version of the game that you're looking at buying. Not the old game, not some non-existant "perfect version of Rust," just the actual game that you can buy and play right now.
In my opinion, the game is terrific. I've purchased a dozen other titles in similar genres and I always come back to Rust. The building system is the most interesting I've found so far (no stupid blocks) and no gameplay experience is ever the same. I'm assuming the people who are complaining about the XP system are the ones who want to play this game like it's Counterstrike; they want to get to endgame ASAP, unlock the best weapons, and go blow stuff up. I'm perfectly fine with the progression of the XP system. Sure, if I'm playing solo, there's little chance that I can make a giant fortress that no one will raid. But you can use -strategy- to work with the mechanics of the game rather than trying to be a one-man clan. There's nothing stopping you from building tiny hidden bases that don't compel everyone on the server to murder you. Or you can skip bases altogether by burying hidden stashes in the ground. There are options...if you're willing to adapt to the situation.
TL;DR - I'm glad I didn't listen to all these naysayers. This is one of the most addictive games I've ever played.

Remember how you always dreamed of the perfect RPG? With a heart-breaking,heart-warming and heart-crushing story all at the same time? With characters that you love more than your real family? With hilarious jokes? The best sound track EVER? And even then, it still looks like it was made in 1995?
This is that game.
The game has a battle system that allows you to either FIGHT, ACT, ITEM or MERCY. FIGHT is self-explanatory. ACT: Different hostile enemies have different "Actions", some allowing enemies to be sparable, or some that effect the battle in any way. ITEM: Use an item to revive your health or equip armour as protection. And MERCY: attempt to spare (or sometimes flee from) an enemy to avoid attacking them.
Undertale has 3 main routes: Neutral, True Pacifist and Genocide. Neutral: Kill or Spare enemies at your free choice.
True Pacifist (can only be obtained after a pacifist neutral run, where no enemies are killed): Befriend characters and kill nobody. And Genocide: Kill everything that moves. Show no mercy.
Each route feels like a different game. Undertale is anything but linear. Any and Every choice you make can and will affect how you play the game. So be careful.
If you hate video games: play this. If you live in your mother's basement playing League of Legends all night: play this (and get a life, but play this first). And if you're homeless: well, you should probably try to get a job before playing this. Sell the dog, the house, your grandma, etc. This deserves all the money you have.

So where do I even start with this game? Wow, I don't think that words can even do justice to the way this game made me feel. Undertale succeeds not only as a video game, but at connecting on an emotional level more so than any other game I have ever played. Undertale is the definition of a game that is much greater than the sum of it's parts. Undertale is a rare situation when an idea is executed with such love and such skill along with every piece coming together in such an excellent way. From the characters, to the music, to the story and gameplay itself, everything stands out as being absolutely fantastic, something that I think rarely ever happens in gaming. Combine this with Toby Fox's incredible writing and world building, and you get Undertale. Undertale creates a world that keeps you engaged constantly, be it the humor, it's lovable characters, or maybe just the mysteries surrounding the game.
It's really hard not to become invested in the incredible world. Toby marries the concepts of storytelling and gameplay in interesting ways the entire way through, creating countless memorable battles and moments, such as the battle with Papyrus, where earlier expectations are shut down and an entire new experience is created. Couple these great moments with the morally ambiguous decisions that don't hold your hand and tell you what's right, but will make you question the way you feel about Undertale and maybe even life in general. The themes of friendship and compassion ring true throughout the entire game, and lead to some truly great emotional moments if you let yourself become invested. Topping off everything, the game has multiple different paths the player can choose to go down, and some of them having very severe consequences if the player decides to do so. The game is also absolutely full of secrets that you can easily miss, but they are that much more satisfying to find because of it. While being a linear RPG, these secrets, along with many changes that occur from playthrough to playthrough, keep the game highly replayable, even with it's short 6 hour length.
It's clear that Toby Fox poured his heart and soul into this game, and I believe it stands as one of gaming's great achievements, and because of this, it is a game that you would be doing yourself a great disservice not to experience for yourself.

there could be more things added to make it even more enjoyable... more PVE side, More weapons, Building types ETC... but as it is, you can still get many hours of enjoyable playtime out of it, and many more with friends!
i have read some reviews about the new XP system being bad and "ruining" the game... i dont see any reason to why this would be true. its changed, its made the game more difficult to gather gear, you no longer start up a game. fine a c4 blueprint, weapons and raid some guys/girls base and youre already ahead of everyone else. its takes the easy, lazy players out of the game and leaves dedicated players. Cons:
Easy raiding (i see this as a con)

Overall an amazing game, one i always come back for more.

Undertale is a game best experienced, and any attempt to describe the game beyond its basic functions and premise spoils what is a truly wonderful experience. So, it's a retro-style 2D turn-based RPG about a small child who falls underground into the kingdom of monsters, and must find a way to leave.
Nothing inherently special in that description. But Undertale is especially special. You haven't played anything like it.
It is by far the most charming game you'll ever play, filled to the brim with lovable and endearing characters, a fascinating, engaging world, and a story that transcends the computer screen.
Though the battles may seem straightforward enough, don't be fooled into taking the easy way out, and simply attack and kill your enemies; indeed, a more fulfilling experience is to be had through pacifism. Each fight suddenly becomes a puzzle, rather than a violent engagement, and they are equal parts amusing and interesting. Such nonviolent options can be, at times, vague and frustrating-- especially during boss fights-- but are more often than not simply a matter of thinking outside of the box, and soon enough you'll find yourself slipping into the mental state required by the game with little difficulty.
If there is one complaint about the game, it's that any combat, be it violent or pacifistic, requires you to engage in a "bullet-hell" sort of minigame, and this is where all difficulties with the game lie. To the game's credit, they're tense and often funny, but can be downright infuriating, especially if you're taking a violent route through the game.
If nothing else, play Undertale because all your friends and half the Internet can't shut up about it. But really, play Undertale because it will make a slight, wonderful change to your life. You will close this game feeling as if your life has improved slightly, simply having played the game.
That is, until you start a Genocide run.

Undertale is a game best experienced, and any attempt to describe the game beyond its basic functions and premise spoils what is a truly wonderful experience. So, it's a retro-style 2D turn-based RPG about a small child who falls underground into the kingdom of monsters, and must find a way to leave.
Nothing inherently special in that description. But Undertale is especially special. You haven't played anything like it.
It is by far the most charming game you'll ever play, filled to the brim with lovable and endearing characters, a fascinating, engaging world, and a story that transcends the computer screen.
Though the battles may seem straightforward enough, don't be fooled into taking the easy way out, and simply attack and kill your enemies; indeed, a more fulfilling experience is to be had through pacifism. Each fight suddenly becomes a puzzle, rather than a violent engagement, and they are equal parts amusing and interesting. Such nonviolent options can be, at times, vague and frustrating-- especially during boss fights-- but are more often than not simply a matter of thinking outside of the box, and soon enough you'll find yourself slipping into the mental state required by the game with little difficulty.
If there is one complaint about the game, it's that any combat, be it violent or pacifistic, requires you to engage in a "bullet-hell" sort of minigame, and this is where all difficulties with the game lie. To the game's credit, they're tense and often funny, but can be downright infuriating, especially if you're taking a violent route through the game.
If nothing else, play Undertale because all your friends and half the Internet can't shut up about it. But really, play Undertale because it will make a slight, wonderful change to your life. You will close this game feeling as if your life has improved slightly, simply having played the game.
That is, until you start a Genocide run.

This game is not for the faint of heart. It is ruthless, brutal, and above all, very unforgiving. You will throw your keyboard at the wall and slam your headset on the desk. That's just how terrible this game can be. However, that being said, I can't recommend it enough to anyone who asks me. There are ways to get around the clan problems. Play on small community made servers or solo/duo/trio servers until you get a feel for the game. You will farm a lot, but it all depends on what kind of gamestyle you enjoy playing. I see lots of negative reviews from people with thousands of hours, and granted, while I used to be one of them, I don't quite understand them. I have had some of the most infurating moments playing this game, and my friends can't vouch enough to the number of times I have yelled at them, and they back at me. You will die, at lot. You will be farming for hours, and lose it all in minutes. You will finally get gear, only to run into people with better gear. However, every now and then you will do the same to someone else, and it feels oh so sweet. You will somehow win a rock fight with a geared man and he will be carrying an entire base worth of materials on him. It makes the game worth it.
The developers are constantly updating on a weekly basis, and they listen to feedback from the community and come of with creative ways to make the game more fun to play. If I had a complaint, it would be the night cycles. Just get rid of them please? Those who own NVIDIA graphics cards will be able to manually adjust the gamma from the NVIDIA control panel and see in game. AMD users like myself will not have this luxery. Night time is used to craft, and unless you take advantage of what is, in my mind, an unfair move in the game, you will spend 20 minutes afk in your house crafting or doing nothing, when you're trying to play a game and relax. Nearly the entire community has been complaining about nighttime, and please developers, if you see this, just shorten it or remove it completely. Nobody is going to care about the associated realism, because I think we are past that.
Overall, a great game, if you're new to it I recommend watching many of the diverse rust youtubers there are to get a good feel for building and early game rust before you dive straight in. There is NO TUTORIAL, and asking fresh spawns or other players will ALWAYS (for safe measure) result in death.

I want to like DayZ so much. I spent countless hours with the Arma 2 mod, dealing with the clunky design and perplexing systems because they were obvious concessions that had to be made when creating a mod. But DayZ has been out on Steam Early Access for over 2 years, and I can't shake the feeling that the team behind it just doesn't know what its doing.
Many of the bugs and design issues that came packed with the game at launch are still in place. Zombies still rubberband around buildings and walk through doors. The awful desync issues that plagued the Arma 2 mod are also in the standalone version, and they still plague the servers 2 years later. The new loot engine is great, I will give them that, but it feels too little too late.
Dean "Rocket" Hall claimed he would not depart Bohemia until DayZ entered beta at the minumum, but he has now been gone for over a year with no end to the alpha in sight. What does that tell us about his confidence in this product, and the development team behind it? DayZ may be a financial success, but as a game, it is a failure.

Rust is a survival game that can be played in whatever way you want to play it, which in it's self is an achievement. The game has no clear story or set goal for you to reach so when you start out you can be a little bit lost, but after a few hours of playing you soon get to grips with how the mechanics work and what you have to do, the recent arrival of the XP system shook up the game and how it is played for many people but I would argue that this makes the game much friendlier for new players which is a positive for me as I would really love to see the game continue to grow. As i've played the game i've noticed that groups have the advantage over solo players which is as it should be because as the saying goes "There's strength in numbers" but I do think that solo players should be given a fighting chance of surviving or even winning a fight against a group of players, even if the liklihood of that win is very low.
The Positives (In my opinion):
-The game is very fun and has a good replay value as every wipe you start again.
-There is always the factor of wanting to come on to see how your base is or go and get some loot so you always seem to want to play more and more.
-The community is overall pretty decent but you have to remember the #1 Rule of rust which is 'Trust Nobody', which I have found to be an accurate way to go about things.
-System that rewards prolonged periods of play so playing the game for a long while will put you at an advantage over people who don't. This gives you a sense of achievement.
-Relatively cheap.
-Thousands of servers.
-Survival game with a strong theme of PVP.
-Very easy and intuitive buliding mechanics that make you think.
-Fun and Challenging combat ranged and hand to hand.
-Very regularly updated with new gear and general updates to FPS and such to enjoy nearly every week.
-Entertaining YouTube community featuring the likes of RhinoCrunch, Faceless, Ser Winter, Vertiigo and more.
-Fun player to player interactions.
-Great anti hacking features.
-Making friends is very easy.
The Negatives (again in my opinion):
-Clans have a massive advantage over the solo player meaning that you are likely to be steamrolled by groups on busy servers very regularly.
-The game is relatively demanding on your PC.
-The game can get a little repetitive if you don't mix up how you play.
-Some people in the community are out to ruin others experience, but this exists in every multiplayer game.
-Hackers and aim botters are still existent even with the anti hacking features.
-Pookie Bear is too rare.
This is my first review on a game and I probably wrote this horribly but gimme a break.

Compared to other reviews, my play time is incredibly short. I have learned in that short time that this game absolutely hates small groups/solo players, which I fall under.
This game suffers from the Survival genre's tropes of people killing you on sight. People with guns killing people without guns for no reason, even if you insist that you mean no harm. fresh spawns often mindlessly kill one another just to get a tiny leg up just to get brained themselves a minute later.
I wish the dev team would implement a system that penalize late game players for murdering a fresh spawn. Someone without a base that has a cabinate and a sleeping bag within, or a wanderer with a bow or adequate ranged weapon to defend themselves with. If you see a person with a gun advancing towards you the likely result will be death, even if they say they're friendly, they often want you to stay still so they can use less ammo to slaughter you.
The EXP system is a terrible idea for a server based game. All progression does not transfer from server to server even on official ones. Not to mention that admins will restart the entire server making everyone's progression start from square 1. This advantages people with big groups, due to the EXP system sharing amoungst friends/allies in close proximity to one another or shared tools.
The aggressive wild life are real♥♥♥♥♥♥kickers as well. Bears often appear out of no where and have almost no sound when chasing after you. You need the situational awareness of Widow Maker 24/7 if you don't want to be blindsided by a bear or wolf. Both bears and wolves will outpace you, so running is never the option and standing your ground against a bear or wolf, solo, is certain death for fresh spawns.
Edit: (playing beyond 17 hours)
I continued my playtime beyond 17 hours. I had decent fun talking to people while I collected resourses for a small house which too approximately 7 hours stright. Most of that time was spent dying to fellow players, the ones that would never speak to you, and looking for a location for said  house. I logged back in 20 hours later to find I have no sleeping bag and the kill message saying I was murdered by a weapon I stored away for an emergecy.
I get this game is still in EA. But 3 years is an unacceptible amount of time to be in perpetual beta. It is a lazy way to free a game from any criticism.

While many will be turned away from this game due to the fanbase surrounding it, I believe that should not matter when looking for a quality game. Undertale is, at the start, quite bland. The art style does not take full effect until later; many turn away just from the graphics alone, but trust me on this: Undertale is beautiful. The many ways you can choose to forge your path through the underground really makes it feel like it is truly YOU, not a character you are just controlling. The bosses and characters are all extremely creative, and, depending on the route you chose to go, lots of little life-lessons can be learned. The game does not always take itself too seriously, but, when it does, it drives a real message through.
Of course, Undertale wasn't the first game to have consequences and different routes, but the way it handled it was very unique. I have never played a game like Undertale, and I probably never will again. Undertale is full of easter eggs and references to other products and games, clearly being inspired by them, but the game doesn't feel like a copy or ripoff, it really is special. I highly recommend it for people who want a new experience that still manages to feel nostalgic.

In 2014 I played over a hundred hours of Rust, the version that is now considered 'Legacy'.  I enjoyed that game and thought it was well worth my dollar, despite its flaws.
But these days its a different game with some new flaws, but also the same old flaws.
I love not having any control over the look of my character.
I love starting the game naked with only a rock and a torch.
I love the crafting and XP system.
Your first few hours in Rust, which if your lucky are during the daytime, will be a little intense. You'll need to gather some wood from the many trees around.  Then you'll need some stone and if you're lucky there are some boulders nearby that you have harvest.  Now you have the materials to make a pickax and hatchet to replace your starting rock.  But now starts the hard part, food, clothing, shelter.  If your lucky there will be a pig nearby that you can kill, but often there will be nothing and you will have to search it out.  Once you start finding and killing animals you can start making clothes, remember you're completely naked when you start.  You also will want to gather more and more wood and stone so you can build a shelter.  You're going to need a place to store things when you go out exploring and looting.
A lot of that sounds like most games of this type, its a pretty standard method of getting your feet wet.  For my return to Rust I played up to level 10, to see how this new system feels.
My first life was taken almost as soon as it started by a bear who felt I was too close.
My second life went much better, I lasted almost thirty minutes before dying of starvation.
On my third life I made an attempt to find my last corpse, I don't know what the despawn timer for them is, I ran for maybe five minutes or more to get to the derelict power plant.  But failed to find/remember where I was when I died.  I did however manage to build a small shelter on a beach, where I left most of my things and went out hunting/exploring when the game crashed.
When I came back the next day I learned that I had been killed and got the pleasure of respawning.  But since I knew where my house was I simply ran naked across the map to the beach.  When I got there I found half my little house missing and my storage chests empty.  Such is the life in these games, so I trudged on. Gather, hunt, build.  I built a larger house and learned some new crafting recipes, and even learned how to turn my wood structure into stone.
Once again returning to the game I learned that while I was away I had been robbed of just about everything.  The only things left in my house was some charcoal and bone fragments.  I tried to see if I could get myself on my feet again, but I hadn't even a Rock for harvest with.  And while I had a crafting recipe for one it required a small amount of Stone, and I had no means to gather any...  So I swam as far into the ocean as I could before I drown.  Respawned and ran back to my house and repeated most the the prior days activities.
When I came back the next day it was the first time that I wasn't starting a step backwards.  I had ample food and clean water.  I had a lot of the various resources, except for stone.  Stone is almost as essential as wood but is far more difficult to gather.  You can chop any tree for wood, but you can't get stone from any rock.  There are certain rocks that spawn in the world that you get your various minerals from(sulfur, metal, high quality metal, and stone) and that's fine.  I should also be able to gather stone from the massive boulders that are all over the place, but no.  So as I traversed the wilds looking for the right boulders the game crashed.
And I haven't been back since.
Rust is not a bad game. Its good, its hard, and its unforgiving.  And its just like I said two years ago "unless you play Rust everyday, you'll have to start over every time". And that's just not what I'm looking for in a game.  I don't have the 4-5 hours of single sitting playtime to get myself into a safe place so I can walk away from the game for a day or two.  And I want to actually feel like I'm making progress.
For me there are other games in this genre that I'd rather play, but this might be your thing.
Also I did bludgeon someone to death on a beach with my rock, and then ate them. How many games let you do that?

I used to play Rust in 2013. This game was really nice, the base building was aight, whole hunting, looting, raiding bases it was great. Even when I played solo I was able to defend my base or raid others.
Now this game has LVL system and clans. You can't craft specific item, for instance a bow to defend yourself, you have to ♥♥♥♥ing grind through 30+ levels (it takes a lot of time) to unlock all recipes, then you have to grind for materials and finally craft items. When you spawn on the world you have a rock and a torch. You will see a lot of armored players with guns or even a freshspawned guy with bow (he has played this game already, before you) so you are going to die a lot of times, just to get the experience to craft items. Okay, even if that wasn't a big problem there is next one. Clans. It takes about 2-3 or more hours to gather all starting items and to build a small, wooden or stone base. After that you might want to take a break from this game and do something different. When you come back you will probably see that your house got destroyed, all your items are stolen and you might be killed or just left by raiders, just to disrespect you.
But if you didn't want to take a break and you want to continue playing soon you will see like 3-10+ players around your small house trying to get inside and rob you. You basically can't do anything in this game alone until you will join a clan. Even with a group of 2-3 people it's almost impossible to build a base and keep upgrading it, because always one clan will see you and will try to kill you and get all your items. This game doesn't require skill, as I said you can't reach anything without joining a clan. Of course you can play on low populated servers, like 5-10 people but is this fun, the map is really big and there would be a small chance to meet other player.
I understand that this is an Early Acces game but it looked very different when it came out, this is a team game, which isn't based on your skills, it just depends how many people is in your clan.

Group-oriented grind-fest.
If you try playing alone, you'll find yourself hitting trees and rocks for hours, only to get killed by some high-tier player with an AK-47. But don't worry, he can take all your loot, and the game will spawn you on the other side of the world, so any progress you've made is nullified, and you can once again enjoy the wonderful sound of a rock hitting a tree. What is that? It's the superbear. It goes through trees, walls, and climbs mountains in the blink of an eye. Don't worry, after it has mauled you, the game will take care of you by teleporting you miles away, so any resources you've collected can't be recovered.
Seriously though the game is horrible for solo-play. In the time I'm writing this review I'm 15 hours in, and still haven't passed through the early phase. And not in the good sense. You can get most of the enjoyment in most games for 15 hours, what I saw in Rust for 15 hours is trees, rocks, and bullets to the face.

However the game I was trying to help was a zombie survival game, not a PVP-only game with a couple of zombies in it.
It has now been 2 years and all that Bohemia has done is add vehicles, weapons and other stuff that enhances the PVP aspect, instead of focusing on actually having to survive the environment and the hordes of zombies that should be in the game.
I'm aware that this is an alpha build, but there is such a thing a priorities and in my opinion it should be to have a game that runs well and has the core aspects of a zombie survival game.
- Can have hilarious moments due to the unscripted nature of the game.
- Playing with friends or a squad makes the PVP quite fun.
(This is where 90% of my game time comes from).
- Alpha... 2013, 2014, 2015 and most likely all of 2016 too.
- Old and frankly crappy engine so the game runs pretty bad, even on high end systems.
- Very buggy and scarce amounts of Zombies. (Which SHOULD be the focus)
- KOS (Kill on Sight) is VERY common, and there is no repercussions in killing other players.
The list of cons can be made quite long, but I think you get what I mean.
If you were looking for a post apocalyptic ZOMBIE SURVIVAL, I'd look elsewhere.
If you are looking for PVP action, go play CS:GO or something similar.

It's really hard to write a review about Undertale - as the featured Courator shorty says, "To explain exactly why Undertale is truly special would require spoiling the experience, so I urge you to look past the hype and just play it yourself."
Technical explanation AKA what to expect as gameplay first, and a little about the story and characters later. I'll try to keep it as spoiler free as I can - I'll likely give general description about a character or two, avoiding the actual plotlines and happenings.
It's a really one of a kind of a game of the current times. Controls come from the NES era - four directions + two buttons. If you attack an enemy, you need to stop a bar running through a scale - the closer you are to the middle, the more damage you do, and certain weapons have different attack "patterns" - with the basic stick you just smack them, with the tough glove you can deliver a couple less damaging hits, dealing somewhat more damage overall. I don't know about the other weapons as I was only playing the pacifist route, and I think that's the more intresting one, because of it's mechanism.
A really small dive into the lore of Undertale: Monster's soul is closely linked to their bodies - weakening their will of fight will weaken them, and you literally can win a fight without raising your hand once for anything other than a hug or pet. While you try to figure out how you can make your enemy happy, less miserable, comfort them etc, you need to dodge their attack in a bullet-hellish scenario. It never gets boring, as each of the enemy types have at least one unique pattern - and by unique, I MEAN unique. One of my favourites was is one of the earliest enemy, a cockroach-like monster: if he had company he swarms the screen like the bugs do, but if he's alone, he just starts awkwardly dancing a wave. Almost all the bullet hell patterns are linked to the actual characters in theme, pattern or shape of the weapon/form of the monster, introducing changed movement against some enemies as well.
What was the most fun in the game for me? Two different, but linked things:
First, the pacifist route's way of defeating enemies. Just as a random example: you can across a monster named like Blurghartarmut , looks as a giant horse figurine from chess, says something to you and then good luck, figure out how to defeat it! Sometimes the name, sometimes the form or the quote helps you to pick out the option to defeat it - some bigger enemies require a specific order of "acts".  In this example of the chess-horse/knight, what do you do? Treat it like a horse, combing it's mane, give sugar cubes, compliment on his speed, or tell him that the other coloured King is defeated, there is peace, no need to fight?  Bear in mind that if one action is enough to defeat an enemy, then there is only one correct answer, and you need to figure it out based on the response. I think it's a really nice little mindgame.
And the second favourite thing of mine is: the whacky writing, and the really, really creative world, character building and what a funny tone the game can have. It's a little like you take one really creative person who then makes jokes, situations and a world out of the jokes and image of the world of a 6 year old. There are a lot of puns in the game, lot of funny situations, and surprisingly, it's full with double-meaning content, and usually you need to take things literally to get through things, but it's just... not always obvious, which is great! It's like putting up a note on a wall at 5M, waiting someone to get a ladder to be able to read it, to find a message " I can't believe you made so far for nothing / how's the weather up here? / Yes, you did it! Now what?"  It's somewhat random, but not the trollface, ohlololol level of being annoying, but the way that after a few hours you realize that if a character tells you a generic-sounding "Come and drop by my place" then you don't question whether you can go or not, you immediately go to find out what quirky/funny stuff the game has to show to you. Sounds really weird, but basically exploration and curiosity is rewarded with joy and fun.
And about the characters: there are a couple of NPCs who only have a few lines of talk, but they usually still give some information about the area, or have some connection to the story if you pay attention - like how a monster wishes for the school to close because of re-activated puzzles, and later you can see a new's cast telling the schools are closed for the very same reason. There are a couple of traders in the game, and you can talk to them about the world/themselves, they can contribute more to the story - at a point there's like a mini-plot going on between two traders, so it's intresting to explore it.  And finally, the "main" NPC characters - they are as different as they can get. Puzzle-obsessed kool guy skeleton, pun loving skeleton, hardcore fight-loving guard, eccentric scientist, the mysterious King you hear a lot about during your journey... they very, very often have interactions between them, various connections, friendships and rivalries that are subject of change during the game.  It's a rare thing to say, but I think in this game not the player character has character development, but all of the main NPCs - if one's willing to spend time with the game and the characters, it can give so much more character-wise than an average RPG, as multiple stories are told, and you can have a part in all of them.
Not to mention that the game has a
lovely music selection, areas and main characters, important enemies all have an awesome soundtrack of their own - if you want to check them out, you can find them on Youtube. Just be careful, comments are ridden with spoilers about the game, don't check them before playing it.
So yes, I can totally recommend the game if you like the base concept available as a description.
You can also download the demo of the game from the official website of:
. Keep in mind that according to the Undertale wiki "The Undertale Demo is extremely brief, buggy, and less detailed compared to the final game. [...] the demo has a much higher encounter rate in the first area compared to the final game."  But it's still a good way to get a first-hand impression of the game without buying it.

Honestly, the game Undertale was good, but not worthy of it's massive fanbase.
The first thing you realize is the game's style. Made by one guy, it's pretty fine and even a good idea to have an art style like this. It's simple and not too complicated, while it can make the sprites or characters easier to draw for any artists in the fanbase. But then again, it's not the best graphics you could have.
Besides this, the fanbase seems to be panicking about it's plot and characters. But, as an opinion,
(SPOILERS)
....I find most of these characters stereotypical. It helps to have stereotypes, as they're easy to understand, but the fandom may as well twist them once they get bored (Sans, anyone?). There's the nerd (Alphys,) the jock/lesbian (Undyne,) taller younger brother (Papyrus, Luigi), the fatter smaller older brother (Sans, Mario,) the mom character (Toriel,) and so on. It helps to understand these characters together, but, I don't want two height-mixed spaghetti-loving brothers found together in another game like this. Nintendo already did it, and Toby Fox decided to do it as well, probably unintentionally. But the characters aren't bad, not as stereotypical as a lot of media, and may be found worth their effort.
The next thing is the story. Sure, there's games with good stories. But good lord, is this a story game. Without it's story, Undertale would be next to s**t. The story manages to tie all of the characters together into one bundle that sticks together and stays that way. The story itself is a good one, whereas
(MASSIVE SPOILERS)
having Asriel as a point of finishing the game finishes the gameplay off with feels, if you're in for that sort of story thing. Or, you could go Genocide route, where you kill every single monster in the game and end up as Chara, who crashes your game. You finish Genocide, ten bucks wasted. No chance of playing the damn thing ever again. There's also neutral, but that's seen less as the other two routes are more interesting. The story itself is good, and pulls at the heartstrings, but I wouldn't say it's the best I'd ever seen. It's more of a short story format, with the way it's displayed, compared to the extensiveness of the main story line of a Bethesda game, perhaps.
The music of the game, however, is a lot like the art style. With Toby Fox working on the audio for Homestuck, he's had some experience before and even manages to use Megalovania.
For the third time.
Most of the songs are slightly bitcrushed but have been enjoyable in the battles when you don't just sit there and listen. Sitting there and listening to the music isn't worth it. But there is some great, even fantastic, opportunity for remixing these songs. Most of the chances you get to mix them are good enough and it can start someone off on a creator of music, being simpler and pixelated tunes. With the art style, the blocky feel of it matches up perfectly.
The entire game ties together incredibly well.
On a final note, I'll say that you should play Undertale. Take one route, try another. But it won't last forever, however. It seems playable for only a little while until you know the odds and ends of the game (Which you learn quickly, by the way,) and then it gets boring.

This game is not only fun, it's highly discoverable and surprisingly stable. I had a memory leak crash leaving it open overnight, and it often crashes on exit when it doesn't matter, but I've really experienced no other problems. I have a kind of weird, semi-budget PC (FX8350, 2xZotac 950 AMP! in SLI) and I can crank up the quality at 1920x1200 and get good frame rates. The down side is that you will get massively griefed even on servers that claim to be against griefing... which to me pretty much ruins the experience. So I wouldn't pay for this game (I got is as part of a humble bundle) but I would play it... on a private server. Unfortunately, there is no other single player mode but to run your own server, wihch requires that you download the game all over again as usual. Ah, Steam. If you don't like getting griefed, you will need a private server, period.

Rust is a good game if you've got a group of friends to play with, but if you're by yourself you're better off avoiding this like the plague. Like all PvP survival games, the community is almost exclusively made up of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who randomly murder other players because <insert arbitrary reason here>, so the only way to survive is to murder other players before they can murder you, creating a random deathmatch feedback loop.
There are absolutely no deterrents in the vanilla game to keep high level players from ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over low level players, meaning casual players will often find themselves quitting within a few hours (why wouldn't they? when their experience consists of being shot by other players and mauled by hyper-aggressive bears and wolves they can't progress), leaving nobody but more "hardcore" players.
Every now and then you may get lucky and run into a friendly player who doesn't shoot first, and may even offer you some supplies to help you get started, but such players are very few and far between, because this game discourages any style of gameplay that isn't flexing your trigger finger at anything that moves.
More casual players could try a community PvE server, but let's face it, this game is designed to be PvP - which would be perfectly fine if the PvP was limited to clans raiding each other and maybe the occasional mugging, but as I said before there are no deterrents to keep large clans from just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over new players.

Honestly, the game Undertale was good, but not worthy of it's massive fanbase.
The first thing you realize is the game's style. Made by one guy, it's pretty fine and even a good idea to have an art style like this. It's simple and not too complicated, while it can make the sprites or characters easier to draw for any artists in the fanbase. But then again, it's not the best graphics you could have.
Besides this, the fanbase seems to be panicking about it's plot and characters. But, as an opinion,
(SPOILERS)
....I find most of these characters stereotypical. It helps to have stereotypes, as they're easy to understand, but the fandom may as well twist them once they get bored (Sans, anyone?). There's the nerd (Alphys,) the jock/lesbian (Undyne,) taller younger brother (Papyrus, Luigi), the fatter smaller older brother (Sans, Mario,) the mom character (Toriel,) and so on. It helps to understand these characters together, but, I don't want two height-mixed spaghetti-loving brothers found together in another game like this. Nintendo already did it, and Toby Fox decided to do it as well, probably unintentionally. But the characters aren't bad, not as stereotypical as a lot of media, and may be found worth their effort.
The next thing is the story. Sure, there's games with good stories. But good lord, is this a story game. Without it's story, Undertale would be next to s**t. The story manages to tie all of the characters together into one bundle that sticks together and stays that way. The story itself is a good one, whereas
(MASSIVE SPOILERS)
having Asriel as a point of finishing the game finishes the gameplay off with feels, if you're in for that sort of story thing. Or, you could go Genocide route, where you kill every single monster in the game and end up as Chara, who crashes your game. You finish Genocide, ten bucks wasted. No chance of playing the damn thing ever again. There's also neutral, but that's seen less as the other two routes are more interesting. The story itself is good, and pulls at the heartstrings, but I wouldn't say it's the best I'd ever seen. It's more of a short story format, with the way it's displayed, compared to the extensiveness of the main story line of a Bethesda game, perhaps.
The music of the game, however, is a lot like the art style. With Toby Fox working on the audio for Homestuck, he's had some experience before and even manages to use Megalovania.
For the third time.
Most of the songs are slightly bitcrushed but have been enjoyable in the battles when you don't just sit there and listen. Sitting there and listening to the music isn't worth it. But there is some great, even fantastic, opportunity for remixing these songs. Most of the chances you get to mix them are good enough and it can start someone off on a creator of music, being simpler and pixelated tunes. With the art style, the blocky feel of it matches up perfectly.
The entire game ties together incredibly well.
On a final note, I'll say that you should play Undertale. Take one route, try another. But it won't last forever, however. It seems playable for only a little while until you know the odds and ends of the game (Which you learn quickly, by the way,) and then it gets boring.

As of writing this review, most of the recent negative reviews are because people don't like the XP system (Though I prefer it over the Blueprint system) or can't run the game on their low-end hardware. As far as open-world survivals go, Rust runs better than most.
Now, for an actual review.
Once you find a decent server to join based on the ping and population, you start out by spawning on a beach. You are naked, but you at least can't spawn in the frozen north or the desert south. For whatever reason, you have a torch and a rock with you. For a while, the rock will be your only real tool. The torch, however, is mostly just a great way to get yourself spotted and killed. Your goal is to find enough resources to not starve or get murdered.
From here there is 2 main paths you can take: you can try to build a base, upgrade it to wood, stone, and metal, amass resources while leveling up, and only killing players for self-defense. OR you can be a hunter, going around to monuments and landmarks (in which every one is referred to as a Rad Town by older players (Not to be confused with the actual Rad Town)) to break barrels and loot boxes and crates, hoping to get lucky and find some valuable resources/weapons. This method involves killing everyone on sight. You won't make any friends doing this, but it's high risk, high reward.
And while that is the basis of the gameplay, Rust has a lot of good things going for it. The dev team, figureheaded by Garry Newman, and lead by a guy named Helk, are usually very open about their plans for Rust and listen to community feedback to make (and revert) changes. The team is constantly doing what they can to improve performance while also updating the graphics and visuals.
You will get mad. You will get murdered. You will murder people. You might even make some friends to murder others with and take control of servers with them. Which, in turn, will make others want to kill you.
Rust is an experience you simply cannot get anywhere else, and it's one hell of a time sink.

Rust is a good game if you've got a group of friends to play with, but if you're by yourself you're better off avoiding this like the plague. Like all PvP survival games, the community is almost exclusively made up of ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s who randomly murder other players because <insert arbitrary reason here>, so the only way to survive is to murder other players before they can murder you, creating a random deathmatch feedback loop.
There are absolutely no deterrents in the vanilla game to keep high level players from ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over low level players, meaning casual players will often find themselves quitting within a few hours (why wouldn't they? when their experience consists of being shot by other players and mauled by hyper-aggressive bears and wolves they can't progress), leaving nobody but more "hardcore" players.
Every now and then you may get lucky and run into a friendly player who doesn't shoot first, and may even offer you some supplies to help you get started, but such players are very few and far between, because this game discourages any style of gameplay that isn't flexing your trigger finger at anything that moves.
More casual players could try a community PvE server, but let's face it, this game is designed to be PvP - which would be perfectly fine if the PvP was limited to clans raiding each other and maybe the occasional mugging, but as I said before there are no deterrents to keep large clans from just ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ all over new players.
This game has been in "alpha" for about 3 years now, don't waste your money because Facepunch is one of the slowest developers out there, and while the game is MASSIVELY better from a technical standpoint than it was 3 years ago, nothing has changed on the community's end (and it won't, because this game is by ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s, for ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥s).

As of writing this review, most of the recent negative reviews are because people don't like the XP system (Though I prefer it over the Blueprint system) or can't run the game on their low-end hardware. As far as open-world survivals go, Rust runs better than most.
Now, for an actual review.
Once you find a decent server to join based on the ping and population, you start out by spawning on a beach. You are naked, but you at least can't spawn in the frozen north or the desert south. For whatever reason, you have a torch and a rock with you. For a while, the rock will be your only real tool. The torch, however, is mostly just a great way to get yourself spotted and killed. Your goal is to find enough resources to not starve or get murdered.
From here there is 2 main paths you can take: you can try to build a base, upgrade it to wood, stone, and metal, amass resources while leveling up, and only killing players for self-defense. OR you can be a hunter, going around to monuments and landmarks (in which every one is referred to as a Rad Town by older players (Not to be confused with the actual Rad Town)) to break barrels and loot boxes and crates, hoping to get lucky and find some valuable resources/weapons. This method involves killing everyone on sight. You won't make any friends doing this, but it's high risk, high reward.
And while that is the basis of the gameplay, Rust has a lot of good things going for it. The dev team, figureheaded by Garry Newman, and lead by a guy named Helk, are usually very open about their plans for Rust and listen to community feedback to make (and revert) changes. The team is constantly doing what they can to improve performance while also updating the graphics and visuals.
You will get mad. You will get murdered. You will murder people. You might even make some friends to murder others with and take control of servers with them. Which, in turn, will make others want to kill you.
Rust is an experience you simply cannot get anywhere else, and it's one hell of a time sink.

RUST!
I really like this game and have been playing it since its release a few years ago.
I think in its core it's one of the few best games that were ever made.
You start out with only a rock and try to build yourself tools, a house and eventually real guns and ammunition with the resources you are gathering.
Although building can be a creative outlet on its own for some, PVP is what gives this game its character and makes it exceptional and unique.
---------------------------
Now, why the negative review?
It's not the hackers, although there are some (like in every other game ever). You can avoid this mostly by playing on community servers with active admins. Also the developers are doing their part to make this better: in the legacy version of Rust there was literally no anticheat. Now with EAC it has become a lot better.
It's also not the kill-on-sight mentality of the community, which is quite toxic one has to admit. But somehow a toxic community is just the right thing for Rust. After all it's about surviving and teaming up with random people will and should most of the times get you killed from behind.
If you really want to team up with somebody, get to know them first and try to build a connection OR play with people you already know.
It's also not the aspect, that people who want to play on their own without a team or clan have no chance in this game, which is not entirely true. If you are alone and have to fight vs 2 or even more enemies, it ought to be harder for you. I agree that it was a bit easier to play on your own in ealier versions of this game (no reviving, more skill involved in taking down enemies with guns, you heal to 100hp at campfires without needing other people to stand near you, ...).
But the recent trend of the developers is to make it fairer for solo players (picking up people now takes 6 seconds and you have to stand still, always 5 minutes cooldown on sleeping bags you recently put down, ...).
What the real problem is - and I think it's not only me - is, that every once in a while there is a ♥♥♥♥♥♥ update that makes the game literally unplayable or atleast takes a lot of fun out of the game.
The new arrowhead, which made aiming with the bow and crossbow impossible; the crossbow nerf, which made it useless; and last but not least the XP system, which took all the fun and also all the possibilities out of the game.
Now with the XP system you have to chop trees and mine rock nodes not for getting the resources but solely to get more XP, which is seriously the most boring thing ever (and it still takes ages to level up).
If you don't do this, you can't build higher tier building stuff, guns and all kinds of other stuff, which means you stand no chance vs the other players.
You don't get XP for playing the game and doing what you normally would do, that is building, hunting down and killing people, raiding, smelting ore, walking around and finding monuments on the map. Instead you get XP for only some stuff, like gathering resources, killing animals (which are quite rare not only due to this), looting barrels and crates.
All in all the XP system needs a lot of improvement.
Don't get me wrong, I know it's an early access game, but that doesn't mean you can just do whatever as a developer.
---------------------------
So how to solve this?
Use the current prerelease version of the game properly and test the♥♥♥♥♥♥out of it. Report and fix every issue there is. And only then, when everything is fine (and there is nothing GAME BREAKING in it anymore) and ONLY then release it to the main client.
This goes to both players and developers.
And if there is something game breaking in the latest patch and it cannot be fixed in a few days, then do a rollback to the last version and test some more.
One thing: make it easier to switch between release and prerelease version, so you don't have to download files everytime you want to play the other version.
---------------------------
The players have always had many ideas to implement into the game (mostly on reddit). The developers need to listen to those people and of course decide what is to be implemented and what not.
In the recent weeks they did listen and good things came out of it and also will come out of it in the future.
When the current problems (XP system) are fixed I will reevaluate the game and update the review. In its current state I CANNOT recommend this game.
---------------------------
TL;DR
One of the best games ever made. Game breaking patches every once in a while.
More testing needs to be done by both the players and developers before releasing patches.
CANNOT recommend game in its current state.

Rust is a Realistic Survival MMO.
Gameplay:
In Rust you start out with a rock and a torch, from there the first things to do is collect some wood using your rock. Throughout the game you will get killed many times if you are playing on a popular server. After putting in some time you will have collect enough wood and stone to start creating tools to speed up how long it takes to gather resources. Overall it will be challenging to get started but after a while you will learn more of what to do and how to craft items in Rust.
Graphics/ Sound:
Rust has some really nice graphics if you have some of the setting turned up. Rust also has some music during the loading screen and throughout the game
Multiplayer:
Rust has a very active community on a range of different servers. Some servers are just plain vanilla and have no mods at all. Other servers may have things like 3X XP or other perks to help speed up the process of creating tools and a base.
Cost:
Rust is priced at $20 at the time of this review and I think that Rust is priced well for what it offers right now. But i would suggest picking Rust up when its on sale for $10. Some sites like Humble Bundle you can even pick up Rust cheaper through their bundles while also supporting charity.
Time:
Rust takes a good 5-10 hours to be at a point where you can go offline without dying.
Pros:
-Realistic
-Active Multiplayer community
-Only $20
-Great Team game
Cons:
-Can be hard to run on lower hardware
-Server wipes
-Time consuming
I would give Rust a 9/10 Total Rating

You know a game is good when the negative reviews are coming from people who have played over 1000 hours.
A movie ticket is $10, and that entertains you for 2 hours... so when your dollar goes hundreds or thousands of times further... its just hypocritical to give a thumbs down review.
And hey, I get it.  When an update comes out that makes you so upset you feel compelled to quit the game, a negative review is your most powerful tool for getting heard and getting results.  At the end of the day, it's the best recourse you have and I can't blame you for using it.
So that being said, if you're new and considering picking this game up, here's what you need to know:
When you remove all the negative reviews from people with several hundred or more hours played, you'll find the status of the reviews to be something like 95%.  It's overwhelmingly positive.
And last time a major gamechanging update came out (XP system) that people hated, the developers fixed the change with a future update.  I'm guessing the same will happen soon for the "twig" update, that everyone seems to hate (for me it has a pretty mimimal impact.)
If you like sandbox games and freeloot PVP... there's just nothing better.  There's plenty of games that explore concepts I like more, but I always find myself right back on Rust.  It's incredibly fun.
Couldn't recommend it enough.  Even when the XP update was killing the game I wrote a positive review, but I deleted it to write this one (unlike some of the other people who wrote "XP update reviews" and still have a thumbs down on the game for an update that no longer exists.)
If your thinking of trying this game... just buy it and give it a shot right now.  It's one of the rare gems that you must try.

I don't want to be another one of those "omg still in alpha" whiners, but I bough this game in May of 2014.  I had very little gaming experience at the time (despite being an adult), and after watching the entire Dayz series of videos from FrankieOnPCin1080p, I just had to have this game.  I bought a gaming PC, and a copy of Dayz.  At first, I was in love, because on the surface the game does appear to be exactly what it advertises - a zombie survival game.  However, as you play more and more, you uncover more and more bugs that you have to find out how to deal with in order to enjoy the game.
I kept playing the game (albeit, while Rocket was still involved), and I had high hopes that one day the game would be fixed beyond it's ridiculously clunky/laggy/unresponsive controls.  I put in over 300 hours of play up to one point in early 2015.  Then I stopped playing for other endeavours, but would still launch the game whenever I would catch wind of a noted update.  I would always hop in hoping to see vast improvements in gameplay, controls, mechanics, etc.  But nope, over time they have added a lot of clotching, food items, slightly polished crafting/gardening/harvesting system, and now vehicles.  It took 2 years before even the first vehicle was launched into the game, and it was a bug-fest that was hardly worth playing for.  The mechanics of that were slightly tweaked and more vehicles added in - and it's still nearly unplayable.
At least now the zombies only take 2 hits to kill - even though absolutely nothing about the combat system has been improved for fixed.  Devs simply made it easier to not die.
Overall, this is the biggest dissappointment of my gaming experience.  I had very high hopes in the beginning, but now, nearly 2 years after I bought the game, it still boots up with the "Early Access Alpha" warning.  Never before have I seen a game so slow in development.  At this point, I doubt it will ever be released as a full title - but I also don't even care anymore.  I am happy that I was able to take part in making a small dev team filthy rich for virtually nothing....  But it would have been nice to at least get even half of what was initially promised.
Anyone who defends this game against my post is going to completely overlook what was originally promised by devs.  Every minor update and list of excuses along the way is moot.
This game has been a complete waste of time and money.

I paid $10 to play nearly thirteen hours of gameplay in one almost purely blind run of the game. I didn't realize it at the time that I wouldn't want to replay this game. Not for a long time, anyway. This is one of those games that you wish you could wipe from your mind just to enjoy seeing it over again.
Another review comments that this game is more of an experience than a game. They couldn't be more right.
Undertale is a unique combination of brutal honesty from unexpected places, old school challenges brought back to life like new, subtle psychology that can really make you think, and a true test of dedication to extremes. It plays like I wish every RPG or Adventure game would play; even if every individual choice doesn't completely split the story, it still takes into account your extreme efforts. You can truly be a good guy, if you can stomach the challenge of trying to find a peaceful solution under the worst, sometimes heartwrenching, sometimes heinous circumstances. You can truly be a bad guy, if you can truly remove yourself from your conscience and deal with being treated like a homicidal monster. You can also just be the one who wants to make it through, with no particular need to sway too far, just trying to make it out alive.
Very little in the game is truly so hard that you'll tear your hair out. The little that is, however, is a test of how truly devoted to the path you take. If it's hard, it's because it wants to be hard on you. It wants to test you. It wants to know if you truly want to stick with the path you've taken, no matter the cost and result. Whatever you choose, it better be worth it.
Spoilers: I'm a bleeding heart pacifist who gets unexpectedly attached to favorite characters in games. After I chose and beat my path, I spent an hour just enjoying the results in the game afterwards, if not longer. Just that alone was well worth $10. I only regret not going a neutral route first, to save the best for last.
Whatever you choose, stay determined.

This game could be great.  It has a lot of really fun elements to it but the community is absolutely terrible.  My friends and I all bought this game on humble bundle for $5, so we are not that upset about dropping it.  But I wouldn't have spent a dime on it if I knew how rampant hacking and griefing was.
Basically the game goes like this: you spend about 6 hours gathering and building materials.  Soon after, you start seeing the mouthbreathers and basement dwellers come out of the woodwork.  They continously harass you since they have been playing for years and just drop c4 on everything you own.  You'd think there would be a community like in ARK to at least help get you started or join sides in clan wars.  Nope.  It's "beat up the new guys until they quit the server" which is why most servers only have a handful of people in them.
On other servers we witnessed players float right through our armored codelocked doors and get aimbot headshots while our autoturrets act as if they weren't even there.  We even had other clans teleport to us to witness the hacking and despite everyone calling them on it, the admins did nothing (they probably WERE the admins).  On another server some invisible guy was running around killing everyone and stealing their meager possesions.  You could do nothing to stop it.  No one cares.  Hacking and griefing is the name of the game with this community.
To sum up, Rust has the most pathetic community I've ever wittnessed to what could be one of the best games out there.  And there is no fix for this.  A bad community will ruin the best of games.  We tried a dozen different servers and it was the same across the board.  I feel bad for the developers at FacePunch who have had their beautiful game hijacked by a bunch of obease taco bell sweaties hacking, beating up on noobs, and killing any future growth.  RIP Rust.  You had so much potential.

Ah Undertale, what is there left to say about Undertale that hasn't already been said? It's a smart and successful game, but It's important to know WHY it's successful. Undertale took chances, it took paths where others wouldn't tread, it respected us (the gamers) enough to give us a complicated and satisfying story. Undertale went to great lengths to prove we're all not only pining for new things in the gaming industry; it proved we will pay for them. Hopefully Fox's little project has been taken into account by all those triple A developers that keep feeding us the slop (the Assassin's Creeds, the Call of Duty's, the 2K's) and they'll realize that a good game isn't about the amount of money you put into it. It's about the amount of HEART you put into it.

I actually like this game. No, love it. It's the first time I've played a survival type of game like this, and I'm hooked. It's addicting as hell. There are negatives to this game in my eyes, but first, let's start with the positives.
The game has this original survival build-your-way-up-to-glory aspect that has finally been done with humans and realistic graphics. It's Minecraft done differently, in my opinion. Whether that's better to you is based on what you think. Me? I love it. It's Minecraft done way better. It also has this great atmosphere. You start out hopeless hitting a tree with a rock while butt naked. But once you learn the game and learn how to craft spears, tools, and clothes, you start to like it a lot more. Then you hunt for animals to throw spears at to get food and leather, then you gather lots of wood to start building your own home. At first, it feels tedious and boring, but then it gets a lot better and you get hooked. Soon, you'll be living in a stone house with guns and armor. It takes time to build up to this kind of setup, and it feels satisfying once you do. It's also way more fun if you bring some friends along with you to survive. The graphics are good, aside from the ugly tree leaves and a bit of super muddy textures on some stuff like dumpsters, which I assume is because the game is still in development. I've seen stuff about a future graphical overhaul which will be pretty sweet. The audio is also well done, especially the death screams. Whew, the chills.
Now, are there negatives? Of course. No game is perfect. The game is a bit unoptimized. Luckily, my EVGA 960 with 4GB VRAM can run this game without sacrificing a lot of visual sexiness. The game still looks pretty good with the settings I have which is great. The animals also have the ability to walk up boulders and mountains and walk through walls which is distracting and frustrating, especially when you're chasing an animal with a wooden bow and he gets away by running through a wall that you can't run through. You also can't choose your gender or race. It feels kinda PC but I think it's always been that way. Well, times have to change because I hate it. I'm forced to be a black woman. I want to be able to be a hispanic colored man in a game if I want to, and I'll proudly say that to a feminist's face.
There's also the toxic community I hear about on official servers. They always KOS (kill on sight) with no mercy, and stomp on the little guys that are trying to enjoy the game. Clans raid and slaughter everyone. To their credit, it is how the game is meant to be played, but it's no fun to any newcomers. The best way to avoid these Hitlers is to join empty servers. I always play on modded servers with little to no people on them, and I've actually made a few friends on said servers.
Now, the XP system. My opinion on it is it can work, but it's not good right now. On vanilla servers, XP takes way too long to get. It's annoying and grindy. I always make sure the modded server has at least 3x or more XP gain to get rid of the grinding. The best way to fix this is to take off new items costing XP to unlock and at least double the XP gain to make it not such a nuisence. There's also the blueprint system I hear people talk about all the time, but it honestly doesn't sound good to me.
This game is great. It's fun and is unique to what I usually play. I got this game in a Humble Bundle for $4.96, and it was 100% worth it.

Here's some tips I have put together to get the most out of your Rust experience:
- Empty the Parallax Mapping, Anisotropic Filtering, and the water option bars. I gained 30+ FPS by doing so. Of course, if you have a beast PC, don't worry about this.
- Join empty modded servers to get a singleplayer kind of feel. It's dumb the devs haven't added a singleplayer option like Ark and Minecraft have.
- Look for servers that have a XP multiplier plugin to get rid of the grinding.
- Servers with a map plugin are also nice, although this isn't often.
- Modded servers with a small playerbase are usually nice and don't KOS immediately. If you want a friendly server, those are the best ones to look out for.
- Don't launch the game in DX12 mode. It's laggy and the water was a solid lime color.

When the credits ended, I stared at the screen for the longest time. I stared so long a dog appeared and just stood under the title. You know, that cute fluffy white one? Then I stared even longer. The dog fell asleep. I managed to keep up my staring for a decent ten minutes after that but nothing else happened. I begrudgingly closed the window. I never played a videogame before that reminded me of how it's better to love and forgive than it is to hate and murder. That's the stuff they teach you kindergarten, but mostly because they don't want all of you arguing over the only box of crayons or the last gummy bear in the jar. This game means so much more. I'm an adult now and I've been struggling with a lot of the themes presented within this work. It was so relevant and so beautifully articulated, I didn't have the heart to do what many of peers are pushing me to do: a Genocide Run. I guess I'm not the hard-hearted person I once thought. I can't even bring myself to kill fictional characters (although I did accidentally kill Toriel on my first try and ended up resetting right away. I felt horrible!), much less hate them. I look at my current life now. There's only one person I truly despise, but this game has shifted my perspective. The anger has turned to pity. This game is the best therapy I've ever had (not that I've been to actual therapy). It's true when they say love when you can. Because we all have such a short time here, whether it's up on the surface or down below. Everyone deserves love and mercy. Sorry for getting so sappy. *cough*

When the credits ended, I stared at the screen for the longest time. I stared so long a dog appeared and just stood under the title. You know, that cute fluffy white one? Then I stared even longer. The dog fell asleep. I managed to keep up my staring for a decent ten minutes after that but nothing else happened. I begrudgingly closed the window. I never played a videogame before that reminded me of how it's better to love and forgive than it is to hate and murder. That's the stuff they teach you kindergarten, but mostly because they don't want all of you arguing over the only box of crayons or the last gummy bear in the jar. This game means so much more. I'm an adult now and I've been struggling with a lot of the themes presented within this work. It was so relevant and so beautifully articulated, I didn't have the heart to do what many of peers are pushing me to do: a Genocide Run. I guess I'm not the hard-hearted person I once thought. I can't even bring myself to kill fictional characters (although I did accidentally kill Toriel on my first try and ended up resetting right away. I felt horrible!), much less hate them. I look at my current life now. There's only one person I truly despise, but this game has shifted my perspective. The anger has turned to pity. This game is the best therapy I've ever had (not that I've been to actual therapy). It's true when they say love when you can. Because we all have such a short time here, whether it's up on the surface or down below. Everyone deserves love and mercy. Sorry for getting so sappy. *cough*

DON'T TRUST THE TRAILER!!!
In fact, don't even watch it. Don't even think about watching it. Undertale bears a lot of resemblance to a show called Gravity Falls. It can be serious and intense, has great characters and a lot of heart, but it also breaks the fourth wall and puts the player/viewer into ridiculous situations for laughs. And when your first impression are those ridiculous situations, without any context or without being invested in the characters, it looks dumb. But once you're actually in the game, and you've seen what it is and what it can be, these moments feel a lot more welcome. You're happy to laugh it off for a second.
The trailer doesn't show off the worst aspects of Undertale. In fact, it's funny moments are some of my favorite moments in the game. But when those funny, ridiculous moments are your first impressions of the game, when you're lead to believe the entire game is like that, it seems stupid and not worth your time. Which Undertale is not!
I mean, come on. If all you'd seen of Gravity Falls was the scene where Dipper imagines himself dancing with Wendy, would you really watch it?
So yeah. Ignore the trailer. Don't even go near it. Instead, just believe me when I tell you that Undertale is an incredible experience that will leave you wanting more. Unless you're a soulless monster, or unless the trailer put you in the wrong frame of mind.
Honestly, the game is best experienced blind, so blind you don't even know that you're playing a game when it first starts up. So just buy it and play it. I promise you won't regret it.
Also, I recommend being able to make spaghetti before playing.

Undertale. A game where you don't have to hurt anyone. But the fanbase does. I reccomend the game, but not the fanbase. It's full of screaming children fangirling/boying over Sans.
P R O S:
1. The game is so story rich, especially when you beat it.
2. Three possible outcomes for an ending.
3. 16-bit graphics are extremely nostalgic, especially for those 80s-90s kids out there, like myself.
4. It gives you that nice, indie feel.
5. Great sense of humor.
6. Great character building.
7. Extremely engaging, as the character's are actually pretty accurate to universal personalities.
C O N S:
1. God, the fanbase. Just don't get with them, please.
2. A lot of the choppy movements seem forced.
3. The game tries too hard to be funny sometimes.
4. At some moments, the game disobeys itself and moves to 32-bit/64-bit graphics during boss battles, which ruins the feel that it's supposed to give you.
5. No difficulty options.
O V E R V I E W:
Undertale looks pretty bad on the surface. 16-bit graphics, the fanbase, and the popularity it's getting. I was in that state, looking over Undertale as I would Five Nights at Freddy's. Both games are similar. Terrible fanbase, rich story, seemingly childish story, the list goes on. Amazing game though once you get into it; it's pretty easy to learn, too. No learning curve, it goes at a good pace. Of course, no game is flawless. The combat is fairly tedious, repeatedly pushing buttons. It's unique, sure, but not an extravagant unique. You don't have to fight, and that's a great idea, but Tobyfox doesn't pull it off amazingly. Like I said, it's mashing buttons, which isn't really that different from fighting... LOVE the artstyle. Truly a beautiful game.
