Garry should've stayed lead and it's pretty apparent now.
It all started in July of 2016, when the developers removed the blueprint system. Under the BP (Blueprint) system, you would collect fragments to piece together blueprints which you would consume to unlock the ability to craft a specific item. The better the item, the more blueprint fragments it required. They replaced the BP system with the XP system. Under the XP system, you would receive experience for completing tasks (basically just grinding: hitting nodes, chopping trees, picking up crates, and whacking barrels) and you would then consume the points to unlock the ability to make a specific item.
So, XP was a mess for a lot of months. Mostly because Helk decided he didn't like XP, and wanted to overhaul again, but it took 4 months for them to come up with a new system. So for 4 months, from July 2016 through November 2016, Rust was very grindy and in a state of Flux.
The new system that replaced XP in November of 2016, which is still in use to this day, is what's known as the component system. Under the component system, you are able to craft everything right from the start. If you have the apropriate "components" you can craft the item.
This component system has a lot of drawbacks.
1) It made an already grindy game, even grindier.
- Instead of having to collect Wood, Stone, Sulfur, Metal, High Quality Metal, and BP frags, you have to collect Wood, Stone, Sulfur, Metal, High Quality Metal, + Rope, Blades, Semi-Auto Body, Rifle-Body, Springs, Gears, SMG Body, Pipes, Sewing Kits, Tarp, Sheet Metal, Propane Tanks, Tech Trash and Road Signs. You can also craft those components with a research table and scrap.
2) It causes servers to die in 2-3 days
- No progression system tying players to servers. If you get raided, there's no reason to stick around on a server anymore. Wipe these days go like this: Wipe day - Servers are full pop. Next day - Servers are half pop. Day after that - Servers are 10-20 pop. Back during blueprints, and even XP, servers never used to die like this. You could make it a full 5 days with max pop, and even longer with biweekly/monthly servers.
- Community is also gone. Servers used to have a distinct identity. You got to know the people on your server, because they played there every wipe. Now? people switch servers too frequently. Everyone is a stranger.
3) Being 1-2 hours late to a wipe is disasterous.
- With high-tier weaponry being available within the first half-hour of a wipe, if you happen to have a job and you don't get off work until 5 on thursdays, you're going to have to compete against fully-geared players with the nerfed to oblivion bow/crossbow/pipe.
So like I said, these changes were made in November of 2016, and the system hasn't been tweaked at all since. The only
changes have been to HQM costs on auto-turrets, and gear costs on a few items. 8 months is a long time to have to watch a game that was once amazing, turn into a heaping pile of grindfest.
To amplify Rust's problems even worse, gunplay has now devolved into this terrible system where the guns don't really shoot where you're aiming. I cannot describe the feelings associated with wasting your time grinding for weapons and armor, just to be able to PVP and ending up losing all of your gear because your gun wouldn't shoot where you told it to. (This isn't even taking into account the horrible lag spikes that preceed any gunplay. Rust is not optimized. If you have a low-end graphics card you will not be able to achieve more than 20 fps, and if you have a good one you will sit at 100 until any sort of action happens, and you'll spike to 5-10 until you die or happen to be kicked by EAC.)
Due to all of the reasons outlined above I cannot support anyone purchasing this game. There are better uses of $20 at this point. Had you asked me a year ago, I would have raved about Rust. Not anymore.

Undertale is like many other RPGs, but at the same time, it is VERY different.

The battle system is great. Rather than ust exchanging attacks, you are able to physically dodge them. The music is also amazing and stunning.
The game is short and sweet, with emphasis on the sweet. it has an amazing story that will bring a grown man to tears, if you play the pacifist route. You get so attached to the characters, you don't want to restart the game.
The choice is yours - spare everyone, or kill everything.
or, y'know, do whatever you want.

I know what you're thinking. "Is Undertale REALLY that good?", "Should I actually get this game?", "So THIS is what all those people on Tumblr won't shut up about?!"
Well let me answer those questions, with another question, "Do you wanna have a good time?"
Because if you press that Add to Cart button, you REALLY are gonna like what happens next. ;P
I can't say much about the story or gameplay here, sorry. :P If you've somehow managed not to get this game spoiled for you at this point I consider you very lucky. This game is all about subverting expectations, so the less you know about the game going in, the better. What I can say is this game, while the graphical style may be lackluster, it more than makes up for it with its humor and characters. If you're on the fence about getting it I would say at least try it out. Undertale has an interesting take on the RPG genre, not just from a story standpoint, but twists its core fundamental structure into something fun and in some ways even thought provoking.
Now this is very important. No matter what ANYONE says, or what even the game may try to tell you. . . Play the game the way YOU want to during your first run (and use YOUR NAME for the character). Don't look up a guide, or walkthrough, anything. Kill the monsters you want to kill, and if you don't want to kill a monster then don't. After your first playthrough, then you can do whatever type of run you wish, barring you don't spoil the game for yourself. Also I recommend you do the quote on quote "good ending" before the "bad ending", as you will get a more emotional impact from the experience (that and the bad ending is also ridiculously harder to achieve compared to the others).
All in all Undertale is a great game and a great experience, and definitely my Game of 2015.

The first Borderlands was built upon the very simple concept of making a Diablo-esque RPG within a skill-based first-person shooter. The appeal of such a pairing goes far beyond acquiring loot in the form of randomly generative shields, grenades, buffs, and possibly more weapons than every other first-person shooter combined (we still have our mathematical hamsters crunching the numbers).
But what I love about Borderlands isn't the loot addiction. It's that such a system is used to turn the modern shooter on its head. Yes, Borderlands controls and feels nearly identical to Call of Duty. However, the game frequently demands you relearn the genre and discover new strategies for success. Nearly every weapon and enemy makes you approach the game in a different way.
Some guns will become more accurate the longer you hold down the trigger. Others can be thrown when you empty a clip, and they'll fly through the air, chasing enemies like a phantom shotgun. Some enemies will evolve into more difficult forms if you don't kill them fast enough. Others will pop out of treasure boxes and whoop your♥♥♥♥♥so bad you'll wish you left them closed. Pandora is a wild world where you never know what you'll find next, so it's a good thing you have some familiar faces by your side.
I completed the first Borderlands but can't tell you much about the story. I know where it begins and ends, and I also know I didn't follow the rest out of disinterest. But if the visuals and combat of Borderlands 2 are a sensible step forward, the improvements in narrative and writing is a stuntman jumping over the world's longest chasm. Borderlands 2's story is so good that it fools you into thinking the first wasn't so bad. Rather than brushing off the first game, this sequel owns it and carries on the most beloved elements from it: the world of Pandora, the four heroes, and their foul-mouthed, incompetent robot friend Claptrap. Though the heroes are now relegated to being side characters, they feel more fleshed out -- strangely more than the new playable heroes that fill in during their absence.
Just as it's hard to separate writer Eric Wolpaw from Portal, it is hard to look past Anthony Burch's (Hey Ash, Whatcha Playin'?) writing voice and influence all throughout this game. Burch brings us Handsome Jack, who will go down as one of the greatest videogame villains of all time. He has the Joker's indifferent, chaotic attitude and Tony Stark's cool, sarcastic personality, and he's a hellbent jerk who often brings to mind Gary Oldman in The Fifth Element. He's just cruel and twisted enough for you to hate him yet still manages to walk that thin line of being lovable in a GLaDOS kind-of-way. He makes the game special, but he's not the only one who does so.
Almost every quest giver and NPC has their golden line of comedic dialogue, if not more. The proud, rotund mechanic Ellie, gentleman explorer Sir Hammerlock, and Handsome Jack are all very good characters. Some will hold a special place in the hearts of players more than others -- foul-mouthed redneck Scooter is a bit of a cliche, and 13-year-old psychopath Tiny Tina (voiced by Anthony's sister Ashly) is kind of obnoxious, but even they have some great lines. Don't worry: Claptrap still has the best lines of all ("Your ability to walk short distances without dying will be Handsome Jack’s demise!"), and you'll miss him whenever he's not tagging along on a mission.
Unlike the first Borderlands, the great humor isn't limited to the characters. The missions contain the funniest parts of the game, often filled with subtle details and punchlines that will make you laugh out loud. In one mission, which has to be a contender for the shortest mission to ever grace an RPG, a guy begs you to shoot him in the face, so you do and immediately receive a reward. From throwing Claptrap the most awkward birthday party ever (poor guy!) to delivering pizza to some Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles wannabes, Borderlands 2's offbeat humor has a way of making the forgettable side missions into memorable plot lines. Some side missions will even ask you to solve a mystery or riddle, offering a change of pace from spamming bullets at things.
I played the majority of the game solo, and only twice did I have to complete a side missions for additional leveling. Borderlands 2 only has one difficulty setting -- excluding the "new game plus" feature which raises the stakes -- but it's one of the most well-balanced shooters I've played in some time, which is something of a miracle when you consider all the random variables at play. However, that's just my experience. Maybe I'm just good, maybe I just picked the right class (Siren), or maybe I just got really lucky with loot. One thing's for sure: Borderlands 2 is no cake walk, and there is no shame in getting help online. Unfortunately, that doesn't always work as it should.
In addition to experiencing minor lag in some matches, the co-op in Borderlands 2 is unbalanced when you don't play with people the same level. Enemies and loot will be set to the host's current level, which makes for a fruitless affair for higher-level characters and a miserable time for lower-level characters. Unless you are just there to have fun with your friends, it's hard to see why someone would play online with players of varying levels. As a level 18 player helping level 13 players, I only earned 1 XP for each enemy killed and all the loot was old junk. You'll want to start the game with a posse or at least seek out same-level players.
In many respects, the game can be just as unbalanced solo. You'll struggle to kill some of the hardest enemies in the game, which only give you a few XP. Meanwhile, you can acquire major XP from easier enemies elsewhere. What's most frustrating is that the game doesn't level-up enemies alongside you, so going back to past areas often feels like cheating. It's almost comical to jump around with armor that kills enemies just by their striking you, while you kill almost anything with a single shot from a pistol. Meanwhile, other areas become populated with higher-level creatures, so it feels like something is missing. Maybe DLC will repopulate these areas with tougher foes, but that doesn't excuse such an oversight.
While the main story is compelling, the main missions are a bit trite. They all boil down to destroying "all the things," reserving any creativity to the side missions. For a world brimming with so much character, I expected Gearbox to aim higher in its mission design. As much as I loathe the cliche turret and vehicle mission in first-person shooters, it'd at least give Borderlands 2 some much needed variety. Instead, turrets are rare and incredibly weak, while vehicles are used merely for getting from A to B in large areas. Endlessly shooting things still makes a great time, but it does get old after a while, and make no mistake, you will be shooting for a long, long while.
Pandora's new gang of four each play similar roles to those of the first game, but there is now enough customization to set them apart. The tech tree in Borderlands 2 is more fleshed out, letting players lean on defense, offense, or buffs. I'm disappointed that each character only has one main ability, but at least there are dozens of ways to modify it. You can also now customize your character's face and body with collectible skins. You can't make your Siren morbidly obese, but you'll at least stand out from others online.
Everything from the menus to the controls have been improved, but some nagging issues from the previous game remain. A mini-map makes navigation easier, though not easy enough. The waypoints often misguide you, some of the mission hubs are so vast that you won't know whether your objective is below or above, and it's almost always a long trek between the two. The game could also stand to be more generous with its fast travel system -- the kiosks are far and few between

Short review: It's Call of Duty with Bears.
Long review:
Rust is by far the best survival game currently out there. It's also the worst.  Here is the experience you will have, to explain why:
You start naked, cold and hungry armed with nothing but a rock and a torch. With a bit of luck, you can mine resources to craft clothing, fashion crude weapons and hunt animals. Then just when you start a campfire to cook it, someone will shoot you with a crossbow.
"Okay" you think, "my mistake there was obvious - I should build a shelter". So after being killed six or seven times in the attempt, you FINALLY get a shelter together. Nothing special, just a little wooden shack with a sleeping bag, a wooden chest to store resources and a toolbox so no one else can build there. So now the real fun starts! Time to get some resources together for a furnace! But when you get back someone has demolished your house, taken your toolbox and renamed your sleeping bag "noob", or usually something much less polite. Then they shoot you with a crossbow. Then again when you respawn.
You get the idea. There is some amazing content in this game, but 90% of it is pointless. Why build a cool house when only one type of build is optimal? Why craft interesting clothes, or customize anything when your resources are much better spent on defense? Don't bother using anything you just unlocked with the new XP system, because it'll just get stolen by a group or naked people armed with nothing but crossbows. You may be safe in a group temporarily, but sooner or later even the biggest bases will be raided by a clan of 20 people and taken for everything they have.
Most reviews blame the community, but the community is toxic because the game is toxic. The only way to have actual fun in this game is to roam around shooting freshly spawned people. Anything else is an exercise in masochism and futility. The game mechanics are heavily skewed to favour attackers and defense is nearly totally pointless at best, or more likely to kill you at worst. No matter how good your armour, you can still be killed easily by that same person armed with nothing but a crossbow.
The game has come along way, but that aspect has remained unchanged since the very start and is unlikely to change. Yes, it's a survival game. But survival should also heaily reward teamwork, trade and helping others. It should punish those who seek only to destroy and never build. Until that happens it doesn't matter how pretty it looks, or what new content or mechanics are added - this game will forever be nothing more than Call of Duty with Bears.

After playing through legacy, it was find a pick axe, get wood, get stones, build a house, furnace, metal door, a few boxes. Then go out and search for guns/blueprints and kill people. It was a simple foundation, 4 pillars, 3 walls, door way, roof and metal door.
Now it is completely gone in the wrong direction. Firstly it went from legacy to new rust. The new map was good, the way they introduced the same properties as old rust. Jumping was a ♥♥♥♥♥ but they fixed it.
The game started going down hill real fast. Introducing high quality metal ruined the game. Instead of using metal frags to create sheet metal like old rust, they introduced this low drop bs item. It is used to create armored and guns and requires 10 or more to make a simple pistol. Oh btw, only like 1 is mined per metal ore node (unless playing on a super lame x10 or higher server). The game became super grindy and catered to super large groups.
Next they gave a boost to blue prints which is great. You find blueprint frags to make books, etc to make blueprints. You can use this to increase chances of success in researching. Good job on this.
Then they take it all away and add in an experience/level up. They say that this will help with the blueprint finding. No, it doesn't. It caters to those who have been on the server longest. It takes level 3 to make a simple stone hatchet and axe. It takes level 8 to make a furnace. This is the highest I went up to. I asked around and people said that you don't get to make a pipe shot gun until much later. Well i had enough materials to make a relativly large home on a x3 server. The only problem was i was lvl 4. I couldn't make a furnace to start smelting ore. Every server is kos except a pve server which are just lame. Asking for a furnace for trade was like trying to take a binky from a crying baby without the baby crying. Nearly impossible... "oh lets trade" comes over, shoots you.
Lets not forget that once other people are established, they all have guns, can craft guns, but when you freshly arrive, you die 5 times, lose all your stuff. You attempted to fight back with your rock, and cant make a spear until you harvest about 1000 wood to get to lvl 2. Then you can make a spear. Then after that your next level take 3x longer because the more you gather, the less xp you get. Ok so now you have a spear, lets get a bow.... nope need to level up more.... Ok lets try and defend against guns, nope, they out range you and have more fire power + health kits, syringes, armor, etc.
Ok down to the main point. The game caters to the first come first serve. You can just roll into a house anymore as a naked, steal some noobs materials and expect to make yourself a decent home right away. You can try, but good luck making what you need to get a house started. The game got really lame and not worth the money to play anymore.

Undertale is not so much an RPG as it is a puzzle game with RPG elements. Granted, you earn EXP and gain LV like in other RPGs, but thats only if you choose to kill the enemies and bosses you encounter. Take the merciful approach and the enemies become more like puzzles that needs to be solved before you can spare them and advance. And to solve them you need to figure out what makes the enemies tick, how you need to interact with them in order to pacify them whitout killing.
Of course, one of the RPG elements Undertale retains are random encounters. Though it's only in regions you haven't completed, you are going to face the same enemies more than once, which can make the game feel grindy at times. Especially if you want to accumulate enough gold to buy the more expensive items that are being sold by vendors.(I should mention that regardless of wether you kill or spare, you'll earn gold from most of the encounters you resolve).
Now most people that like Undertale are going to say that the game is best enjoyed spoiler-free, and i'm no exception to that notion. But then again, if you do want some first impressions of the game whitout commiting your hard-earned cash first, i won't blame you. In fact, there is a demo of the game available for download on the web. At the very least, i recommend you give that one a try.

This is my very first review on a game that i until recently Enjoyed with great pleasure.
Alright ladies and gentlemen, I shall not keep you waiting, I shall get straight to the point.
Rust is solemnly damned into Oblivion.
Let me compare two average games with each other, why you ask? Because they have two things in common. Yes indeed the other system is based on dinosaurs (hint) and the dino's level up with you. So if you're level 70 the Dinosaurs are lvl 70~ish as well. And the moment a new player spawns in at level 1 they will have an incredibly hard time catching up. So it will gradually impossible to beat said player. (Ark if you haven't guessed it untill now)
See the problem with Rust?
If a new player spawns in at lvl 1 with zero XP points, if he/she meets a lvl 50 player who's got ??? XP points, and has researched nearly everything. The new spawn will have got NO CHANCE at defeating the player with the higher level. Because the new player can't find blueprints which helped a massive lot against Raiders and surprises. Those same Blueprints you could've gotten from the dead person which ambushed you. funnily enough Now when you kill someone whom is attacking you you aren't given the opportunity to even research it. When it breaks it's gone. And as such Rust has turned from a Survival, into an RPG a bad one at that.
I am actually saddened that the Developers F*cked it up so bad, I have very fond memories of this game. But I really wanted to see it flourish.
Sorry my good friend, it's to the trashbin with you.
You shall be missed.... Dearly.
Kind regards Mr.Dickens

The first Borderlands was built upon the very simple concept of making a Diablo-esque RPG within a skill-based first-person shooter. The appeal of such a pairing goes far beyond acquiring loot in the form of randomly generative shields, grenades, buffs, and possibly more weapons than every other first-person shooter combined (we still have our mathematical hamsters crunching the numbers).
But what I love about Borderlands isn't the loot addiction. It's that such a system is used to turn the modern shooter on its head. Yes, Borderlands controls and feels nearly identical to Call of Duty. However, the game frequently demands you relearn the genre and discover new strategies for success. Nearly every weapon and enemy makes you approach the game in a different way.
Some guns will become more accurate the longer you hold down the trigger. Others can be thrown when you empty a clip, and they'll fly through the air, chasing enemies like a phantom shotgun. Some enemies will evolve into more difficult forms if you don't kill them fast enough. Others will pop out of treasure boxes and whoop your♥♥♥♥♥so bad you'll wish you left them closed. Pandora is a wild world where you never know what you'll find next, so it's a good thing you have some familiar faces by your side.
I completed the first Borderlands but can't tell you much about the story. I know where it begins and ends, and I also know I didn't follow the rest out of disinterest. But if the visuals and combat of Borderlands 2 are a sensible step forward, the improvements in narrative and writing is a stuntman jumping over the world's longest chasm. Borderlands 2's story is so good that it fools you into thinking the first wasn't so bad. Rather than brushing off the first game, this sequel owns it and carries on the most beloved elements from it: the world of Pandora, the four heroes, and their foul-mouthed, incompetent robot friend Claptrap. Though the heroes are now relegated to being side characters, they feel more fleshed out -- strangely more than the new playable heroes that fill in during their absence.
Just as it's hard to separate writer Eric Wolpaw from Portal, it is hard to look past Anthony Burch's (Hey Ash, Whatcha Playin'?) writing voice and influence all throughout this game. Burch brings us Handsome Jack, who will go down as one of the greatest videogame villains of all time. He has the Joker's indifferent, chaotic attitude and Tony Stark's cool, sarcastic personality, and he's a hellbent jerk who often brings to mind Gary Oldman in The Fifth Element. He's just cruel and twisted enough for you to hate him yet still manages to walk that thin line of being lovable in a GLaDOS kind-of-way. He makes the game special, but he's not the only one who does so.
Almost every quest giver and NPC has their golden line of comedic dialogue, if not more. The proud, rotund mechanic Ellie, gentleman explorer Sir Hammerlock, and Handsome Jack are all very good characters. Some will hold a special place in the hearts of players more than others -- foul-mouthed redneck Scooter is a bit of a cliche, and 13-year-old psychopath Tiny Tina (voiced by Anthony's sister Ashly) is kind of obnoxious, but even they have some great lines. Don't worry: Claptrap still has the best lines of all ("Your ability to walk short distances without dying will be Handsome Jack’s demise!"), and you'll miss him whenever he's not tagging along on a mission.
Unlike the first Borderlands, the great humor isn't limited to the characters. The missions contain the funniest parts of the game, often filled with subtle details and punchlines that will make you laugh out loud. In one mission, which has to be a contender for the shortest mission to ever grace an RPG, a guy begs you to shoot him in the face, so you do and immediately receive a reward. From throwing Claptrap the most awkward birthday party ever (poor guy!) to delivering pizza to some Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles wannabes, Borderlands 2's offbeat humor has a way of making the forgettable side missions into memorable plot lines. Some side missions will even ask you to solve a mystery or riddle, offering a change of pace from spamming bullets at things.
I played the majority of the game solo, and only twice did I have to complete a side missions for additional leveling. Borderlands 2 only has one difficulty setting -- excluding the "new game plus" feature which raises the stakes -- but it's one of the most well-balanced shooters I've played in some time, which is something of a miracle when you consider all the random variables at play. However, that's just my experience. Maybe I'm just good, maybe I just picked the right class (Siren), or maybe I just got really lucky with loot. One thing's for sure: Borderlands 2 is no cake walk, and there is no shame in getting help online. Unfortunately, that doesn't always work as it should.
In addition to experiencing minor lag in some matches, the co-op in Borderlands 2 is unbalanced when you don't play with people the same level. Enemies and loot will be set to the host's current level, which makes for a fruitless affair for higher-level characters and a miserable time for lower-level characters. Unless you are just there to have fun with your friends, it's hard to see why someone would play online with players of varying levels. As a level 18 player helping level 13 players, I only earned 1 XP for each enemy killed and all the loot was old junk. You'll want to start the game with a posse or at least seek out same-level players.
In many respects, the game can be just as unbalanced solo. You'll struggle to kill some of the hardest enemies in the game, which only give you a few XP. Meanwhile, you can acquire major XP from easier enemies elsewhere. What's most frustrating is that the game doesn't level-up enemies alongside you, so going back to past areas often feels like cheating. It's almost comical to jump around with armor that kills enemies just by their striking you, while you kill almost anything with a single shot from a pistol. Meanwhile, other areas become populated with higher-level creatures, so it feels like something is missing. Maybe DLC will repopulate these areas with tougher foes, but that doesn't excuse such an oversight.
While the main story is compelling, the main missions are a bit trite. They all boil down to destroying "all the things," reserving any creativity to the side missions. For a world brimming with so much character, I expected Gearbox to aim higher in its mission design. As much as I loathe the cliche turret and vehicle mission in first-person shooters, it'd at least give Borderlands 2 some much needed variety. Instead, turrets are rare and incredibly weak, while vehicles are used merely for getting from A to B in large areas. Endlessly shooting things still makes a great time, but it does get old after a while, and make no mistake, you will be shooting for a long, long while.
Pandora's new gang of four each play similar roles to those of the first game, but there is now enough customization to set them apart. The tech tree in Borderlands 2 is more fleshed out, letting players lean on defense, offense, or buffs. I'm disappointed that each character only has one main ability, but at least there are dozens of ways to modify it. You can also now customize your character's face and body with collectible skins. You can't make your Siren morbidly obese, but you'll at least stand out from others online.
Everything from the menus to the controls have been improved, but some nagging issues from the previous game remain. A mini-map makes navigation easier, though not easy enough. The waypoints often misguide you, some of the mission hubs are so vast that you won't know whether your objective is below or above, and it's almost always a long trek between the two. The game could also stand to be more generous with its fast travel system -- the kiosks are far and few between

Alright. Let me tell you how this game plays out.
You wake up. Naked. Nothing but a rock and a torch to your name. You don't know where you are. All you know is that you must survive. So, with your rock you begin bashing at a tree and collecting wood when suddenly...BANG! Someone has shot you for no reason. You have died. Respawn. You start again, still eager to get into the game. You bash a tree, bash a rock and make a stone hatchet. With that hatchet you can get wood faster and faster. Soon you have enough for a building plan and begin working on your base. SInce you are new, you don't want to build too big, so you build a small base. 2x2 or 2x1. Yay now you have a place to live. By now you're starving so you go hunting. What's that over there? A pig! Mmmm...bacon...you run to the pig, waving your rock or hatchet violently. You want that bacon. You need it. However the pig runs which is to be expected. The pig approaches a rock and you think you have it cornered when it just...shoots up over the rock. Gone. So you settle for some nearby corn or mushrooms. Now, night approaches, it's getting darker by the second. You hear the howl of a wolf and the screech of a...something. "Time to go back inside." you say to yourself. You make your way back to your base and enter your place of living. Now, the game tells you that you're cold...so you make a campfire and set it in your house. The fire brings light and warmth. But wait. What's this? You hear rustling? What could it be? A bear, a wolf? WRONG. Your fire has attracted another player. They shoot through your base and kill you. Respawn. *sigh* Now, let's say that you finally have gotten a pretty good base. You've found some items and have everthing fortified. Cool beans! Now you log off to go do something else. You come back the next day and you're dead. Someone raided you when you were offline. Wash rinse and repeat. That's the game.
Regardless of that, I still love it. You can find a server with only five people on it and stay there. That way you don't have to worry about asshats taking your stuff. I hope this was helpful to someone or at least a bit informative or funny. :P

Rust is one of those games that you either play for 5 minutes and swear that you'll never touch it again, or you'll play for 5 days straight and have to return to it like a drug.
The first time I fired up the game, I was promptly murdered by a fellow naked player with a rock. Many new players are frustrated by this aspect of the game. You will be killed, and other players aren't there to hold your hand and play patty-cake. It is a true survival game and nothing is off-limits on most servers in terms of gameplay. The community is filled with every kind of player, from the folks who are generous and helpful to new players to the kill-on-sight-because-I-can sociopaths. There are much more of the latter, and it may get frustrating if you don't have a good strategy.
If I had to compare the game to others, I would say it has elements of Day-Z, The Forest and Minecraft (I know I'll get flak for mentioning the last one). The primary focus is on survival by defending yourself from the elements, other players, other threats. You spend a lot of time gathering food and resources to craft building materials, tools and weapons. Once you have sufficient defense and weapons, you can raid other players or conquer the attack helicopter that flies around the island once per day.
This game will give you elation when you finally craft or find that prized piece of loot. This game will also make you rage with the burning of a thousand suns when someone sneaking up behind you decides that they want to shoot you in the head for said piece of loot, and now you start (essentially) from scratch. You will be excited, anxious, angry and in the depths of despair all in an hour (similar to being married, strangely).
But as with marriage, if you stick with it, it will probably turn out okay.

It tends to remind me of games like the Mario and Luigi series, where each attempt at finishing a battle (attacking, spells, etc) felt like a minigame.
3) The dialog was phenomenal. I haven't played very many games that actively make me laugh out loud. Incredibly likable characters that made the experience just that made better.

Firstly, I'd like to say that I am a DayZ vet. I've got 410 hours on DayZ SA and well over 1000 on the mod.
Now, let's go back 2 years into the past, December 16, 2013 to be exact, when DayZ SA just dropped the ball. I was not even remotely excited for DayZ SA but was still going to get it because of how much I played the mod with my crew. (Didn't even end up buying it, one of my crew members bought it for me for Christmas, what a bro). Now, as I was saying, I had been following the DayZ development process since the standalone was announced, and at first I was thrilled, but as time progressed and how I saw Dean handling most of it, the idea of DayZ SA went kind of sour in my mouth. Thus, when DayZ released my expectations couldn't have been any lower for it.
Then I was surprised, my expectations were so low, I was quite intrigued at the games quality at the time of release. However, putting many hours and going through many updates the game just got worse and worse. It just kept going down hill with every update, with no hope on the horizon. My crew and I eventually stopped playing and didn't look back.
Fast forward about a year, at the least, and something miraculous happened, the .59 update. I had some friends 100% rehyped about the game, telling me to re-download it and give it another try. I reluctantly pressed the install button for DayZ SA.
The first thing I noticed was that I was getting 50 frames! That has never happened before! My rig is very bad, erm, at least it was, currently adding new upgrades and the like. But when I retested DayZ, with the rig I had, I was astounded. Not only was there a huge frame boost (probably thanks to the new renderer) but everything just felt so much smoother, I can't really explain it, but at DayZ's worse everything felt clunky as could be.
Heli crashes are back in 100%. You can find the AUG and the M4 on American heli crashes and the SVD/VSS on russian ones. I've waited a long time to write this review, because I didn't think a bad review would have been warranted at the time, because I followed the development of DayZ and knew it would be a rough road.
Since they changed the engine, added a new renderer, brought in vehicles and so so much more, the game has improved from it's release by about 10 times and from it's lowest point (for me anyway, which was a few months after release) about 100 times.
The reviews from the plebs not even explaining why the game is bad don't even know how bad the game was at one point, most of these people bought the game more recently.
The game shouldn't have been released on Dec 16, 2013 but should have been released Dec 16, 2015. The game is much better, and it really deserves a chance now.
Being a vet, I can see how hard the dev team has worked with the .59 update.
Now, if you're looking for a COD shooter this isn't it. You will be spending hours trying to get geared and will likely lose it before you can use it. This games learning curve is huge, so if you're a noob but want to buy it and try it out, you'll likely have to put in 100hours before you can even say you're decent at the game. That being said, I have played with people with over 1000 hours and have no idea what they are doing, so keep that in mind.

Alright. Let me tell you how this game plays out.
You wake up. Naked. Nothing but a rock and a torch to your name. You don't know where you are. All you know is that you must survive. So, with your rock you begin bashing at a tree and collecting wood when suddenly...BANG! Someone has shot you for no reason. You have died. Respawn. You start again, still eager to get into the game. You bash a tree, bash a rock and make a stone hatchet. With that hatchet you can get wood faster and faster. Soon you have enough for a building plan and begin working on your base. SInce you are new, you don't want to build too big, so you build a small base. 2x2 or 2x1. Yay now you have a place to live. By now you're starving so you go hunting. What's that over there? A pig! Mmmm...bacon...you run to the pig, waving your rock or hatchet violently. You want that bacon. You need it. However the pig runs which is to be expected. The pig approaches a rock and you think you have it cornered when it just...shoots up over the rock. Gone. So you settle for some nearby corn or mushrooms. Now, night approaches, it's getting darker by the second. You hear the howl of a wolf and the screech of a...something. "Time to go back inside." you say to yourself. You make your way back to your base and enter your place of living. Now, the game tells you that you're cold...so you make a campfire and set it in your house. The fire brings light and warmth. But wait. What's this? You hear rustling? What could it be? A bear, a wolf? WRONG. Your fire has attracted another player. They shoot through your base and kill you. Respawn. *sigh* Now, let's say that you finally have gotten a pretty good base. You've found some items and have everthing fortified. Cool beans! Now you log off to go do something else. You come back the next day and you're dead. Someone raided you when you were offline. Wash rinse and repeat. That's the game.
Regardless of that, I still love it. You can find a server with only five people on it and stay there. That way you don't have to worry about asshats taking your stuff. I hope this was helpful to someone or at least a bit informative or funny. :P

Alright ladies and gentlemen, I shall not keep you waiting, I shall get straight to the point.
Rust is solemnly damned into Oblivion.
Let me compare two average games with each other, why you ask? Because they have two things in common. Yes indeed the other system is based on dinosaurs (hint) and the dino's level up with you. So if you're level 70 the Dinosaurs are lvl 70~ish as well. And the moment a new player spawns in at level 1 they will have an incredibly hard time catching up. So it will gradually impossible to beat said player. (Ark if you haven't guessed it untill now)
See the problem with Rust?
If a new player spawns in at lvl 1 with zero XP points, if he/she meets a lvl 50 player who's got ??? XP points, and has researched nearly everything. The new spawn will have got NO CHANCE at defeating the player with the higher level. Because the new player can't find blueprints which helped a massive lot against Raiders and surprises. Those same Blueprints you could've gotten from the dead person which ambushed you. funnily enough Now when you kill someone whom is attacking you you aren't given the opportunity to even research it. When it breaks it's gone. And as such Rust has turned from a Survival, into an RPG a bad one at that.
I am actually saddened that the Developers F*cked it up so bad, I have very fond memories of this game. But I really wanted to see it flourish.
Sorry my good friend, it's to the trashbin with you.
You shall be missed.... Dearly.

About a month and a half ago I purchased Undertale based off of a recomendation from a friend and of all the press it was getting. It seemed like my kind of game. I like RPGs and the character designs really caught my eye. However I didnt play it for a few weeks. Then I got news about my father who was terminally ill and passed a few days after I returned home. I was an emotional wreck and my depression was worse then ever. We were very close and It was one of the hardest things I have ever had to go through. I barely talked to my family or friends afterwords and shut myself out of the world. So during this, I decided to try and play some games to keep my mind off of it, hoping to distract me from my emotions and coming to terms with what happened. Thats when I decided to play Undertale.
I knew a little about the game when I first started, and watched some Lets-plays on the first dungeon before going through. I decided to go through as a pacifist run for my first playthrough since it seems to be one of the main selling points of the game. I went through the entire game without killing a single monster, and got rewarded with one of the most emotional and suprising playthroughs Ive ever had. This game actually brought me to tears on a lot of instances and events throughout and I know i wont forget them for a very very long time. However the best thing I can say about this game is that it has given me the strength to move on and come to terms with my father's passing. The story of Asgore and Toriel is one of sorrow and hope, something that I needed. The hype was worth it.

About a month and a half ago I purchased Undertale based off of a recomendation from a friend and of all the press it was getting. It seemed like my kind of game. I like RPGs and the character designs really caught my eye. However I didnt play it for a few weeks. Then I got news about my father who was terminally ill and passed a few days after I returned home. I was an emotional wreck and my depression was worse then ever. We were very close and It was one of the hardest things I have ever had to go through. I barely talked to my family or friends afterwords and shut myself out of the world. So during this, I decided to try and play some games to keep my mind off of it, hoping to distract me from my emotions and coming to terms with what happened. Thats when I decided to play Undertale.
I knew a little about the game when I first started, and watched some Lets-plays on the first dungeon before going through. I decided to go through as a pacifist run for my first playthrough since it seems to be one of the main selling points of the game. I went through the entire game without killing a single monster, and got rewarded with one of the most emotional and suprising playthroughs Ive ever had. This game actually brought me to tears on a lot of instances and events throughout and I know i wont forget them for a very very long time. However the best thing I can say about this game is that it has given me the strength to move on and come to terms with my father's passing. The story of Asgore and Toriel is one of sorrow and hope, something that I needed. The hype was worth it.

Undertale is honestly one of the best games I've ever played.
You play as a human who falls down into the world of monsters. You then journey through the world, meeting monsters you either become friends with or completely obliterate. EVERYTHING you do affects the game, so replaying the game a few times is also recommended.

It's also really good at showing off the consequenses of choice, so you can play either as a peaceful pacifist or a relentless killing machine.
I also love the way Undertale breaks the fourth wall and really goes beyond the game in many ways you will have to discover for yourself. :P

My son and I had built a twig house one square in size to survive our first night. We had found an air drop and lucked out on an automatic pistol, we had also found a bolt action rifle. We had a wooden door and a lock and had built a furnace and a fire. we had some meat and a bit of food, a water tank and a roof over our heads.
In the middle of the night our front door and wall burst in and a stranger was in our house. In panic we shot him again and again. Dead we took all his stuff. He was loaded with at least 12,000 stone and 5,000 metal.  We quickly started to upgrade our home and put on some metal doors as we thought he would be back. Within a minute he was back, with another gun. We didn't know what was going on so we shot him in the head.
Heart pounding we finished our house and as the sun came up we laughed and felt relief at surviving our first night.
One of us hung around the house with our new weapons picked up off the bad guy, while I went scavenging.
On the way back I saw a figure looking up towards the house. It wasn't my son.
He was crouching in the grass watching our house. I snuck up behind him. My son ran around up by the house keeping him distracted then i attacked. I struck him three or four times with my sword but he used his assault rifle to pepper me and I died. My son revenged me and got him, but there was more than one!
When the fire fight was over he was standing and the enemy was dead.
My spawn wasn't too far away and I was soon back. We now had lots of weapons and gear. But we now had enemies that knew where we were and they would come for us.

Undertale is the game that anyone who's ever enjoyed games wished they had made. It is best going into it with as little foreknowledge as possible and just enjoying the experience.
If you are someone who has played games for their whole life, you will like Undertale. If you are someone who plays games casually, you will like Undertale. If you've never played a game in your life and this is your first one, you will like Undertale.
If you've ever thought about video games as their own medium of expression; interactive experiences that have the potential to be so much more than simply shallow diversion or electronic input challenges to be overcome, you will love, admire and pine after Undertale.
Take my enthusiasm with a grain of salt; I have just finished the game completely and am on a high, and the game is super hyped at this point, so look at it this way: Undertale is a game made in RPG maker than combines turn-based combat and bullet hell shooters. It has a heavy focus on story, fun gameplay that is challenging without being frustrating and a great soundtrack. And it was made by one guy in under 3 years.
On a side note: if you're into business or just like the self made man story, then think on this: Toby Fox (the developer) launched a kickstarter campaign for Undertale on June 24th 2013, asking for $5000. He pitched it as "A traditional role-playing game where no one has to get hurt". He quickly made $50,000 on kickstarter. Toby then proceeded to work on the project for the next few years, doing 99% of the work himself, with some art done by a friend. The game releases in September 2015 to incredible critical success. By now, in March 2016, 6 months down the road, the game has sold over a million copies, with the game being priced at $9.99 and the soundtrack being priced around the same. Figure that one out.
Basically, just drop what you're doing and play it. You'll see what I mean.

As 97% of the current reviews say - Undertale is a GREAT indie-RPG!
Undertale is a nice mix between RPG and "Bullet-Hell", it's also a short (~5h for one playthrough) and very story-driven game.
You'll play a human who fell into world filled with monsters - and from start to finish it's all up to you if you spare them or kill them - That's right! You can spare (almost) every enemy you'll encounter! I found this to be an extremely rewarding and nice feature - mostly because I never encountered it in any RPG I've played before! The different characters that you'll encounter have strong personalities and will react on you in different ways, depending on how many monsters you have killed or spared thus far! This makes the game extremly replayable... The story is also excellently made and consits of many twists as well as fourth-wall-breaking moments, and the game is filled with funny characters and jokes which made me chuckle quite often!
The soundtrack of the game is great, it reminded me a lot of old gameboy-games - and some tracks are extremely catchy... The graphics are - as you can see on the store page - all in 2D, but they sort of give the game a nice "retro"-feeling and I think they're also quite variable and nice, despite being not on modern days level... I think it's also mentionable that there is basically no grinding needed to complete the game - at least on 2 of the 3 possible paths you can take!
As said, the fighting-system consists of the typical RPG-combat-menu with an option to fight and an option to act (and befriend the monster to spare it). Combat is turn-based and on the enemies turn you'll have to play short minigames which mostly consits of dodgin bullets (like, for example, in the Binding of Isaac)...
If you like story driven games and oldschool-RPGs you should ceratinly check out Undertale - I purchased it for the full price and regretted not a single cent!
tl;dnr?: Undertale is a great RPG, if you liked Earthbound or Earthbound-likes, or even story driven games in general you should certainly buy it!

So I decided to change my review. My choice to change it happened when I realized that the developers are working not only to get new skins in the game, but also to make the game run more smooth. It seems to me they are always trying to find a way to improve the game. I only noticed the design and "feel" of the game developing previously. Now I'm finally experiencing it. This game now runs smooth on the minimum recommended specs, maybe not on ultra settings, but still. Smooth. And the developers are not afraid of trying new things. The most major change was when they implemented a level system, but maybe the most interesting time was when they removed it after a while, realizing Rust wasn't that kind of a game.
Also, I'm a PVE player, allthough 95% of my time has been on PVP servers. With the new items and the desire to implement new stuff, such as power and powersources, more and more PVE servers seem to pop up. In the end you shouldn't be surprised if the whole system has changed from being mainly a PVP game to a game where settlers sometimes NEED to co-operate. But that's only speculating. I am very excited about this game and the future of it. I highly recommend people to start playing now. This has proven to be a great journey so forth.

As 97% of the current reviews say - Undertale is a GREAT indie-RPG!
Undertale is a nice mix between RPG and "Bullet-Hell", it's also a short (~5h for one playthrough) and very story-driven game.
You'll play a human who fell into world filled with monsters - and from start to finish it's all up to you if you spare them or kill them - That's right! You can spare (almost) every enemy you'll encounter! I found this to be an extremely rewarding and nice feature - mostly because I never encountered it in any RPG I've played before! The different characters that you'll encounter have strong personalities and will react on you in different ways, depending on how many monsters you have killed or spared thus far! This makes the game extremly replayable... The story is also excellently made and consits of many twists as well as fourth-wall-breaking moments, and the game is filled with funny characters and jokes which made me chuckle quite often!
The soundtrack of the game is great, it reminded me a lot of old gameboy-games - and some tracks are extremely catchy... The graphics are - as you can see on the store page - all in 2D, but they sort of give the game a nice "retro"-feeling and I think they're also quite variable and nice, despite being not on modern days level... I think it's also mentionable that there is basically no grinding needed to complete the game - at least on 2 of the 3 possible paths you can take!
As said, the fighting-system consists of the typical RPG-combat-menu with an option to fight and an option to act (and befriend the monster to spare it). Combat is turn-based and on the enemies turn you'll have to play short minigames which mostly consits of dodgin bullets (like, for example, in the Binding of Isaac)...
If you like story driven games and oldschool-RPGs you should ceratinly check out Undertale - I purchased it for the full price and regretted not a single cent!
tl;dnr?: Undertale is a great RPG, if you liked Earthbound or Earthbound-likes, or even story driven games in general you should certainly buy it!

Well... now that i have almost 1000 hours of RUST in less than 4 months ( that scares me, specially cause i also work), i should definitely post a review on this awesome game.
I started playing last March and it's been a hell of a ride, from the 1st weapon found to the 1st chopper shot down.
It has multiple layers of fun, and the small bugs and glitches often help with that: the exorcist bears, the constructor eyeballs, etc...
It's a fast paced game, specially if you are already experienced with the first steps after the wipes. (All servers wipe at least once a month, on the 1st thursday)
At first you will hate the wipes, but as soon as you get more into the game you'll love them... OH the fresh starts!! :)
It's a harsh world if you go to high populated servers: people will shoot first and ask after.
Don't get attached to your precious stuff, you will eventually be raided and lose it all. OMG NOT MY PRECIOUS M249!
The ONE rule: DO NOT TRUST ANYONE! (with a few exceptions ofc :))
It doesn't have the best graphics nor the most complex crafting system, the graphics are good and the crafting and bulding is user friendly and optimized.
Thank God the inventory limits to slots and not weight... some players may prefer the weight system, but i find it pretty annoying.
Lacks more PvE! The chopper is the only PvE fight in game at the moment, so expect PvP to be your main activity right after the gathering of resources.
It has no vehicles so expect long walks in the bigger maps. Read somewhere the devs are planning to let us ride the 'now'  wild horses.
Who's gonna ride your wild horses, Facepunch? That be me, kk?
The maps are procedural, so there's no 2 servers with the same map and it changes every wipe cycle.
Crashes some times, has a few glitches (some are funny!) and residual cheating problems, but every thursday we see new improvements and the Devs working actively in fixing and adding. It's Alpha folks!
With the new XP system going live next thursday 7th of July 2016, some of the above might change. I think the game will be better leveled for all players and should go Beta pretty soon after this.
Buy the game :) it's fun and addicting. I don't remember having so much fun and spend so many hours gaming since the vanilla WoW back in 2005. Check my plays.tv, got a few videos there :)
Best regards,
Zaranza

This is the game that convinced me not to buy early access games again. Of course I understand that I was buying a game which was still in development (bugs, missing features, etc), but even so, this is a let-down due to the lack of development progress not feature completeness.
Or put another way... where is the incentive to finish a product when the unfinished version has already been bought by most people that will buy it? From a finance point of view, it logically doesn’t make any sense to spend more money completing a game when everyone has already bought it. Especially if the customer has no way of getting any money back or complaining about broken promises (i.e. I will give you money on the promise that you give me a finished game at a reasonable point in the future).
Steam is also guilty of profiting from the sales and then pushing the blame / responsibility onto the developers (usually hiding behind “it’s an early access game, you know the risks”). I feel that my agreement / purchase was made between me and Steam and it’s their problem that their suppliers let them down, not mine.
I think there is plenty of room for improvements / lessons learnt about the whole early access programme. But my advice; Buyer beware – don’t buy anything on the promise of getting it in the future, there are too many examples of the product either not being delivered or not living up to its hype.

Unfortunately my review will probably be washed down by the large amount of negative reviews this game has received, however I will take a stab at getting my voice out there to the people. First off, however, I want you to look at how many hours I have logged into this game. The amount of time I have spent in DayZ Standalone far surpasses any other game I have played on Steam, and for good reason. There is a lot of misconception going around the Steam reviews, and quite frankly many of the negative comments are filled with bigot hate towards the developers and a lack of understanding for how the early access model works in DayZ. Hopefully I can clear some of the confusion and give potential buyers some clarity on the title.
Let's rewind the clocks back to late 2013, a year after DayZ mod was released on Arma II. The survival sandbox genre had just exploded into the videogames scene, and every developer was trying to claim their stake in the land of the survivalist games. At the time, Bohemia Interactive had in their hands the most popular survivalist game on the market. Thousands of people played DayZ mod, and people loved the idea of an open-world survival game in which the elements and players are pitted against you. DayZ mod set the tone for what a survival game should be: challenging, unforgiving, and hard to top. Bohemia wanted to take the title and make it something greater, something much bigger and smoother than what the original mod intended to be. They knew that releasing a full version of the game on that clunky Arma II engine wouldn't cut it, so they had to make major improvements to bring the title into 2016 and beyond.
Instead of releasing the full DayZ Standalone game on the horrible Arma II engine, Bohemia made the decision to completely re-gut the engine and build a new one from scratch. FROM. SCRATCH. There are a few legacy modules that are getting carried over, but for the most part every aspect of the game is new (render, physics, lighting, etc). Anyone who has had any kind of development experience in video-games understands that this is a daunting task, a momentous task, a task that doesn't happen in one month or one year; No, creating a brand new engine takes years to develop, and this is where the root of the "problem" started.
DayZ Standalone went into early access in late 2013, and this is where they made their big mistake. The game simply wasn't ready. With no new engine components even being started on (plus it hit early access only 4 weeks into the development timeline, dear god), many early access players were left in disappointment when new features could not be pushed right away. People cried "fix zombies", but the zombies could not be fixed yet because an entirely new AI system was being created. People cried "fix FPS", but no FPS fix could be put in place because they were busy developing the new renderer. People wanted new vehicles, but vehicles could not be added yet because the physics system was being re-worked. There's no point in providing a "fix" for a mechanic in the game when that mechanic is going to be entirely replaced down the line anyways.
And so people got ♥♥♥♥♥♥, and fed up. "$20 for a Standalone title, and there's no fixes for these bugs?" Even I was at the point of rage, often times quitting DayZ Standalone for months at a time. People started saying that the developers weren't doing anything, that they "took the money and ran". But the real reality was that they were simply hard at work laying out the foundation for the title, unfortunately not being able to fix most bugs and issues at the time because they were so busy writing up new systems for the game to play on.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
SO LET'S FAST FORWARD. It's late 2015 now, nearing 2016. DayZ Standalone has been in development for 2 years now. Has the game changed? Are any of the new engine models finished? Are zombies even fixed yet?
You bet your ♥♥♥ they are. If you were to ask me when I think the game should of been released to the public as early access, I would have said right now (version .59) would have been the time to do it. FINALLY, after 2 years of development, Bohemia Interactive is getting around to completing all of the upcoming engine changes and new foundation for the title. Let me make a quick list to get your hype train rolling:
New Renderer is nearly finished, should have "30 - 40 % FPS boost overall"
Zombie AI is brand new and fixed, zombies now have sense of smell and sight, don't clip through walls, are actually a challenge
Four vehicles currently in game: V3S, Sedan, Hatchback, and Bus. Arial vehicles confirmed, as well as bikes and boats
New vehicle physics system taken from GTA V (Bullet SDK). Full vehicle maintenance and parts
All servers persistent. Camps and items are saved after restart. You can create large camps now.
Tents, Barrels, vehicles, protector cases, and backpacks can all be used as base storage now. Stays persistent through server reset
Loot respawn fixed. Loot spawns in areas that make sense now, it is very hard to get access to good weapons and ammo
Sickness and Disease now a major factor of gameplay
Tons of new animals in the game with new Animal AI. They react to sight and sound, as well as naturally roam the map looking for ponds and fields to graze in.
Predator animals confirmed, including wolves and bears
map changes and new northern towns expand the map greatly from mod
Softskills soon to be implemented, aka the more you run the more fit you get. skills develop over time
Every building now enter able with loot
A ton of new weapons and cosmetic items (clothing) added into the game
character wear progession, such as growing beards and getting dirt / blood on yourself, soon to be implemented
Contaminated Zones confirmed and being worked on, the first being a military base up north
And soo so so much more. I could keep the list going forever but it honestly doesn't cover how much they've added into the game since launch.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
Conclusion
Anyone who says DayZ Standalone is dead, or that the developers have "taken the money and ran", or that the community is dead, quite frankly is full of ♥♥♥♥. The game is very much alive and so much better than it was when it started. Even though DayZ SA has been slow off the start compared to other survivalist games (H1Z1, Rust, ARK, Unturned, Miscreated, etc), I strongly believe it will come out on top as the best survivalist game when it is finished. No other survival game has this much attention to detail and realism as DayZ. No other survival game has the kind of studio resources and money that Bohemia has to put out a strong title. No other survival game has mastered the hardcore aspect of survival and struggle better than DayZ. Well, my thoughts toward this game are mixed. Having just finished it, I want to point out it's strong sides and the ones which I consider to be utterly stupid.
What's appealing:
1) Depth of possibilities. For such a small game it possesses plenty of possible things to do, secrets and surprises.
2) Humour. Check. A lot of times you'll end up smiling at a good joke and sometimes it's impossible not to laugh.
3) Characters. They do really make strong feelings towards them appear, be it positive or negative ones.
4) The plot. The storyline features plenty of totally unexpected twists and turns, so that it will take your breath.
5) Music. Some tunes really touched my heart.
6) Possibility of totally pacifistic walkthough is an interesting option.
What's awful:
1) Ending. Imaging yourself to be a child, which daddy's helping him to make a model toy yacht. The boy feels excited and happy, and when the only thing left is to attach a small flag, the daddy suddenly pukes on it, jumps and crushes it with his feet. Any other ending, even the most stereotypical ones, would had been WAAAY more appealing.
But is it only for me? Who knows..
Totally worth buying, though. Check it yourself.

Wow... this game blew me away. It's got an amazing soundtrack, many different endings, and just a very friendly feel to it. The graphics are nothing to muse at, and I will admit, this game maybe isn't for everyone, but one thing's for sure. It's stolen the hearts of many people, including me. Once you play it, you'll be taken in by the humor, serenity, all of it. It's got a unique combat system giving you a choice. A choice weather to spare or kill your enemies. Your choice has a great impact on the game and that's one thing that makes it amazing. Just note this: it will play with your feels. So anybody with a super tender heart or an allergy to any LOLCAT type things should probably stay away.
All in all, it's just an amazing game that one should definitely try out! Graphics:6/10. Story:9/10. Soundtrack: 10/10. Honestly. You can't have an amazing game without an amazing soundtrack. Amazing soundtrack are underrated.

Edit: I still love Undertale a LOT but this review is embarassing. I apologize in advance.
This game has surpassed my expectations for what a game can be.
Just... wow.
Let's start with the worst part: the graphics. I personally think the 8-bit aesthetic was a decent choice on art style, as some parts of the game would look kind of cheesy with higher quality cartoon sprites. My three complaints are that the first area is an ugly shade of purple, the battles aren't very colourful, and the player character is a little crude-looking. That out of the way, every (non-Ruins) environment looks absolutely beautiful, and the main cast of characters look nice in their overworld sprites. The battle sprites are more detailed to help display more of the characters' personality, but like I said, they aren't as colourful as one could want.
The second part is the actual gameplay. the overworld is like any other RPG, with random and not-so-random encounters littering the area. The battles themselves are enjoyable: you avoid attacks like in a bullet-hell shooter and time your own attacks like in a Mario & Luigi game. I love them, especially the boss battles. They even let you spare enemies instead of killing them. Even the Zelda-style puzzles that are occasionally thrown in are usually enjoyable. (I usually don't like those.)
Now, the reason that I believe Undertale to be the best video game I've ever played: the story. Without spoiling anything, it's interesting, emotional or hilarious at almost any moment. You get a different ending if you kill nothing, kill everything, kill nothing and befriend everyone, or do a combination of any of those. It takes a lot of inspiration from Earthbound. I really don't know what else to say without making it a less enjoyable experience for those who read this. It's best experienced blind-ish, so don't go browsing the internet for memes like I did.
In fact, just buy it. Buy it now.

Well... now that i have almost 1000 hours of RUST in less than 4 months ( that scares me, specially cause i also work), i should definitely post a review on this awesome game.
I started playing last March and it's been a hell of a ride, from the 1st weapon found to the 1st chopper shot down.
It has multiple layers of fun, and the small bugs and glitches often help with that: the exorcist bears, the constructor eyeballs, etc...
It's a fast paced game, specially if you are already experienced with the first steps after the wipes. (All servers wipe at least once a month, on the 1st thursday)
At first you will hate the wipes, but as soon as you get more into the game you'll love them... OH the fresh starts!! :)
It's a harsh world if you go to high populated servers: people will shoot first and ask after.
Don't get attached to your precious stuff, you will eventually be raided and lose it all. OMG NOT MY PRECIOUS M249!
The ONE rule: DO NOT TRUST ANYONE! (with a few exceptions ofc :))
It doesn't have the best graphics nor the most complex crafting system, the graphics are good and the crafting and bulding is user friendly and optimized.
Thank God the inventory limits to slots and not weight... some players may prefer the weight system, but i find it pretty annoying.
Lacks more PvE! The chopper is the only PvE fight in game at the moment, so expect PvP to be your main activity right after the gathering of resources.
It has no vehicles so expect long walks in the bigger maps. Read somewhere the devs are planning to let us ride the 'now'  wild horses.
Who's gonna ride your wild horses, Facepunch? That be me, kk?
The maps are procedural, so there's no 2 servers with the same map and it changes every wipe cycle.
Crashes some times, has a few glitches (some are funny!) and residual cheating problems, but every thursday we see new improvements and the Devs working actively in fixing and adding. It's Alpha folks!
With the new XP system going live next thursday 7th of July 2016, some of the above might change. I think the game will be better leveled for all players and should go Beta pretty soon after this.
Buy the game :) it's fun and addicting. I don't remember having so much fun and spend so many hours gaming since the vanilla WoW back in 2005. Check my plays.tv, got a few videos there :)
Best regards,
Zaranza

I have logged close to 600 hours in this game at this point. Here are some of the pros and cons:
Pros:
- Beatiful, open world maps and interesting monuments to explore. Player generated structures are fascinating and each wipe cycle brings a new map and a new round of buildings created by players.
- Scratches a survival itch that other games haven't been able to for me.Hearing the footsteps of other players, especially when you are vulnerable, is terrifying. No zombies needed in this game, other people are the scariest threat of all. There is nothing like the feeling of leaving the protection of your base to venture into the great unknown, and nothing like that of closing that door behind you when you return to safety. (Unless, of course, you are in your base and hear the dreaded BEEP BEEP BEEP of a timed explosive charge stuck an outside wall...)
- The pvp is VERY challenging. If you engage with other players you have the opportunity to form alliances, neighborhood comradery or enemies. Plenty of opportunity to make enemies with the community this game has. Player to player interactions are my favorite part of this game. Make sure you have a mic and be prepared to die. A lot.
- Building a secure base that is difficult to raid is appropriately challenging. The more you build the better you will become at raiding other bases and predicting design elements that compromise security or make a base stronger.
- Very active development team. The changes that have been made to the game since November 2015 when I started playing have greatly improved gameplay. It has been a priviledge to play this game during its development and watch it grow.
Cons:
- The community is absolutely brutal. KOS mentality abounds and it will take lots of effort to get a base built on most higher population servers. Gameplay favors groups. If you have a friendly personality and are willing to put yourself out there, you can absolutely make friends in-game to team up with. Many people are very relieved to meet a friendly person that wants to join forces. This being said, large clans will always dominate servers.
- Some of the guns need some tweaking in terms of cost and performance, but it does seem as though the developers are working on this.
- VERY grindy. I love gathering resources in games, but even I feel a little too much gameplay is dedicated to smacking trees or stone nodes. This tends to promote more KOS mentality, it's easier for fully geared groups to massacre unarmed resource farmers than it is to farm the resources yourself.
Overall: I bought this game while it was on sale, this is the most fun I've had for $9.99 in my life. While other players are the cause for much grief (literal and figurative) in this game, they are also what makes gampley so interesting, complex, and addicting. I keep coming back for more because of the unpredictability of Rust.

As of the time I write this review, I have played 65 hours of this game, and 33 of those within the past week or two.  I played through tons of single-player, tons of co-op with friends, and a bit of the matchmaking stuff.  I also never played the first Borderlands, and didn't even find this game interesting till about a month or 2 ago.  Just letting people know those parameters before I start.
I love Borderlands 2.  I currently have 2 characters, Axton (37) and Zer0 (21).  I have played through the main story and some of the DLCs.  It is a very interesting game.  It has an easy to get around economy, and the guns can be incredibly interesting at points.  You can play this game both willy-nilly, as well as tactically serious.  It caters to many different styles of play for each character.  Axton can be played in 3 trees (Guerrilla, Damage, Survival), which I believe are titled by the playstyle.  I chose guerrilla, so I mainly focus on running in, landing my turret, it doing some damage, and me shooting from cover.  About halfway through it's run, I run back to it, and turn it off, prancing away as my cooldown becomes incredibly shortened due to me taking my turret back early.
Matchmaking isn't a disaster.  The exact opposite.  It is incredibly user friendly.  Unfortunately the actual matches with strangers themselves are somewhat random.  Not much strategy, most people I played with did not care about others playing with them.  Although this rugged individualism works in single player, when you play with 3 others and the enemies are 3 times as difficult to kill, team work is a must (this is where the willy-nilly goes out the window).  Sometimes you get some good people, but mostly I did not have good experiences with the people in matchmaking.
Luckily, playing with friends is so much more fulfilling.  Co-op is the same as matchmaking, except it's with people you most likely know.  The benefit of this is that when you are lower level and your friends are at a higher level, they can "power level" you to a higher level.  I was level 1 to start out with.  By the time I got to level 12 with friends about an hour had past.  Alone, this would have taken quite a bit more time, such as 3-4 hours.
Overall, it is simply an FPS that can be played with friends, yet it is not so simple.  Very fun, hilarious at points.  The Claptrap character is stupid as well as oblivious to sadness, even speaking out how he is programmed to be happy and excited all the time, even during the most depressing of historical events such as funerals or genocides.  This review could not do him justice.  Moxxi probably has a tie to every single character in the game, but they are all through sexual encounters of sorts (ALL of them).  The only legitimately normal character in the entire game is Roland, who is the leader of the faction you will be fighting for.

TL;DR: Technical issues aside, my biggest problem with the game is best explained with a cake metaphor: The title implies that zombie-killing is the cake, with player interaction and survivalism as the icing. In reality, the player interaction and survivalism is the half-baked cake, and the zombies are the icing, which is made from literal sh*t. Steer clear, people.
An MMO zombie game sounds like every zombie-killing gamer's wet dream. This can't be too bad, right?
...
...right?
I'm sorry, but this take on the concept is just terrible, even for Early Access. Since its initial release forever ago, there has been no real fixes for some of the biggest problems in the game that affect the core gameplay and overall performance. The dev team's idea of updating this game seems to be occasionally fixing random bugs and dumping random heaps of unpolished content into the game. I'm sorry, but adding content should be VERY low on the priority list when there is already a grotesque fustercluck of problems with performance and the core gameplay that DESPERATELY need fixing. Can't exactly enjoy all that shiny new content if you can't see it through all the problems with the friggin' core gameplay.
But the horrendously inefficient development process and other usual Early Access issues aside, this game suffers from the same problem as the Walking Dead. Namely, the fact that there is a much bigger focus on interaction between characters and boring survivalist mumbojumbo than the actual zombie killing. Seriously, engaging in zombie-related entertainment for character interaction and survivalism is like going to McDonalds for salad. Heck, this game is straight-up called "Day-Z" (implying that the zombies are the primary focus of the game) and it just doesn't deal in zombies a whole lot. So it's more like going to a fast-food joint called "Delicious Hamburgers" or something of that nature, only to discover that they primarily serve salad and their hamburgers are actually terrible.
This lack of focus on the actual zombies is further exacerbated by the completely broken combat system, whether you are dealing with other player characters or zombies. I don't know if it has something to do with networking problems or inefficient/crappy coding of the game itself, but I don't think I can find the words to describe how atrociously clunky and broken the combat (and the entire game as a whole, I should add) feels.
The terrible zombie combat is made EVEN WORSE by the fact that there is poor feedback in combat.
