Unfortunately my review will probably be washed down by the large amount of negative reviews this game has received, however I will take a stab at getting my voice out there to the people. First off, however,
The amount of time I have spent in DayZ Standalone
surpasses any other game I have played on Steam, and for good reason. There is a lot of misconception going around the Steam reviews, and quite frankly many of the negative comments are filled with bigot hate towards the developers and a lack of understanding for how the early access model works in DayZ. Hopefully I can clear some of the confusion and give potential buyers some clarity on the title.
Let's rewind the clocks back to late 2013, a year after DayZ mod was released on Arma II. The survival sandbox genre had just exploded into the videogames scene, and every developer was trying to claim their stake in the land of the survivalist games. At the time, Bohemia Interactive had in their hands the most popular survivalist game on the market. Thousands of people played DayZ mod, and people loved the idea of an open-world survival game in which the elements and players are pitted against you. DayZ mod set the tone for what a survival game should be: challenging, unforgiving, and hard to top. Bohemia wanted to take the title and make it something greater, something much bigger and smoother than what the original mod intended to be. They knew that releasing a full version of the game on that clunky Arma II engine wouldn't cut it, so they had to make major improvements to bring the title into 2016 and beyond.
Instead of releasing the full DayZ Standalone game on the horrible Arma II engine, Bohemia made the decision to
re-gut the engine and build a new one from scratch.

There are a few legacy modules that are getting carried over, but for the most part every aspect of the game is new (render, physics, lighting, etc). Anyone who has had any kind of development experience in video-games understands that this is a daunting task, a momentous task, a task that doesn't happen in one month or one year; No, creating a brand new engine takes
to develop, and this is where the root of the "problem" started.
DayZ Standalone went into early access in late 2013, and this is where they made their big mistake. The game simply wasn't ready. With no new engine components even being
on (plus it hit early access only 4 weeks into the development timeline, dear god), many early access players were left in disappointment when new features could not be pushed right away. People cried "fix zombies", but the zombies could not be fixed yet because an entirely new AI system was being created. People cried "fix FPS", but no FPS fix could be put in place because they were busy developing the new renderer. People wanted new vehicles, but vehicles could not be added yet because the physics system was being re-worked. There's no point in providing a "fix" for a mechanic in the game when that mechanic is going to be entirely replaced down the line anyways.
And so people got♥♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ and fed up. "$20 for a Standalone title, and there's no fixes for these bugs?" Even I was at the point of rage, often times quitting DayZ Standalone for months at a time. People started saying that the developers weren't doing anything, that they "took the money and ran". But the real reality was that they were simply hard at work laying out the foundation for the title, unfortunately not being able to fix most bugs and issues at the time because they were so busy writing up new systems for the game to play on.
--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------
. It's late 2015 now, nearing 2016. DayZ Standalone has been in development for 2 years now. Has the game changed? Are any of the new engine models finished? Are zombies even fixed yet?
You bet your♥♥♥♥♥they are. If you were to ask me when I think the game should of been released to the public as early access, I would have said right now (version .59) would have been the time to do it. FINALLY, after 2 years of development, Bohemia Interactive is getting around to completing all of the upcoming engine changes and new foundation for the title. Let me make a quick list to get your hype train rolling:

Be nice to everyone. Some of the best experiences I've had playing this game were helping randoms out in the wild and becoming survival buddies, sometimes even neighbors. I know it's scary not shooting everything that moves because you don't want to lose your gun, but some barely clothed/naked dude is not gonna hurt you, even if you have something as low tier as a waterpipe shotgun. Treat people how you want to be treated.

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

If your looking for a review on this game you've come to the wrong place, but if your looking for an outstanding lemon bars recipe you've come to the right place.
Ingredients:
1) 2 cups Flour
2) 1/2 cup Sugar
3) 1/4 teaspoon Salt
4) 2 sticks (1 Cup) Salted Butter, Cut Into Small Cubes
5) Filling
6) 1-1/2 cup Sugar
7) 1/4 cup Flour
8) 4 whole Large Eggs
9) Zest And Juice Of 4 Medium-sized Lemons
10) Powdered Sugar, For Sifting
Directions:
1. For the crust: Preheat the oven to 350 degrees F. Grease a 9-by-13-inch pan with butter.
2. Stir together the flour, sugar, and salt. Add the butter to the bowl and use a pastry cutter to cut it all together until the mixture resembles fine crumbs. Press into the prepared pan and bake until golden around the edges, about 20 minutes.
3. For the filling: Stir together the sugar and flour. Crack in the eggs and whisk to combine. Add the lemon zest and juice and mix until combined. Pour over the crust and bake about 20 minutes.
4. Allow to cool in the fridge for a minimum of 2 hours, then sift powdered sugar over the top before cutting into squares.
(Use an 8 x 10 pan if you'd like the layers to be a little thicker.)

It was... I don't remember what day it was. Thadeus had bought me a game he loved. Undertale it was called. For a while, I didn't really want to play it. I mean, the graphics seemed... not that impressive and all I knew about it was that it was influenced by Mother/Earthbound, which granted are some of my favourite RPG's, but for some reason, I held off on playing the game.
I sat down one day, Thadeus eagerly sitting on Steam chat, awaiting my reaction. I fired up the game, commented how I could tell it was made in Game Maker, cause of the collision detection. Commented how I wish the music wouldn't constantly change styles. I kinda half♥♥♥♥♥played it, not really paying full attention. I met Flowey, he of course was creepy as all hell, letting me know it was "kill or be killed". I killed some enemies. That's what you do in RPG's, right? I earned some EXP and felt pretty good. This character Toriel took me in, she seemed very nice. I liked her. In fact... I started to enjoy her company. Then I wanted to leave her place and move on. She blocked my way, said she was going to test if I was ready.
Then I killed her.
Realizing what I'd done, realizing I had killed a character who was friendly, I panicked. What happened? In other games, friendly NPC's wouldn't die if you fought them. They would stop, not let you kill them, something would keep it from happening. Yet here I sat, watching Toriel vaporize in front of me after the most blood chilling speech I've ever seen from someone friendly.
I cried, I felt rotten. I felt ashamed. I reloaded the game so I could get her back. The next fight the game told me I thought of letting Toriel know I watched her die, and she said she felt like a ghost when I looked at her. Finally figuring out how to spare her I moved on. Then... Flowey appeared again. He let me know he was aware I had reloaded to try and save Toriel. I felt a chill down my spine unlike anything I've ever felt in any game. I knew it was possible for game characters to break the fourth wall but this felt like Flowey was speaking directly to me. Not the sprite on the screen, but the player controlling the sprite. Instantly I felt like I couldn't play anymore. I was scared, way out of my comfort zone. I had just played a game that held me directly responsible for taking the life of a friendly character. I shut down the game and didn't touch it again for a long time...
I deleted my save file... manually... complete reset of the game... then I went back one day. Thadeus urged me to go back to it, struggling not to spoil it for me.
I had an experience that changed my entire view on games. What games can do to you, how they can impact you. Undertale takes every trope, every preconception you might have about games and turn them entirely on their heads. Instead of killing everything, you are urged NOT to kill, but to use non-violent solutions. The game has no limits on who you can kill. You can kill everyone if you so desire. It is up to you if you want to kill everyone or make friends. So on my second playthrough, scarred by my initial experience, I didn't hurt anyone. And the rest of the game was honestly one of the most unforgetable experiences I've had in gaming ever, something that will truly stick with me forever.
Undertale proves that 8bit sprites on a computer screen can feel as real as you and me, it proves that killing is a horrible thing and holds nothing back to push that point home. It proves that in the end, the only thing that matters is what you choose.
So choose wisely...

Positive:
For a player that generally don't care all too much for story based games or RPGs, Undertale was an funny, emotional and exciting experience. Never knowing what the game was going to throw at you, this game was a journey uncomparable to antyhing I've played before. From a purely story-based perspective, this is the best game I have ever played.
Critique:
That being said, there is more to enjoying a game than a good story and good character devolopement. Gameplay wise, I found it just a little lackluster, leaving me sometimes bored from just reading, and wanting satisfying gameplay. But this is not what Undertale's main motive is. Undertale is a game for the person who loves a great story game, or the type of person who thinks that there are few things better than an amazing film. If you are that type of person, this will be your favourite game.
But to conclude my experience from playing this game, I fell in love wth the characters and the story, laughed a lot and never knew what to expect. At time I felt that the gameplay paled, and ended getting bored at parts. Apart from that, a genius game in every right, Undertale takes home the cake and delivers an amazing experience for anyone to enjoy!

Gameplay is really simple and so are rpg elements combined within (character class with basic skill tree, weapon stats etc.) but I guess that makes "Borderlands 2" special. Completely agree with the other reviewers that the community is toxic..so I highly recommend starting your own server and inviting friends and friendly new folks to play, or joining a server with active admins that try to rein in the toxic behavior by setting rules or banning folks that are clearly just jerks that should be playing COD.  You can even restrict who joins your server in the first place with Steam groups if you so choose, though I think it's better to allow random folks to join and lay down the law just to diversify the server.  Running your own server lets you see who is dying and how, how many folks are on, what's being said in chat even if you're not actively playing, and more so you can really keep an eye out for folks that may ruin the game for others.
The mods you can add to a server are great and help improve the game tremendously.  From making it easier to find your dead body, to slowing down some of the more ridiculous decay timers (a nicely built wooden house should not decay that fast), to things like allowing you to go spear fishing, and more.
So, once you've either found a server like that or done all that to allow folks to truly enjoy what the game has to offer, I would most definitely recommend it.  There are plenty of bugs (animals glitching into your homes and murdering you in your sleep for one) but between the visuals, the gameplay, the audio and the general atmosphere they all create ti's a great game.  That daggone patrol helicopter just about gives me nightmares, it can be rather relentless.

text: Sans' Shortcuts brought me to an Overrated UnderTale
I'm not even gonna write a proper review. I just want to know how many other people cried when playing the ending.

This game was very sad, and also, very happy. I went on the genocide run first, without thinking about what I was doing, and I thought that that's how the game had to go, you kill, gain LV and stats, and things like that, but you don't think about what you're doing. You're going through the game, as if it is another rpg where you kill everything, and level up, but when you realize at the end, that your actions have consequences, it hits the sweet spot with moral and ethical values. The Frog at the very beginning of the game even pleads for mercy for himself, and all monsters alike, and when you go out and kill a monster, you slowly become a monster yourself by the end of the game, and not metaphorically, I mean, literally. So I went on a pacifist run, where I usually talked my way out of battle, or fled, or spared monsters, and needless to say, my efforts were rewarded in a very satisfying happy, yet bittersweet ending. I have been told though that there are lots of other secrets to be discovered, so if you like games that have mystery, or adventure, this one is for you.
I also found a whole lot of the music very calming, and peaceful, for instance, I was traveling through Snowdin, and the town was magical, the characters, given little dialogue and narration, seemed fleshed out among the other Snowdin villagers, and they just 'belonged.' It was like walking through a fantasy for most of the game, walking through the puzzles and braving the stronger opponents in the game. It was as if all of my literal dreams were being visualized, and, I will admit I used to dream and fantasize about things like that when I was a kid. From wacky characters such as Papyrus, to the bold and peaceful king at the ending of the game, every character had It's place in this big world, and I was so frustrated to find some of the choices very hard to choose. Even in the little things, like deciding which is better, crossword, or word jumble? Every single dialogue choice, big or little, has an amazing impact on things like, how Papyrus acted, or if I stayed friends with Sans, and weather I would have to fight Undyne.
And the soundtrack just added to the mystical tone of Undertale, as I fought Toriel, or battled Papyrus, or heard one of Sans jokes, all of the music just fit in somehow, to a game this small, yet so big. The sound effects were not the best, and neither was the music, but the way that they utilized what they had to make the game, and build it into what it is now, is amazing. I wish the music was more cinematic, or theatrical, but when I think about what the game might be if the music were like that, then that would ruin the art style, or at least just seem out of place, next to it. It is like an old NES game, or an old nintendo game, in that it has simplistic graphics, and movements, but it's not like it had to be completely realistic.
The fights are my personal favorite parts of the game, because it has some fast parts, and some slow parts, and some really just confusing moments, but it's not to fast for the style of the game, and not too slow either. I found a lot of what the monsters said really funny, and really inspiring, and that filled me with determination(no pun intended).
All in all, this game is not perfect, but for me, it certainly is, and I enjoyed every minute playing this game. I recommend it for an adolescent audience, or a young adult audience, because there are some things that kids should not play through.

After owning this game for a long time, I have had quite a few friends purchase this game and either love it or hate it, and that is what anyone who is purchasing the game has to think about. I personally love it, I think that it is a unique game in which every single time you play can be different. However, losing everything when you die is a real turn off for quite a lot of people - and it sounds bad - every time you die, you lose everything you worked hard for, there's no reward system. But, this is what makes the game more thrilling - feeling a rush as try and shoot it out with another person, both of you knowing that everything is on the line...
There are a lot of negative comments which state that it is still in alpha and that the game is bad - and as I said before, you either love it or hate it. However, you cannot blame the developers for this - they warned you that it is still in alpha and there are going to be bugs, so using this as a reason to not recommend the game just isn't fair to the game.
Summary of the game:
DayZ is a post-apocalyptic zombie survival game - you start with a shirt and some pants and have to search for supplies to survive. Although this is a zombie survival game the zombies are not the main focus of the game, the main attraction of this game is player interactions - every single person acts differently in game, people want to shoot you, handcuff and torture you, be your friend, or even wait until your guard is down to take advantage of you - you have to constantly be on your guard.
Advice to anyone about to/thinking of purchasing the game to make your experience better:
I feel that DayZ is what you make it, there are many ways that you can play the game, and as you get more hours on it you will start to discover the ways of playing the game which you find entertaining. So I am listing a few thoughts that I have to players which will hopefully make them understand more and get more enjoyment out of the game.
1. The developers continuously update the game - they have weekly maintenance and are continuously testing on the experimental server to create new content and make the game better. There are bugs/issues - however these can be reported to the devs to let them know and help them in their process of fixing the game. If you wish to purchase DayZ you will have to keep all of this in mind - there are times where bugs will annoy/frustrate you, however as development continues the number of bugs will decrease and the game will be optimized.
2. DayZ is only as fun as you make it... - This means that if all you do is look for items and run from city to city you are probably not going to have much fun. Player interactions help to make this game unique and I encourage anyone who is wanting to play this game to interact with players more - not everyone just wants to kill you and you will get a lot more enjoyment out of the game this way. (But still, don't trust anyone :P)
3. Don't hold on to your character - if you do find yourself in possession of some cool items, try not to get emotionally attached to your character, it may sound stupid but after you have spent a long time on one life dying can cause you to not feel like playing, this is DayZ, you could die at any second and you have to be prepared for that.
4. Try and play with someone else - I started off playing DayZ by myself, I found it fun but not as fun as when I was in teamspeak/skype with other people. As I stated above  - player interactions make this game - so having your own group, even if its just one other person, can really help your game experience - having other friendly players makes the more tedious parts of DayZ like running more entertaining - and having some extra backup never hurts.
5. You NEED a mic - it is not a game requirement to have a mic, but there is in game push to talk chat - most of the players use this, and a lot of the time the way a person sounds (either suspicious or friendly) can impact on how you interact with them. As well as this, a lot of people choose just to kill people who don't have a mic as they cannot judge what kind of personality that player has. So although it is not a game requirement, I strongly recommend it.
6. Finally, play with a mission - in DayZ you can do many different things, there is a lot of content in the game and the devs are continuously adding more. If you do not play with a goal in mind, a task to do or even a kill count you want, then you are going to find yourself eventually becoming bored. I encourage you to search the wiki while you play - if you search on the wiki when finding items that you haven't seen before or using interactions that you haven't done before then you may discover their intended use or something new that you want to try out.
So, just to conclude, you are going to either love or hate DayZ - that is the way it has been built, and this is not a review encouraging you to buy the game, but intstead a review that is aimed at enhancing the entertainment you get out of DayZ, so to everyone who is planning on buying this game, get the most out of it and I hope it treats you well.

Game does not expect any approach from a player and you can enjoy it as you wish, which is a great advantage these days, especially for a fps title. Not to mention great DLCs that offer different experience while still sticking to the story and some known characters. One of the best modern fps titles.

Borderlands 2 is a highly addictive FPS, made all the more accessible by it's compatibility with OS users. It combines beautiful cell-shaded graphics (you may not love them, but they are certainly distinct and a refreshing break from the modern desire for the ultra-real) with an easily accessible style of game play, and throws in an element of the RPG with the ability to customise the skills you acquire (level 5 and higher) and the weapon combinations that you can use. The story line is really quirky, and it has a decent amount of side missions that blend vehicular and strategy-type objectives. The overall world map is expansive and features a range of different enemies and bosses that keep you very much involved.
Good Bits (there are a whole host, so here are a few):
- All characters can use all weapon classes (you don't have to play the assassin to use a sniper rifle)
- Characters have unique skills to acquire
- The story is unpredictable and engaging
- The variety of weapons is pretty amazing
- It's a stunning game
- It's easy to play (i.e. pick up and play) but the levels are challenging and pitched at the right level
- There's a plethora of regen-points to every mission, so you don't have to start a mission from the beginning
- You can replay boss battles once you have beaten them the first time
- DLC is available, that actually delivers decent additional maps/characters, making it worth the money
Bad Bits:
- Some story missions are very long and don't have the option to save and quit halfway through
- For the casual gamer, the additional characters don't really offer much more to make you want to replay the game with them (no different story paths etc)
Overall, it's a brilliant game and definitely worth spending the cash. It pops up in the sales, so pick it up for a bargain!

Thomas Jacob "Jack" Black (born August 28, 1969) is an American actor, comedian, musician and producer. His acting career has been extensive, starring primarily in comedy films. He is known for his roles in High Fidelity (2000), Shallow Hal (2001), School of Rock (2003), King Kong (2005), The Holiday (2006), Nacho Libre (2006), Kung Fu Panda films (2008, 2011 and 2016), Tropic Thunder (2008), Bernie (2011) and Goosebumps (2015). He has been nominated for two Golden Globe Awards. Black is the lead vocalist of the comedic rock group Tenacious D, which he formed in 1994 with friend Kyle Gass. They have released the albums Tenacious D, The Pick of Destiny, and Rize of the Fenix.

Early life[edit]
Thomas Jacob Black[1] was born on August 28, 1969, in Santa Monica, California,[2] the son of two satellite engineers, Judith Love (née Cohen), who worked on the Hubble Space Telescope and is also a writer, and Thomas William Black.[3][4][5] His mother was born Jewish, and his father converted to Judaism. Black was raised in the Jewish faith, attending Hebrew school and celebrating a Bar Mitzvah.[6][7] On a guest appearance on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno, he said his surname may have come from the occupational name of blacksmith.[8]
Black's parents divorced when he was 10; Black moved to Culver City with his father and frequently visited his mother's home. As a child, Black appeared in a commercial for the Activision game Pitfall! in 1982.[9] This was shown during his later appearances as an adult actor on Jimmy Kimmel Live! and again on The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien.[citation needed]
For high school, Black's parents enrolled him at the Poseidon School, a private secondary school designed specifically for students struggling in the traditional school system.[10] Black also attended the Crossroads School, where he excelled in drama. He later attended UCLA[11] but dropped out during his sophomore year to pursue a career in entertainment. Fellow UCLA student Tim Robbins later cast Black in Bob Roberts. Black gained recurring roles on the HBO sketch comedy series, Mr. Show.[citation needed]
Acting career[edit]
Early roles[edit]
Black first acted in a television commercial at age 13 for the video game Pitfall!.[12] Black's adult career began with acting on prime time television. He played roles on shows including Life Goes On, Northern Exposure, Mr. Show, Picket Fences, The Golden Palace and The X-Files. Black appeared in the unaired TV pilot Heat Vision and Jack, directed by Ben Stiller, in which he played an ex-astronaut pursued by actor Ron Silver. He was accompanied by his friend who had merged with a motorcycle, voiced by Owen Wilson.[citation needed]
Black later took on small roles in Airborne (1993), Demolition Man, Waterworld, The Fan, The Cable Guy, Mars Attacks!, Tim Robbins' Dead Man Walking, The Jackal, Enemy of the State, and others. He had a small role in True Romance as a security guard, but the scene was deleted.[citation needed]
Leading roles[edit]
In 2000 Black appeared in the movie High Fidelity as a wild employee in John Cusack's record store, a role he considers his breakout.[13] He soon gained leading roles in films such as Shallow Hal, Nacho Libre, Tenacious D in The Pick of Destiny, Year One, and Gulliver's Travels. He received particular praise for his starring role in the well-received School of Rock, earning critical acclaim and a Golden Globe nomination for Best Actor – Musical or Comedy.[14]
He starred in one of his few dramatic roles as the obsessed filmmaker Carl Denham in Peter Jackson's 2005 remake of King Kong, a performance he based on Orson Welles. He voiced the title role in Kung Fu Panda, which grossed US$20.3 million on its opening day, June 6, 2008, as well as Kung Fu Panda 2 and Kung Fu Panda 3; this is his favorite role and he praises the tutoring of co-star and two-time Academy Award winner Dustin Hoffman.[15] His next film, The Big Year, a competitive birdwatching comedy co-starring Owen Wilson, Steve Martin, and JoBeth Williams, was released in October 2011.[citation needed]
Jack garnered a second Golden Globe Award nomination, this time in the category Best Actor in a Comedy, for his 2011 starring role in Richard Linklater's black comedy Bernie, as real-life murderer Bernie Tiede, a funeral director in a small East Texas town, who befriends and eventually murders a rich widow, played by Shirley MacLaine. Black's subdued portrayal, authentic East Texas accent and musical talent – he sings several gospel hymns as well as "Seventy-six Trombones" — had Roger Ebert describing Black's work as "one of the performances of the year."[16]

Black guest-starred on The Office along with Cloris Leachman, and Jessica Alba in a movie within the show. He also guest-starred in iCarly, in the episode "iStart a Fan War".
Black has appeared numerous times on the "untelevised TV network" short film festival Channel 101, created by Dan Harmon and Rob Schrab, starring in the shows Computerman, Timebelt, and Laserfart. He also provided an introduction for the unaired sketch comedy Awesometown, donning a Colonial-era military uniform. In the introduction, he claims to be George Washington (and takes credit for the accomplishments of other American Presidents such as Thomas Jefferson and Abraham Lincoln). Black also guest starred in the Cartoon Network's Adult Swim show Tom Goes to the Mayor, as a bear-trap store owner. Black also guest-starred on Dan Harmon's show Community.
Hosting work and appearances[edit]
Black took part in the Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? celebrity edition along with Denis Leary, Jimmy Kimmel and others and was handed the prize of US$125,000 in October 2001.[17] On December 14, he hosted the 2008 Spike Video Game Awards. Black has hosted the Nickelodeon Acceptable.TV.[18] He presented the tribute to rock legends Led Zeppelin when the band were named as 2012 recipients of Kennedy Center Honors. [19]

Thomas Jacob "Jack" Black (born August 28, 1969) is an American actor, comedian, musician and producer. His acting career has been extensive, starring primarily in comedy films. He is known for his roles in High Fidelity (2000), Shallow Hal (2001), School of Rock (2003), King Kong (2005), The Holiday (2006), Nacho Libre (2006), Kung Fu Panda films (2008, 2011 and 2016), Tropic Thunder (2008), Bernie (2011) and Goosebumps (2015). He has been nominated for two Golden Globe Awards. Black is the lead vocalist of the comedic rock group Tenacious D, which he formed in 1994 with friend Kyle Gass. They have released the albums Tenacious D, The Pick of Destiny, and Rize of the Fenix.

Early life[edit]
Thomas Jacob Black[1] was born on August 28, 1969, in Santa Monica, California,[2] the son of two satellite engineers, Judith Love (née Cohen), who worked on the Hubble Space Telescope and is also a writer, and Thomas William Black.[3][4][5] His mother was born Jewish, and his father converted to Judaism. Black was raised in the Jewish faith, attending Hebrew school and celebrating a Bar Mitzvah.[6][7] On a guest appearance on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno, he said his surname may have come from the occupational name of blacksmith.[8]
Black's parents divorced when he was 10; Black moved to Culver City with his father and frequently visited his mother's home. As a child, Black appeared in a commercial for the Activision game Pitfall! in 1982.[9] This was shown during his later appearances as an adult actor on Jimmy Kimmel Live! and again on The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien.[citation needed]
For high school, Black's parents enrolled him at the Poseidon School, a private secondary school designed specifically for students struggling in the traditional school system.[10] Black also attended the Crossroads School, where he excelled in drama. He later attended UCLA[11] but dropped out during his sophomore year to pursue a career in entertainment. Fellow UCLA student Tim Robbins later cast Black in Bob Roberts. Black gained recurring roles on the HBO sketch comedy series, Mr. Show.[citation needed]
Acting career[edit]
Early roles[edit]
Black first acted in a television commercial at age 13 for the video game Pitfall!.[12] Black's adult career began with acting on prime time television. He played roles on shows including Life Goes On, Northern Exposure, Mr. Show, Picket Fences, The Golden Palace and The X-Files. Black appeared in the unaired TV pilot Heat Vision and Jack, directed by Ben Stiller, in which he played an ex-astronaut pursued by actor Ron Silver. He was accompanied by his friend who had merged with a motorcycle, voiced by Owen Wilson.[citation needed]
Black later took on small roles in Airborne (1993), Demolition Man, Waterworld, The Fan, The Cable Guy, Mars Attacks!, Tim Robbins' Dead Man Walking, The Jackal, Enemy of the State, and others. He had a small role in True Romance as a security guard, but the scene was deleted.[citation needed]
Leading roles[edit]
In 2000 Black appeared in the movie High Fidelity as a wild employee in John Cusack's record store, a role he considers his breakout.[13] He soon gained leading roles in films such as Shallow Hal, Nacho Libre, Tenacious D in The Pick of Destiny, Year One, and Gulliver's Travels. He received particular praise for his starring role in the well-received School of Rock, earning critical acclaim and a Golden Globe nomination for Best Actor – Musical or Comedy.[14]
He starred in one of his few dramatic roles as the obsessed filmmaker Carl Denham in Peter Jackson's 2005 remake of King Kong, a performance he based on Orson Welles. He voiced the title role in Kung Fu Panda, which grossed US$20.3 million on its opening day, June 6, 2008, as well as Kung Fu Panda 2 and Kung Fu Panda 3; this is his favorite role and he praises the tutoring of co-star and two-time Academy Award winner Dustin Hoffman.[15] His next film, The Big Year, a competitive birdwatching comedy co-starring Owen Wilson, Steve Martin, and JoBeth Williams, was released in October 2011.[citation needed]
Jack garnered a second Golden Globe Award nomination, this time in the category Best Actor in a Comedy, for his 2011 starring role in Richard Linklater's black comedy Bernie, as real-life murderer Bernie Tiede, a funeral director in a small East Texas town, who befriends and eventually murders a rich widow, played by Shirley MacLaine. Black's subdued portrayal, authentic East Texas accent and musical talent – he sings several gospel hymns as well as "Seventy-six Trombones" — had Roger Ebert describing Black's work as "one of the performances of the year."[16]

So i'm just going to cut to the chase:  The main thing keeping you from purchasing this game right now is probably the main thing that was stopping me:  The price.  10 dollars for a fairly short game is what you're probably thinking, right?  How can I possibly justify spending 10 dollars on a 5 - 8 hour game when you could spend (for example) 15 on a 100 hour long RPG adventure?
I'll tell you why: Quality over quantity.  The game may not be long, but you'll want to play it over and over again.  Not just because the game is THAT good, but because of all the content you missed.  Undertale does something that very few games actually do:  Lock you out of content, forcing you to do multiple playthroughs.  Normally if a game does do this, the games are so long that you don't want to miss a thing, or at least want to get the best possible result on your first playthrough, because the chances of you actually playing the game again are extremely small.  There's nothing wrong with that.  Why would you want to play through a 100 hour adventure again just to experience a few lines of dialogue or maybe a short quest that you may have missed?  Because undertale is so short, you can justify playing just one more playthrough to see that one little tiny thing you may have missed.  What happens if you say this to that person?  what happens if you kill this monster before this scene?  There are three main endings in the game, but between that there is tons of variety not just in the storyline, but in the epilogue as well.  In fact there is plenty of AMAZING content that you can COMPLETELY miss if you dont backtrack a couple of times.  Luckily there are plenty of "quick travel" mechanics implented to make this not a complete pain.
Oh, and the game loves to mess with you.  If you're on your second playthrough or have to redo a section because you died, you may notice a few changes.  Because of this, you can do all three playthroughs without any part of the game being exactly the same (except maybe the ruins, the first section of the game.)
Either way: I would suggest MINIMUM to play at least two playthroughs of this game to get the two more popular endings (neutral and pacifist).  That alone is about 10-16 hours, which is at a minimum 1 dollar per hour.  I think that's well worth the price, especially considering how good it is.  Compare that to a modern day AAA game, which is about 40-60 dollars for 8 hours of singleplayer that's only worth going through once.  10 dollars doesn't seem so bad anymore, does it?
Oh and if you're not satisfied with that, there is one more ending, but trust me:  If you do that, you're gonna have a bad time.

I've had lots of good times in Rust since legacy, but it's the same thing over again. It's only a survival game for the first hour or so, then it becomes a raid-race. Harvest, build, craft as fast as possible so you can be stronger than everyone else then raid or be raided. Rinse and repeat. Keep doing this for 2 weeks and the servers will wipe. Now, you can start all over!
Pro's:
- Alot of content. Albeit, many of the unlockables are stupid signs and canvases to paint on.
- Graphics look good but I keep my graphics low so detail is lower and its easier to see people. Yeah, you can look like youre hiding in the beautiful grass on your screen, but not on mine and most other decent players.
- They've clearly put a lot of work into it
Con's:
- You have to build 50,000 doors and walls to keep people from raiding you. There has never been a balance of defense vs raiding. Too often I spend hours upon hours of playing to get raided within minutes by someone who has an♥♥♥♥♥load of time to build C4.
- This is not for individuals. You must play with an active group or people will just offline raid you or outgun you.
- Too much crappy content. You spend lots of time getting blueprint fragments only to be rewarded crap.
- Servers wipe every 2 weeks. If you start playing within those two weeks, all your effort will be wiped away when the wipe cycle comes around.
- There are too many details that you have to learn the hard way and it never seems to stop. Close windows with something so people don't boost in, put multiple cupboards all around to keep people from exploiting the cupboard system, turn your walls around right so weak side isn't outside, etc. Always some BS to mind. As if it isn't bad enough I have to harvest like a mofo to build all those doors. Additionally, door and wall HP don't match. You have a wood wall that's 250 HP but wood door is 125 HP. You have a metal door that's 250 HP and stone walls that are 500 HP. OH! But you have an armored door thats 800 HP and metal walls that are 750 HP. And then there's armored walls at 1000 HP. Why would I want armored walls when my door is only 800? Why would I have a stone base if my  door is only 250 or 750? If it's 250, they'll blow through the door, if its 750, they'll blow through the wall. Like I said, you have to build a giant base or people will just blow through your walls with C4 or the god-damned rockets.
- Don't worry guys, if you save your blueprint fragments you may get a gun! Yeah, I get a crappy laser sight and the other guy gets an AK. How am I suppose to kill him with a laser site?
The devs have done a lot to make the game good but then some stuff I still scratch my head about and wonder, "WTF are they thinking?". Eventually, you'll get raided through some BS tactic even though you put hours on end to build a defenseable base. In most cases, you will not get to defend it at all and all your work will be for nought.

Thomas Jacob "Jack" Black (born August 28, 1969) is an American actor, comedian, musician and producer. His acting career has been extensive, starring primarily in comedy films. He is known for his roles in High Fidelity (2000), Shallow Hal (2001), School of Rock (2003), King Kong (2005), The Holiday (2006), Nacho Libre (2006), Kung Fu Panda films (2008, 2011 and 2016), Tropic Thunder (2008), Bernie (2011) and Goosebumps (2015). He has been nominated for two Golden Globe Awards. Black is the lead vocalist of the comedic rock group Tenacious D, which he formed in 1994 with friend Kyle Gass. They have released the albums Tenacious D, The Pick of Destiny, and Rize of the Fenix.

Early life[edit]
Thomas Jacob Black[1] was born on August 28, 1969, in Santa Monica, California,[2] the son of two satellite engineers, Judith Love (née Cohen), who worked on the Hubble Space Telescope and is also a writer, and Thomas William Black.[3][4][5] His mother was born Jewish, and his father converted to Judaism. Black was raised in the Jewish faith, attending Hebrew school and celebrating a Bar Mitzvah.[6][7] On a guest appearance on The Tonight Show with Jay Leno, he said his surname may have come from the occupational name of blacksmith.[8]
Black's parents divorced when he was 10; Black moved to Culver City with his father and frequently visited his mother's home. As a child, Black appeared in a commercial for the Activision game Pitfall! in 1982.[9] This was shown during his later appearances as an adult actor on Jimmy Kimmel Live! and again on The Tonight Show with Conan O'Brien.[citation needed]
For high school, Black's parents enrolled him at the Poseidon School, a private secondary school designed specifically for students struggling in the traditional school system.[10] Black also attended the Crossroads School, where he excelled in drama. He later attended UCLA[11] but dropped out during his sophomore year to pursue a career in entertainment. Fellow UCLA student Tim Robbins later cast Black in Bob Roberts. Black gained recurring roles on the HBO sketch comedy series, Mr. Show.[citation needed]
Acting career[edit]
Early roles[edit]
Black first acted in a television commercial at age 13 for the video game Pitfall!.[12] Black's adult career began with acting on prime time television. He played roles on shows including Life Goes On, Northern Exposure, Mr. Show, Picket Fences, The Golden Palace and The X-Files. Black appeared in the unaired TV pilot Heat Vision and Jack, directed by Ben Stiller, in which he played an ex-astronaut pursued by actor Ron Silver. He was accompanied by his friend who had merged with a motorcycle, voiced by Owen Wilson.[citation needed]
Black later took on small roles in Airborne (1993), Demolition Man, Waterworld, The Fan, The Cable Guy, Mars Attacks!, Tim Robbins' Dead Man Walking, The Jackal, Enemy of the State, and others. He had a small role in True Romance as a security guard, but the scene was deleted.[citation needed]
Leading roles[edit]
In 2000 Black appeared in the movie High Fidelity as a wild employee in John Cusack's record store, a role he considers his breakout.[13] He soon gained leading roles in films such as Shallow Hal, Nacho Libre, Tenacious D in The Pick of Destiny, Year One, and Gulliver's Travels. He received particular praise for his starring role in the well-received School of Rock, earning critical acclaim and a Golden Globe nomination for Best Actor – Musical or Comedy.[14]
He starred in one of his few dramatic roles as the obsessed filmmaker Carl Denham in Peter Jackson's 2005 remake of King Kong, a performance he based on Orson Welles. He voiced the title role in Kung Fu Panda, which grossed US$20.3 million on its opening day, June 6, 2008, as well as Kung Fu Panda 2 and Kung Fu Panda 3; this is his favorite role and he praises the tutoring of co-star and two-time Academy Award winner Dustin Hoffman.[15] His next film, The Big Year, a competitive birdwatching comedy co-starring Owen Wilson, Steve Martin, and JoBeth Williams, was released in October 2011.[citation needed]
Jack garnered a second Golden Globe Award nomination, this time in the category Best Actor in a Comedy, for his 2011 starring role in Richard Linklater's black comedy Bernie, as real-life murderer Bernie Tiede, a funeral director in a small East Texas town, who befriends and eventually murders a rich widow, played by Shirley MacLaine. Black's subdued portrayal, authentic East Texas accent and musical talent – he sings several gospel hymns as well as "Seventy-six Trombones" — had Roger Ebert describing Black's work as "one of the performances of the year."[16]

Black also guest starred in the Cartoon Network's Adult Swim show Tom Goes to the Mayor, as a bear-trap store owner. Black also guest-starred on Dan Harmon's show Community.
Hosting work and appearances[edit]
Black took part in the Who Wants to Be a Millionaire? celebrity edition along with Denis Leary, Jimmy Kimmel and others and was handed the prize of US$125,000 in October 2001.[17] On December 14, he hosted the 2008 Spike Video Game Awards. Black has hosted the Nickelodeon Acceptable.TV.[18] He presented the tribute to rock legends Led Zeppelin when the band were named as 2012 recipients of Kennedy Center Honors. [19]

Handsome Jack, the antagonist, seemed to make me laugh more than anyone else. I thought this game was only goofy and comedic, especially when I met Tiny Tina. Instead of an average side mission, like 'Collect 25 Flowers' or 'Kill 25 Enemies' each side mission contains its own story. Whether it be competely humorous or extremely depressing and sad, every side mission was unique in its own way. Another fantastic thing this game is the amount of loot and different weapons. If you finish all of the side missions and story missions, the game is constantly being given new DLCs (Downloadable Content) containing tons of missions and hilarious campaigns. If you are looking for tons of fun either by yourself or with friends, Borderlands 2 is for you.

GAME: This game is a game reminiscient of EarthBound, with retro graphics, quirky humor, and lovable characters. Humans and monsters lived in peace before the humans got scared of the power of the monsters. A war broke out, and the human wizards casted a strong magical spell to create a barrier around a mountain, and sealing the monsters inside the mountain (Probably not the best solution). 6 children wandered up the mountain and fell in, being killed by the once passive king of the monsters. He collects thier souls, and once 7 human souls have been acquired, the spell can be broken and the monsters can wage war on the humas again. Then, you come in. You are the 7th human to fall into the mountain, and can change the story in 3 different ways.
- You can kill everyone and destroy the world
- You can kill a few monsters or no monsters to leave the mountain
-You can save everyone, become friends with the main characters, and break the barrier once and for all, leading the monsters to a happy life aboveground.
REPLAY VALUE: 9/10
MUSIC: 10/10
GRAPHICS: Depends on wheter you like retro graphics or not
STORY: 9/10

Pro's:
- Alot of content. Albeit, many of the unlockables are stupid signs and canvases to paint on.

Con's:
- You have to build 50,000 doors and walls to keep people from raiding you. There has never been a balance of defense vs raiding. Too often I spend hours upon hours of playing to get raided within minutes by someone who has an♥♥♥♥♥load of time to build C4.

Close windows with something so people don't boost in, put multiple cupboards all around to keep people from exploiting the cupboard system, turn your walls around right so weak side isn't outside, etc. Always some BS to mind. As if it isn't bad enough I have to harvest like a mofo to build all those doors. Additionally, door and wall HP don't match. You have a wood wall that's 250 HP but wood door is 125 HP. You have a metal door that's 250 HP and stone walls that are 500 HP. OH! But you have an armored door thats 800 HP and metal walls that are 750 HP. And then there's armored walls at 1000 HP. Why would I want armored walls when my door is only 800? Why would I have a stone base if my  door is only 250 or 750? Borderlands 2 is continuation of the mercenaries looking for the vault while fighting Handsome Jack, this time with new characters. That aside, the game is more of the same hilarious over the top style action. BL2 doesn’t try to be serious; it knows it’s a joke. Packed with geek and popular culture references such as Dr Who, Teenage Mutant Ninja Turtles, Snow White and Fantasia as well as memes and viral YouTube videos (double rainbow etc), BL2 is full of quirks and side stories expanding its already vast world.
BL2 has many RPG elements such as the questing system and the loot system. Quests can have several outcomes based on your actions with further quests unlocking as you progress. The weapons within the game are all unique. You might find two guns of the same “brand” and level yet one will do more damage while the other is more accurate. Many of the guns have side effects such as setting the target on fire or electrocuting them, some even explode when you reload them. Roaming the vast open world leads to finding more and better loot. Want a scoped pistol that shoots corrosive goop? Or perhaps a shotgun that shoots rockets? Borderlands has them, and more.
BL also features classes (4 +2 DLC at time of writing) and unlock trees (3 different per class) allowing you to bend any character to your play style – no particular character has a weapon perk initially. Regardless of if you prefer rifles, smgs, shotguns, pistols or rocket launchers, the class system lets you be anyone.
What’s more, the NPCs bring their own humour and amusement to Borderlands. The dialogue and missions within the game are well written and the voice acting it superb. Not to mention the pleasant array of PC specific options including field of view and PhyzX effects for fluids and explosions. Crouched behind cover you can soon find yourself surrounded with shards and shrapnel while knee deep in spent cartridges and shells, when a rocket explodes next to you throwing all the debris smashing into the surrounding area.
You can easily sink 300+ hours into this game, it’s definitely value for money. Definitely worth checking out.

First of all, let me just say, this is a game full of feels. I cried a bit during this game, especially towards the end of the pacifist route. I'm gonna warn you, it is impossible to get the pacifist route the first go, since the game is created that way, but when you do get the good ending, have a box of tissues with you. I cried. A LOT. I'm replaying it to see any of the little things I could have missed throughout the game, and overall this was a very well made game. The music is beautiful, comforting, fun, exciting, and some of the music just gives you feels depending on whats happening in the game at that moment. The characters are extremely loveable, and its almost as if they are real. Some of the characters you can talk to over and over, and they always come up with something new or funny to talk about. Also, some of these characters are extremely relateable in many ways~ It makes it much more interesting and exciting to play through and in a way makes you more attactched to these characters. I don't  have the heart to do the genocide route. Not after having built relationships with these characters. This game really plays with your emotions, but in a more positive way. Honestly this is one of my favorite games, and I will always remember this game. If you are hesitating on getting this game because it has become so "Mainstream", I suggest you get it. It is popular for a reason. Don't try and be the hipster outcast just because this is a game everyone likes. If most people like it, its usually for a good reason! I admit I was hesitating about getting it for that reason, but having played it, I realized that a lot of times, if something has gained a lot of fame, its usually because it earned it. This is one of those games that honestly earned all the popularity that it is getting. I hope more games like this will start coming out. This is one of those games where you know the creator put a lot of heart and thought into it, and I am very thankful for that~ So many wonderful aspects to this game, there is something for everyone in Undertale.  :)
Happy gaming~

First of all the basics (you might have heard all of this about a dozen times already, but for the sake of completion, I'm gonna tell you anyway):
You play as a young child that's fallen down into the realm of the monsters. A long time ago, humans and monsters used to live together in harmony but after a war broke out, the humans trapped the monsters underground. Now that you're down there, you're trapped as well and your goal is to escape. But your way through the depths of the underground is filled with dangers, vile puzzles and menacing foes (some of which might seem a bit "odd") that you need to overcome.
The special thing Undertale does so damn well is the whole journey and the developements that result of your choices on the way. It is a game that's meant to be played through at least twice but you'll most likely gonna complete it three or more times. As the game is designed this way, you can complete it rather "fast" (about 4-8 hours, depending on your personal speed). Don't worry, this is intentional!
Undertale uses a very clever and novel combat system. While it is structured like a typical turn-based RPG system(Attack/Special/Item/Run), it has certain mechanics that make Undertale stand out from genre classics.
First of all when an enemy attacks you, it's possible to dodge their attacks in an interactive mini-game. You can fully avoid taking any damage in almost every encounter just by skill, reaction and concentration. This makes for a very rewarding learning-curve and makes you stay on your toes in every encounter.
The second aspect that defines Undertales combat is its way of making you interact with your opponent. Every single type of enemy you encounter can be interacted with in a certain way. While some of these actions are plain goofy and somewhat reminiscent of Earthbound, some make for a very entertaining way of manipulating your opponent (like breaking their concentration, making them assist you or forcing them to yield).
Talking about Undertales OST is hard. While most people can agree that it's outstanding, nobody can really explain where all the fine details lie. The entire score has a wide range of themes, ranging from happy or encouraging over weird and creepy to foreboding and dramatic. It fills a wide array of emotions and Toby Fox (who composed all of the soundtrack by himself) did an amazing job of making the individual tunes fit their respective encounters / situations. I'd really love to go on about all the little details and what made it so damn special for me but that alone would fill an entire book. My best advice for you is to listen to it yourself and enjoy the beauty that lies within. And if you have the extra bucks to spare, please buy the game with soundtrack and don't just listen to it on youtube (trust me, you will).
I know, if you played through Undertale already or know enough about the game, this review might seem a little impersonal and sparse. But this is only to prevent any spoilers whatsoever.
To be honest, this game is far more than I ever expected it to be. Don't get me wrong, I knew before playing that it was very good and darn funny. I have tried since day one to like this game. A bad omen. I have been biting my tongue telling myself that it is alpha for ages now... and i have finally come to a conclusion. This game is a cash grab. Avoid it. Don't get me wrong it has core mechanics mostly in place and it will eventually release... with no single player campaign and as of Christmas 2015 no enemy AI. Not even zombies. This is a huge problem. Fan boys will cry foul and say its alpha but the fact is that zombies are not a "feature" in DayZ they are a CORE MECHANIC.
I have sat by and watched as the devs have heaped loads of new code into this game making amazing models for the weapons and characters adding vehicles and re.texturing all of Chernaurus. Ive explored most of the new buildings and hiked North to Misty mountain and drove through Cherno and it was all well done, but it doesnt change the fact.
The Fact is that they are using a recycled map and a ten year old game engine to create a "game" that has no campaign, no plot, and no point. And no zombies..... ALPHA ALPHA ALPHA!!! I can hear it already. If you dont have at least one working zombie in year three of development and have added all manner of new content it is going to create problems when the real AI is added in. They were having problems with the burden zeds were causing on servers. I would like to know what they plan to do about those place holder zombies (without horde ai or client side hit detection) when they are replaced. Will the new improved zeds be even more stupid than before to "optimize"? It reeks of cynycism to me and I cannot endorse it.
So to re.cap my stance, this game is nothing more than a cash grab initiated by a young and naive would be lawyer. When the heat picked up and real work was required he packed up and shipped out, leaving an impossible mess of bad decisions for the new guard to sort out. It is unfortunate that the real talent arrived so late. This game was stagnating up until Rockets departure and since then has been struggling to put it all back together. Some great work has come out of the modelers and animators and the ui is much better. I enjoy the emphasis on survival and civilian weapons as well as the multitude of functional gear, but seriously I didnt buy the Alpha of Barbie Camping Adventure.
This is not a complaint just about zombies but about the the overall direction of DayZ. I invested in this greenlight because I saw potential for another blockbuster out of Bohemia, a zombie survival game based on the ARMA engine.. what I got was Barbies PVP Sandbox of Slaughter. Here's hoping that the devs see this problem and put a strong effort into adding AI (zeds, civies, scum) and at least make a single player random instance map or something for release. Not doing these things is like selling half of a game. (a refurbished one at that)

I bought this game over a year ago, and and first I was blown away.  It was an amazing concept.  Sure it was buggy, but it's in early access, I told myself, soon we'll get to see this masterpiece fleshed out.  The idea of being dropped into this huge world, with other players, just fighting for survival, no goals, no quests, just living.  It was a lot of fun...for about an hour.
Over the past year I've come back to this game time and time again, to check on progress, and the times that updates ARE made, they make the game significantly worse than it was before.
Furthermore, the whole idea of this huge map is exhausting, because 99% of the map is just emptiness.  There's buildings, hell, whole towns to explore.  But you may find an item in 1 out of 10 of these.  The idea worked in ARMA, because the vehicles made it less tedious to get from point A to point B.  In this game, you'll spend an hour walking and never find anything worthwhile.
The biggest problem, however, is the apathy from the developers.  The progress of the game was never fast to begin with, but now it's slowed to a screeching halt, and all of us who spent our hard earned money are left with an empty shell of a game that you can't even call half finished.
This game is the entire reason I will never buy another early access game.  Save your money and learn from my example.

Not too sure what to write here so heres a recipe for Pancakes instead
Ingredients:
1 1/2 cups all-purpose flour
3 tablespoons sugar
1 tablespoon baking powder
1/4 teaspoon salt
1/8 teaspoon freshly ground nutmeg
2 large eggs, at room temperature
1 1/4 cups milk, at room temperature
1/2 teaspoon pure vanilla extract
3 tablespoons unsalted butter, plus more as needed
Now to make it
1. In a large bowl, whisk together the flour, sugar, baking powder, salt, and nutmeg.
2. In another bowl, beat the eggs and then whisk in the milk and vanilla.
3. Melt the butter in a large cast iron skillet or griddle over medium heat.
4. Whisk the butter into the milk mixture. Add the wet ingredients to the flour mixture, and whisk until a thick batter is just formed
5. Keeping the skillet at medium heat, ladle about 1/4 cup of the batter onto the skillet, to make a pancake. Make 1 or 2 more pancakes, taking care to keep them evenly spaced apart. Cook, until bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, and the undersides are golden brown, about 2 minutes. Flip with a spatula and cook about 1 minute more on the second side. Serve immediately or transfer to a platter and cover loosely with foil to keep warm. Repeat with the remaining batter, adding more butter to the skillet as needed.
6. Procedure for adding fruit to pancakes: Once the bubbles break the surface of the pancakes, scatter the surface with sliced or diced fruit, or chocolate chips, nuts, etc. Flip with a spatula and cook for 1 minute more, being careful not to burn toppings.

Like co-op?  If you're looking for a friendly, community game to play with others, this game is exceptional and unbeatable.  It's also the best way possible to introduce someone to first person shooters that perhaps has not been a gamer in the past (in this case, my wife).   Usually co-op is an afterthought, or not thought of at all.  Co-op is the primary focus of this game, and has been absolutely perfected.  Borderlands 1 was excellent, and the best co-op to date.  Borderlands 2 fixes anything and everything that you didn't even realize you missed in 1, and for an experience that is extremely fun for all, easy to join or host, productive on both fronts, and endless fun.  The non-stop add-on content they keep throwing out is great, lots of contests, as well as virtually unlimited loot combinations to make it always worth your while to keep playing.  This has trumped all of my old favorites that are not even the same genre (I typically hate FPS since I can't compete with those that play 24/7/365 and don't have things like a job or responsibilities).  I can't recommend this game enough, you won't be sorry!

When I picked up Borderlands 2 during a Steam sale (summer or spring, cannae mind), I did so because I was listening to my brother and a friend playing it over Skype and it sounded like they were having more fun than should be legal. I hadn't read anything about Borderlands 2, I hadn't look up any articles, reviews or watched any videos, I didn't have a clue what it was about, the characters, the setting, the entire game was new and alien to me. So obviously, I dived right in.
I was skeptical to wether I'd enjoy the game at all, after about an hour the initial wave of nausea from the art style disipated, meeting Claptrap, killing the Bullymongs and then moving onto the bandit fight at Hammerlocks place, I did actually find myself gaining some degree of enjoyment. This part however was merely a skirmish, a bit of light training to get you used to how the game feels, the real fun didn't start until I joined my brother and his friend in their hedonistic joint killing spree. Thats when I finally laid my finger on what makes Borderlands so special; it's Co-op.
I've played Borderlands 2 alone, I actually played through an entire DLC by myself because nobody else had it, and I can tell you that playing Borderlands 2 alone is a lot like getting drunk by yourself... for all the fun you might have dancing around your living room like a♥♥♥♥♥♥ it doesn't really mean much if there's nobody there to share the moment, and film you falling through the glass table you clumsy oaf. Now that I've made that analogy, we can assume that playing Borderlands 2 co-op is like getting drunk with friends, right? Well... yeah... I suppose so. I'm not made of analogies. It's a much better game as a shared experience, when I fought the Badassaurus Rex (google it) nobody was there to share the joy with me... it was a hollow experience, victory felt empty, it was me fighting a debuffed super-boss alone in an arena, just shooting at it endlessly until it finally died. Had it been a team effort, the fight would have been much harder, it woud have been one of much shouting and screaming and cursing, the hair and the blood, it would have been fantastic. And then the loot... the loot would have been much much better, which is one of the many perks of playing co-op. In a way, the game does force you to play co-op, by making the game slightly easier and giving out better stuff... it's likely so the game generates more sales from people pestering their friends to buy it, then the expansions, then the character DLC, then the... it goes on and on, but for the amount of fun that the game is and the enjoyment you get, it's very much worth every penny, sinking 100+ hours into Borderlands 2 is as easy as blinking.

Alright, rust. Is it a good game? Is it worth the money? Well let's find out. Rust is a survival game, like minecraft, but with extremely better graphics and alot of other items an oppertunities to make. It's only avaible in multiplayer, which means that no solo game play can be made except you play on a server solo. And with that said, you will also need friends to play this game. If you don't play with friends, then you will probably play with traitors on servers. As I said, it's a survival game, which means that you need to get shelter, food, water and weapons. You can build alot of different houses and bases which makes the game a very fun experiance if you like building stuff. You can also craft alot of melee and shooting weapons which you can kill both animals and players with. Ok, thats some stuf fabout the game, now do I like it? The answer is a clear yes. It's a extremely fun open world survival game that gives me throwbacks to playing minecraft when I was younger and how I played in the woods as a kid. How ever, in this case, it's even more then that wehn you have so many building materials, weapons etc. If you have a few friends that you can build a base with together then you will have an extremely fun time. The full price is clearly worth it, but get it on a sale if you are close to one. Now there are some bad things, of course. When playing on servers you will of course meet other players, some are friendly and some are not. The ones that are not how ever will probably ruin your base and take your stuff, and after that you are forced to begin on new. This happens about every 3d day and it's very annoying.

I'm not even sure now how I discovered this, "new game with a cool idea". A friend, DayZ-exploring, a flashing Steam store page, who knows. But once I installed it, and loaded it up, I had found a new, exciting video game. The music when loading was incredible, eerie and atmospheric; and this was 'alpha' music? Once I loaded into the world, an island of apparently great size, I enjoyed the experience from the start. Nature, trees, vast distances, animals, ruins, and...people.
For that is what makes Rust tick, people. The first moment, not knowing whether to hide, fight, or try to communicate, is telling, and this is a common thread. And with these first moments, come the first deaths, both expected and not. And so comes the first rule of Rust, don't trust anyone. And with this rule comes the choice you have to make, do you strive to live a solo life? Do you have Steam friends that play and can band together? Or do you try to find some team to take you in? Be ready, you are going to die, a lot.
I made a shelter, and built, and harvested, and hunted. I ventured into dangerous places and survived. Or died. In the end, it was a great experience. Then came the version changes, at first it was good, bugs were fixed. Then, they started over from scratch, and things started getting different from what made it good in the first place. It was good, then bad, then good, then bad.
The game today is worse than it was, a new thing we are seeing in games when they are made to be a service. A game with a golden age, something we used to only see in MMOs. That is why I can no longer recommend this game. I am going to give it a thumbs up, because of my experiences, and that it was worth the money I paid, but now is a different time. Rust is over for me.
Graphics:
Apart from certain updates and small periods, Rust has always looked fantastic. As they moved into Beta and the modern Rust era, the game both looks great, and takes a great system to run. It's one of the games that gets my PC as hot as it can get. Beware!
Sound:
Great music and sounds at first, but inconsistent sound production. Seemed like the staff never settled on consistant sounds/music during the process. To me, this shows a lack of focus, which has been clear from every player since the beta started. This developmental blurriness seems to coincide with when Rust had already made huge sales. Pretty much the team had success, and just went in slow-patch mode. It was less about a work of art, a work that could have defined the team of producers and developers for the rest of their lives, and more about making the project akin to updating the software in automatically flushing toilets.
Community:
It's a multiplayer game, and the community can be tight-knit if you're in good, but overall it's as toxic as it gets. The sadness with Rust comes from both the community and the developers. Nobody is happy, ever. This has bred conflict between players I've never witnessed before. In short, Rust has the worst community of players I have ever seen, and the clear lack of maturity in most players is almost depressing.
Overall:
Rust was a pioneer, and flagship in a tattered lot, but what made it great also destroyed it. When new games are made in its shadow, I hope that someone can capture that essence just once again, and hold it tight until a perfect time to share it with the world.

Alright, rust. Is it a good game? Is it worth the money? Well let's find out. Rust is a survival game, like minecraft, but with extremely better graphics and alot of other items an oppertunities to make. It's only avaible in multiplayer, which means that no solo game play can be made except you play on a server solo. And with that said, you will also need friends to play this game. If you don't play with friends, then you will probably play with traitors on servers. As I said, it's a survival game, which means that you need to get shelter, food, water and weapons. You can build alot of different houses and bases which makes the game a very fun experiance if you like building stuff. You can also craft alot of melee and shooting weapons which you can kill both animals and players with. Ok, thats some stuf fabout the game, now do I like it? The answer is a clear yes. It's a extremely fun open world survival game that gives me throwbacks to playing minecraft when I was younger and how I played in the woods as a kid. How ever, in this case, it's even more then that wehn you have so many building materials, weapons etc. If you have a few friends that you can build a base with together then you will have an extremely fun time. The full price is clearly worth it, but get it on a sale if you are close to one. Now there are some bad things, of course. When playing on servers you will of course meet other players, some are friendly and some are not. The ones that are not how ever will probably ruin your base and take your stuff, and after that you are forced to begin on new. This happens about every 3d day and it's very annoying.
All together, it's a great game!

DayZ is one of those games that went to the top of my wishlist the instant I first learned about it on Steam. Open world, unscripted, zombie-themed sandbox with no rules outside of the game mechanics, where the players set the scene and atmosphere based on their own actions? This game sounded amazing to me!
To be clear there are aspects to this game that I love and I've had some memorable experiences playing the game. I am also aware that the game is in Early Access and as a result my review is based solely on the return on investment a player can expect when taking the cost of the game and the state of the game's development process into consideration.
Overall the concept is sound but there are some fundamental problems with the execution of this concept that need to be addressed before DayZ will be enjoyable on a large scale. Spawn locations, the number of players per server, loot density, and other factors go into creating an experience that is enjoyable at times but largely frustrating and empty 95% of the time (especially given the fact that zombies aren't currently in the game... at all)
When you spawn in DayZ you're placed in an area that is imeediately dangerous for you. There is no transition from newb area of relative safety into more dangerous territory as a semi-experienced novice. You are simply pushed off the deep end out of the gate. Many will find this deeply frustrating. Surviving early on is a matter of running as far from your spawn point inland as possible to both get away from those who are already running around in top gear and to find the most basic provisions necessary to survive for a few days.
You will spend 95% of your time alone in this game unless you play with friends. Even then coordinating meetups with all new players is a nightmare. When you do finally get a decent amount of gear the first 20 interactions you have with other players will end poorly for you in 5 seconds or less. It simply takes too long to gear up a character and interactions with other players are so few and far between that the time needed to learn how to defend yourself properly is artificially and unnecessarily inflated.
The game is ambitious for sure and there are a lot of cool things you can do in the game but the devs need to tune the game in such a way to make it more engaging early on (without it being like lambs to the slaughter for complete newbs) or the only people playing this in two years will be the people playing it right now.

Coming up on the two year anniversary of DayZ and what does the dev team have to show for it?
Honestly, it feels like in order to appease the player base, the devs have devoted more time to adding in weapons and 15 types of headwear rather than fixing the zombies... and the game in general. For example, the game will not exit to desktop a good 2/3rds of the time. It just enters a frozen state and even trying to end the process in task manager doesn't work. You have to restart your computer in order to get it out of your processes tab. That is a fundamental problem but I am glad I can grow enough tomatoes to feed a small African nation within 20 minutes.
It is also not optimized whatsoever. I am able to run Witcher 3 and Arma 3 on full graphic settings (with a reasonable draw distance of 3km for arma 3). DayZ? Nope. I'm lucky to get 30 fps in an open field at night on the lowest settings.
The majority of the actions you take in terms of managing your inventory (like picking things up, reloading, eating) is delayed by a couple seconds to never happening at all because of the nature of the database system. It feels like you are navigating your way through a border checkpoint in order to pick up a can of beans. This is to combat hacking, but if the server's performance drops, reloading your rifle can happen 5 seconds after, or 10 minutes down the road or never at all. In a fire fight, it is kinda crucial NOT to have to deal with that. Especially, when you can lose all of your stuff when you die.
The zombies are a joke. You can be on the roof of the police station and still be taking damage from a zombie that is floating through the ground floor because the server thinks he is hitting you. If you are lucky enough to not be affected by laggy zombies in your many hours playing, they still navigate houses like the Kool-Aid man but without the rubble or the tasty sugary beverage, shifting through walls and doors at you, fists flailing. This is a zombie survival game FFS! I mean... come on.
This is more of a gripe towards the way the game is being developed so take this with a grain of salt, but the systems that are being introduced are becoming more and more convoluted and annoyingly complicated. Realism is good, don't get me wrong, but if you add too much and it starts becoming tedious and boring or people find exploits to get around it. Remember in the mod, when you could just blood bag someone and move on? In DayZ, you have to make sure the blood is the right type as yours now, which means finding a blood testing kit and the right blood bag to match and the level of health it returns is hilariously low. So why go through all that effort? Just eat 15 cans of beans and drink a small lake's worth of water and wait till your health returns! That's ridiculous... The mod is fun because it blends the right amount of realism while keeping it simple enough not to infringe on the gameplay itself. And the devs are bringing in cholera and dysentery so now you have to find water purification tablets to drink water or else you'll have chronic diarrhea and die.
I was lucky enough to buy this on launch so I didn't pay the listed price at the time of writing this review of $38.99 CAD and I have gotten my money's worth in terms of game time, but two years since release to early access on Steam... TWO YEARS... and the game has made little progress.
